title: Case Studies — HSC Business Studies Final Notes
text: Case Studies — HSC Business Studies Final Notes All Topics | Applied case studies for exam responses. Use these in every extended response. How to Use Case Studies in the HSC The HSC exam requires you to apply theory to real businesses . Every extended response and most short answer questions need case study references. Case study framework: Background — industry, size, location, products/services Operations — how they produce/deliver, strategies used Marketing — target market, marketing mix, positioning Finance — performance (ratios), funding, budgets HR — staffing, training, culture Recommendations — based on analysis, justified with theory Apple Inc. — Finance Case Study Background Industry: Consumer electronics, software, services Size: One of the world's largest companies by market cap Products: iPhone, Mac, iPad, Wearables, Services (Apple Music, iCloud, App Store) Global presence: Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, Rest of Asia Pacific Financial Data (2024-2025) Income Statement Highlights: Item Sept 2025 Sept 2024 Change Products revenue $307,003M $294,866M +4.1% Services revenue $109,158M $96,169M +13.5% Total revenue $416,161M $391,035M +6.4% Net income $112,010M $93,736M +19.5% Revenue by segment (2025): Americas 42.9%, Europe 26.7%, Greater China 15.5%, Japan 6.9%, Rest of Asia Pacific 8.1% Revenue by product (2025): iPhone 50.4%, Services 26.2%, Wearables 8.6%, Mac 8.1%, iPad 6.7% Financial Ratios (Apple) Ratio 2025 2024 Trend Current Ratio 0.89:1 0.87:1 Slightly improved but below ideal 2:1 Net Profit Margin 26.9% 24.0% Improved Gearing (D/E) 3.87:1 5.41:1 Improved — less debt reliance AR Turnover 34.9 days 31.2 days Slightly worsened Key Takeaways Strengths: Strong NPM improvement (24% → 26.9%), revenue growth across all segments, services growing fastest (+13.5%), gearing improved significantly, low inventory levels Weaknesses: Current ratio well below 2:1, AR turnover worsened, heavy iPhone reliance (50% of revenue), China market risk How to use in exam: "For example, Apple's net profit margin improved from 24.0% to 26.9%, demonstrating that their revenue growth strategies have been effective. However, their current ratio of 0.89:1 remains below the ideal 2:1, indicating potential liquidity concerns." McDonald's Corporation — Finance Case Study Background Industry: Fast food / Quick Service Restaurant (QSR) Size: Global — 40,000+ restaurants in 100+ countries Business model: Primarily franchise-based (95% franchised) Financial Ratios (Historical) Ratio 2022 2021 2020 2019 Current Ratio 1.43:1 1.78:1 1.01:1 0.98:1 Net Profit Margin 26.65% 32.49% 24.63% 28.20% Gross Profit Margin 56.97% 54.17% 50.77% 52.32% McDonald's 2022-2023 Analysis Ratio 2022 2023 Analysis Current Ratio 1.43:1 1.16:1 Worsened — increase in short-term borrowing Gearing (D/E) -598% -869% Negative due to share buyback Net Profit Margin 27% 33% Improved — increased sales while controlling costs AR Turnover 31.74 days 32.88 days Slightly worsened but close to ideal 30 days Example HSC Response Recommendation: "It is recommended for McDonald's to use cost centres to improve their profitability." Why: Cost centres minimise costs by allowing McDonald's to allocate budgets and responsibilities to each centre to find ways to minimise costs such as buying raw materials locally rather than controlling from head office in America. Marketing link: McDonald's implemented a promotional campaign in 2023 giving away Marvel movie figures with large meals, incentivising more customers and increasing sales from $23,182M to $25,493M. Perfect Fresh Pty Ltd — Operations & Marketing Case Study Background Industry: Food manufacturing, wholesale supply Product: Fresh salads for caterers and wholesale outlets Market: Sydney region Key innovation: Plastic storage bag extending salad shelf life Problems Identified Late deliveries to customers Poor product presentation (packaging) Low productivity and high staff absenteeism Analysis by Business Function Operations — Inputs (Packaging): Packaging is a critical input directly influencing freshness and visual appeal Poor-quality packaging → damage, reduced freshness, poor presentation Solution: High-quality, durable, visually appealing packaging Operations — Transformation (Technology): Modern equipment improves speed, consistency, hygiene Produces uniform, professional look Solution: Upgrade technology to improve productivity, reduce errors Marketing — Product Strategy: Premium, branded packaging strategy Creates strong visual identity, stands out in wholesale settings Reinforces commitment to quality and freshness HR — Staffing Issues: Low productivity and high absenteeism suggest poor motivation Link to motivation theories: Herzberg — ensure hygiene factors (working conditions, job security) are met, then use motivators (recognition, responsibility) Common Australian Case Studies by Topic Topic Business Why Operations Toyota Australia, Atlassian, Cochlear, CSL Innovation, quality management, global supply chains Marketing Qantas, Woolworths, Canva, Thankyou Group Strong branding, segmentation, digital marketing Finance Commonwealth Bank, BHP, Apple, McDonald's Strong financial data, clear ratios HR Google Australia, Salesforce, Westpac Progressive HR practices, diversity programs Tips for Using Case Studies in the Exam Short Answer Questions Always name the business Link theory directly to the case study Use specific data/figures when available "For example, Apple's net profit margin improved from 24.0% to 26.9%..." Extended Response / Business Report Reference the case study in every section Use ratios and financial data to support arguments Compare across years or against industry benchmarks Make specific, justified recommendations Key Formula [Theory/Concept] + [Case Study Evidence] + [Link to Question] = Full Marks Exam trap: Don't just describe the case study — you must link it to the theory and answer the specific question asked . See also: Finance | Marketing | Operations | Human Resources | MOC Notes prepared for HSC Business Studies — Applied Case Studies.

text: Case Study Stats Sheet: Apple, McDonald's and Xiaomi One compact set of evidence for the four Business Studies functions. All financial figures are for 2025. Apple reports in US dollars; Xiaomi reports in RMB. Apple’s financial year ended 27 September, while McDonald’s and Xiaomi’s ended 31 December.[1][2][3] HSC area Apple McDonald’s Xiaomi Marketing Global smartphone shipment share rose from 18.9% in 2024 to 19.7% in 2025, with 247.8 million phones shipped.[4] Global comparable sales grew 3.1% in 2025.[2] Global smartphone shipment share was 13.1% in 2025, down from 13.6% in 2024; 165.3 million phones shipped.[4] Operations FY2025 R&D spending was US$34.55 billion, up 10%. A significant majority of manufacturing is done by outsourced partners, mainly in Asia.[1] 45,356 restaurants at year-end 2025; approximately 95% were franchised.[2] 2025 R&D spending was RMB33.1 billion, up 37.8%.[3] Finance FY2025 revenue: US$416.16 billion; net income: US$112.01 billion; net profit ratio: 26.9%.[1] 2025 revenue: US$26.89 billion; net income: US$8.56 billion; net profit ratio: 31.9%.[2] 2025 revenue: RMB457.29 billion, up 25%; profit for the year: RMB41.57 billion, up 76.3%; net profit ratio: 9.1%.[3] Human resources Approximately 166,000 full-time equivalent employees in September 2025; development includes Apple University and online learning.[1] Over 150,000 company employees, plus over 2 million people working in franchised restaurants in 2025; training includes Hamburger University.[2] 56,531 full-time employees in 2025, including 25,457 R&D personnel.[3] Smartphone market shares are IDC’s preliminary estimates of unit shipments for calendar 2025, not shares of market value.[4] Net profit ratios are calculated as reported profit divided by revenue and rounded to one decimal place. title: Confusing Pairs — MCQ Drill Sheet
text: Confusing Pairs — MCQ Drill Sheet Why this file exists. Across two trials (Killara and Knox), seven of eight MCQ errors were the right syllabus dot point, wrong member of the pair . You aren't missing content — you're picking the neighbour. How to use it. Cover the right column. Say the tell out loud. Anything you hesitate on, star it. Twenty minutes beats re-reading a module. Theory: Operations | Marketing | Finance | Human Resources · Marked papers: Trial Practice Killara 2022 1. ⚠️ The Ten You Have Actually Got Wrong Drill these first. Every one cost a real mark. Paper Pair The tell 2025 HSC 8 Assurance / Improvement ⭐ "Ongoing commitment" = IMPROVEMENT. Assurance is a system that prevents defects, certified against a standard (ISO 9000) — it's a thing you set up . Improvement is a continuous effort to get better — it never finishes. If the stem says ongoing , continuous , always looking to , it is improvement 2025 HSC 19 Operations sequence — which end is the input ⭐ Every sequence option must read INPUT → TRANSFORMATION → OUTPUT . Label each of the three terms before choosing. Product and customer service are outputs ; materials, information, facilities, human resources, customers are inputs ; task design, control, improvement are transformation Killara 4 Resource / Industrial market Resource = where raw materials are sold (farmers, miners). Industrial = businesses that buy inputs to make other goods. Farmers operate in resource, sell to industrial Killara 6 Unfair dismissal / Performance appraisal Dismissal ends employment. Appraisal evaluates it. An appraisal is not a termination Killara 10 Common law contract / Enterprise agreement Common law = individually negotiated, one person. Enterprise agreement = collective, must pass the BOOT Killara 17 Key business function / anything else There are exactly four : operations, marketing, finance, HR. "Employees", "customers", "outsourcing" are not functions Knox 5 Financial cost of change / Inertia The syllabus lists them separately . Financial = redundancy payments, retraining, new equipment, plant layout. Inertia = behavioural resistance, costs nothing directly Knox 10 Administrative / Developmental performance management Administrative = measuring output to decide pay, promotion, retention. Developmental = feedback used to build skills. Data collection with no training attached is administrative Knox 16 Market share analysis / Marketing profitability analysis Only profitability involves cost . Market share compares your sales to industry sales Knox 17 FIFO / LIFO When prices rise, FIFO leaves the fresh, expensive stock on the balance sheet → higher inventory, higher profit 2. Operations Processes Pair The tell Transformed / Transforming resources Transformed = what gets changed (materials, information, customers). Transforming = what does the changing (human resources, facilities) Sequencing / Scheduling Order vs duration Gantt chart / Critical path analysis Gantt shows what and how long, including concurrent tasks. CPA shows what must finish before something else can start, giving the critical path and float Critical path / Longest task list It's the longest path by time , not by number of tasks Float / Critical activity Float is spare time. Critical activities have zero float Lead time / Cycle time Lead = order to receipt. Cycle = time to produce one unit Bottleneck / Defect Bottleneck = lowest-capacity point limiting total output. A defect is a quality failure. Not the same thing Quality and layout Pair The tell Quality control / Quality assurance Control finds defects after the fact. Assurance designs the process so they don't occur Quality assurance / TQM Assurance = a system (ISO 9000). TQM = a whole-of-business philosophy, everyone responsible Design quality / Conformance quality Design = does it match what consumers understand the product to be. Conformance = does it meet the specification Process layout / Product layout Process groups machines by function (job shop). Product arranges them in the sequence of production (assembly line) Fixed position layout The product doesn't move — shipbuilding, construction Inventory Pair The tell JIT / FIFO and LIFO JIT is inventory management (when stock arrives). FIFO/LIFO are inventory valuation (what it's worth on the balance sheet) FIFO / LIFO — rising prices FIFO : higher closing inventory, lower COGS, higher profit . LIFO : lower closing inventory, higher COGS, lower profit EOQ / Reorder point EOQ = how much to order. Reorder point = when to order Obsolescence / Spoilage Obsolescence = outdated. Spoilage = physically deteriorated Strategy and influences Pair The tell Speed / Dependability Speed = how fast. Dependability = how reliably, when you said you would Cost leadership / Lowest price A low-cost producer may still charge a premium . Cost leadership is about your costs , not your prices Outsourcing / Offshoring Outsourcing = external provider. Offshoring = moved overseas, possibly still in-house Outsourcing / Global sourcing Outsourcing contracts out an activity . Global sourcing buys inputs from anywhere Legal compliance / Ethical responsibility Compliance = letter of the law, the minimum. Ethics/CSR = spirit of the law, voluntary. You can be fully compliant and still unethical Compliance cost / Penalty Compliance cost = the expense of meeting the law. A penalty is what you pay for breaching it Economies of scale Lower cost per unit , not lower total cost. Total cost still rises Explicit / Implicit service Explicit = tangible elements (time, expertise). Implicit = intangible feelings (atmosphere, status) 3. Marketing Markets and segmentation Pair The tell Resource / Industrial / Intermediate / Consumer market Resource = raw materials sold (primary producers). Industrial = buy inputs to produce other goods. Intermediate = retailers and wholesalers buying to resell . Consumer = individuals for personal use Mass / Niche market Mass = one product for everyone. Niche = one narrow segment Market segment / Target market A segment is a group with shared characteristics. The target market is the segment you decide to pursue Demographic / Psychographic / Geographic / Behavioural Demographic = who they are (age, income, gender). Psychographic = how they think (lifestyle, values, personality). Geographic = where they are. Behavioural = what they do (usage rate, loyalty, benefits sought) Positioning / Branding / Differentiation Differentiation = making the product distinct. Branding = the name and identity. Positioning = the image relative to competitors in the consumer's mind Influences on consumer choice Pair The tell Psychological / Sociocultural Psychological = inside the individual (perception, motives, attitudes, personality, learning). Sociocultural = other people (family, peers, reference groups, social class, culture) Influences on choice / Marketing strategies Influences = why the customer buys. Strategies = what the business does. Branding and price are strategies , not influences Process and KPIs Pair The tell Situational analysis / Market research Situational = SWOT and product life cycle, where the business stands now . Research = collecting data about customers and the market Primary / Secondary data Primary = you collect it (surveys, observation, focus groups) — specific, current, expensive. Secondary = someone else did (census, industry reports, internet) — cheap, fast, possibly outdated Sales analysis / Market share analysis / Marketing profitability analysis Sales = your sales against objectives. Market share = your sales against industry sales. Profitability = cost of a marketing activity against the revenue it generated Monitoring / Controlling Monitoring measures. Controlling compares to planned, investigates the variance , and takes corrective action Strategies Pair The tell Price skimming / Price penetration Skimming = launch high , lower over time (new tech). Penetration = launch low to gain share, then raise Cost-plus / Market / Competition-based pricing Cost-plus = cost + mark-up. Market = what the market will bear. Competition-based = at, below or above rivals Above the line / Below the line promotion Above = mass media the business pays for (TV, radio, print). Below = everything else (personal selling, sales promotion, PR, direct mail) Publicity / Public relations Publicity = free media coverage, not controlled by the business. PR = deliberate activity the business plans to build image Push / Pull strategy Push = promote to the retailer so they stock it. Pull = promote to the consumer so they demand it Standardisation / Customisation Standardisation = same product everywhere (economies of scale). Customisation = adapted to local tastes Global branding / Global pricing Branding = one identity worldwide. Pricing = one price strategy worldwide Consumer law — the five Law The tell Deceptive and misleading advertising Claims that mislead — false comparisons, fine print, altered product demonstrations Price discrimination Charging different prices to different buyers for the same good without justification Implied conditions Unstated but legally assumed — the good is fit for purpose and matches its description Warranties A promise to repair or replace. Cannot be fake or misleading Resale price maintenance A supplier forcing a retailer to sell at a set minimum price. Illegal Citation: Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) , containing the Australian Consumer Law , enforced by the ACCC . 4. Finance Pair The tell Liquidity / Solvency Time frame only. Liquidity = short term (current ratio). Solvency = long term (gearing ratio) Gearing / Leverage The same thing — proportion funded by debt rather than equity Control of current assets / current liabilities Assets = cash, receivables, inventory (JIT, credit checks, cash budgets). Liabilities = payables, loans, overdrafts (paying on time, seeking discounts, minimising overdraft) Debenture / Mortgage Debenture = long-term debt to the public, unsecured . Mortgage = secured against property Factoring / Leasing Factoring = selling receivables for cash now. Leasing = renting the use of an asset Primary / Secondary market Primary = new shares, the company gets the money. Secondary = existing shares traded, company gets nothing Overdraft / Bank loan Overdraft = flexible, short term, on a current account. Loan = fixed amount, fixed term Operating / Financial lease Operating = short term, owner maintains . Financial = runs for the asset's useful life, lessee maintains Income statement / Balance sheet Income statement = performance over a period . Balance sheet = position at a point in time Cash flow statement / Cash flow budget Statement = record of the past . Budget = forecast of the future Capitalising an expense / Expensing it Capitalising puts the cost on the balance sheet as an asset, written off later as depreciation . This understates expenses and overstates profit now Normalised earnings / Window dressing Normalised = one-off items removed to show underlying performance, but management decides what's unusual . Window dressing = legal techniques to make the position look better at reporting date Window dressing / Fraud Window dressing is legal. Fraud is not Hedging / Derivative Hedging = any strategy reducing financial risk. A derivative is a specific type of hedging contract (futures, options, swaps, forwards) Spot rate / Forward rate Spot = today's exchange rate. Forward = locked in now for a future date Merger / Takeover Merger = both agree to combine. Takeover = one buys the other, which ceases to exist Cost centre / Profit centre Cost centre only incurs costs. Profit centre also generates revenue Appreciation / Depreciation (currency) Appreciation = AUD rises → exports dearer, imports cheaper. Depreciation = AUD falls → exports cheaper, imports dearer The seven ratios LIQUIDITY Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities ideal 2:1 SOLVENCY Gearing Ratio = Total Liabilities / Owners' Equity ideal 0.5:1 to 1:1 PROFITABILITY Gross Profit = (Gross Profit / Sales) x 100 Net Profit = (Net Profit / Sales) x 100 Return on Equity = (Net Profit / Owners' Equity) x 100 EFFICIENCY Expense Ratio = (Total Expenses / Sales) x 100 lowest possible Accounts Receivable Step 1: Sales / AR Step 2: 365 / answer ideal 30 days A ratio without a comparison is a number, not analysis. Always answer compared to what? — over time, industry average, or target. If the paper gives you an industry average, use it. 5. Human Resources Acquisition Pair The tell Job description / Job specification De-S-cription = the po- S -ition. Spec -ification = the spec -ial qualities of the person Recruitment / Selection Recruitment builds the pool . Selection chooses from it Internal / External recruitment Internal = cheaper, faster, known quantity, but no fresh ideas. External = new skills and perspectives, but costly and slower to settle Employee / Contractor Employee = contract of service, business controls how and when, owes leave and super. Contractor = contract for service, controls own methods, invoices for a result Leadership and job design Pair The tell Authoritarian / Coercive leadership Authoritarian = the leader decides and directs ; employees don't participate. Coercive = the leader forces compliance, "whether they want it or not." Who decides vs how compliance is obtained Participative / Delegative Participative = employees are consulted , but the final decision is still the leader's . Delegative (laissez-faire) = employees make the decision Pacesetting / Transformational Pacesetting models high performance and expects imitation — values results more than anything , burns people out. Transformational creates a shared vision and moves people beyond self-interest Job rotation / enlargement / enrichment Rotation = moving between jobs. Enlargement = more tasks at the same level (horizontal). Enrichment = more responsibility and autonomy (vertical) Job satisfaction / Job enrichment Satisfaction is the outcome — how content employees are. Enrichment is the strategy — designing tasks around existing abilities to reduce boredom General / Specific skills (recruitment) General = attitudes and behaviours that are a good cultural fit . Specific = skills required for particular jobs , targeted at skill shortages Development and maintenance Pair The tell Induction / Training Induction introduces to the business . Training improves job performance Training / Development Training = the current role. Development = future responsibilities and promotion Administrative / Developmental performance management ⚠️ Use your teacher's definition. Administrative = HR completes skills audits , identifies training needs, keeps an employee database — it records and audits . Developmental = HR plans and implements training , on and off the job — it plans and delivers Monetary / Non-monetary rewards Monetary = bonuses, commissions, pay increases — financial motivation. Non-monetary = recognition, promotion, flexible working, career development — satisfaction and loyalty . Provide both, because employees are motivated by different factors Individual / Group performance pay Individual recognises outstanding contribution . Team-based encourages cooperation toward common objectives . Using both prevents excessive competition while still rewarding effort Monetary / Non-monetary rewards Monetary = cash or cash-equivalent (salary, bonus, performance pay). Non-monetary = flexible hours, recognition, leave, career development Intrinsic / Extrinsic rewards Intrinsic comes from within the person (satisfaction). Extrinsic is given by the business Piece rate / Commission Piece rate = pay per unit produced . Commission = pay per sale Hygiene factors / Motivators Hygiene prevents dissatisfaction but doesn't motivate (pay, conditions). Motivators actively create satisfaction (achievement, recognition, responsibility) Separation Pair The tell Voluntary / Involuntary separation Voluntary = the employee chooses (resignation, retirement, voluntary redundancy). Involuntary = the business decides (retrenchment, dismissal, forced redundancy) Redundancy / Dismissal Redundancy = the JOB no longer exists. Dismissal = the PERSON is removed. Redundancy attracts severance; dismissal for misconduct does not Retrenchment / Retirement Retrenchment is involuntary — the business no longer needs the role. Retirement is voluntary Summary / Unfair dismissal Summary = immediate, for serious misconduct. Unfair = harsh, unjust or unreasonable Unfair dismissal / Unlawful termination Unfair = harsh, unjust or unreasonable. Unlawful = for a prohibited reason (pregnancy, race, union membership, illness) Constructive dismissal Employee resigns because the employer's conduct left them no choice. Still counts as dismissal Legal and disputes Pair The tell Award / Enterprise agreement Award = industry-wide safety net, applies by default. Enterprise agreement = workplace-negotiated, must pass the BOOT Enterprise agreement / Common law contract Agreement = collective. Common law = individual NES / Awards NES = 11 legislated minimums for all employees. Awards = industry-specific, on top Negotiation / Mediation / Conciliation / Arbitration Escalating intervention: Negotiation = the parties alone. Mediation = a third party facilitates only . Conciliation = Fair Work Australia suggests solutions. Arbitration = a commissioner imposes a legally binding decision Overt / Covert industrial action Overt is visible and deliberate — strikes, work bans, work-to-rule, lockouts, picket lines. Covert is concealed — absenteeism , turnover, sabotage, deliberate under-performance Work to rule / Work ban Work to rule = workers refuse tasks outside their normal duties (e.g. overtime). Work ban = workers turn up but don't perform their normal duties Strike / Lockout Strike = employees stop work. Lockout = employer shuts them out EEO / Anti-discrimination EEO requires decisions on merit and removal of barriers. Anti-discrimination prohibits specified conduct Turnover / Absenteeism Turnover = staff leaving and being replaced. Absenteeism = unplanned days off Span of control / Chain of command Span = how many people a manager supervises. Chain = the reporting lines 6. Same Word, Different Topic These catch people because the word is genuinely used twice with different meanings. Check which module the question is in. Word In Operations In Finance Control Compare actual to planned, investigate the variance , take corrective action Manage the level you hold of current assets and current liabilities Quality control Inspecting output to find defects — Word Meaning A Meaning B Depreciation Writing off an asset's cost over its useful life (Finance) The AUD falling in value (Global) Matching principle Match the term of finance to the use of funds Match revenue to the expenses incurred earning it Differentiation Operations: distinguishing the good or service itself Marketing: the strategy of making the product distinct from competitors Efficiency Operations: productivity, output per input Finance: the expense ratio and accounts receivable turnover 6.1 ⭐ Same words, two syllabus sections The nastiest version of this: the same words appear twice within one module , under different headings. Checked against the NSW syllabus (2010) §10.1–10.4. The words Section A Section B Which one the question wants Control · improvement Operations PROCESSES → "monitoring, control and improvement" Operations STRATEGIES → "quality management: control, assurance, improvement" KPIs, variance, corrective action → process . Defects, inspection, ISO 9000, TQM → strategy Target market · segmentation Marketing PROCESS → "identifying target markets" (step 4) Marketing STRATEGIES → "market segmentation, product/service differentiation and positioning" Which group do we sell to → process . How do we divide the market and position in it → strategy Monitoring · controlling Marketing PROCESS → step 6, "implementation, monitoring and controlling" Finance PROCESSES → "monitoring and controlling — cash flow statement, income statement, balance sheet" Marketing: compare actual to planned sales , revise the mix. Finance: the three statements Placement traps worth memorising: Stakeholders are an HR influence , not part of the role of HRM. Comparative ratio analysis is a named Finance process dot point — the comparison is the syllabus content, not just good technique. Motivation theories (Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor) and organisational structures are not in the HSC syllabus at all. 7. Self-Test Cover the tells above. Write the distinguishing feature for each. Anything you hesitate on for more than three seconds, star and redo tomorrow. Round 1 — the eight you've missed 1. Resource market vs Industrial market 2. Unfair dismissal vs Performance appraisal 3. Common law contract vs Enterprise agreement 4. Name the four key business functions 5. Financial cost of change vs Inertia 6. Administrative vs Developmental performance management 7. Market share analysis vs Marketing profitability analysis 8. FIFO vs LIFO when prices are rising Round 2 — highest-frequency in past papers 9. Sequencing vs Scheduling 10. Quality control vs Quality assurance 11. Transformed vs Transforming resources 12. Lead time vs Cycle time 13. Liquidity vs Solvency 14. Income statement vs Balance sheet 15. Cash flow statement vs Cash flow budget 16. Primary vs Secondary market 17. Job description vs Job specification 18. Recruitment vs Selection 19. Training vs Development 20. Redundancy vs Dismissal 21. Mediation vs Conciliation vs Arbitration 22. Award vs Enterprise agreement 23. Primary vs Secondary data 24. Price skimming vs Price penetration 25. Publicity vs Public relations Round 3 — the trickier ones 26. Outsourcing vs Offshoring vs Global sourcing 27. Capitalising an expense vs Expensing it 28. Normalised earnings vs Window dressing 29. Window dressing vs Fraud 30. Hedging vs Derivative 31. Spot rate vs Forward rate 32. Operating lease vs Financial lease 33. Cost leadership vs Lowest price 34. Design quality vs Conformance quality 35. Process layout vs Product layout 36. Hygiene factors vs Motivators 37. Intrinsic vs Extrinsic rewards 38. Piece rate vs Commission 39. Voluntary vs Involuntary separation 40. Control in Operations vs Control in Finance 8. MCQ Method Four minutes lost to careless reading is four marks. Same as a full extended-response paragraph. 1. UNDERLINE the exact noun the question asks for. "which key business FUNCTION" → only four options qualify "control of current ASSETS" → liabilities options are out "FINANCIAL cost" → behavioural options are out 2. Check for a directional word that flips the answer. SEEKING a discount (you pay) vs OFFERING a discount (you're paid) sell IN a market vs sell TO a market an INCREASE in economic activity (boom only) 3. If two options are from the same pair, ONE of them is the trap. Ask which member the question actually named. 4. On calculations, compare the given figures before deciding. Inventory $15 000 sold for $15 000 = no profit = no change. See also: MOC | Trial Practice Killara 2022 | Operations | Marketing | Finance | Human Resources

title: Crichton Office Supplies Report and Apple Marketing Essay
text: Crichton Office Supplies Report and Apple Marketing Essay Question 25: Crichton Office Supplies Business Report Prompt: Crichton Office Supplies operates out of a warehouse in Western Sydney. They import a range of products and sell them to small businesses, who are mostly business owners ordering office supplies. In order to control costs, the business only has limited amounts of stock on hand and pays their workers the minimum wage under their award contract. While this has led to lower costs, it has had several negative impacts on the business, including delayed customer orders because products were not in stock, low worker satisfaction, and increasing staff turnover that requires recruiting and training new staff. Management is considering changing inventory management, improving worker conditions by moving from an award to an enterprise agreement, and finding other ways to maintain staff. The question is worth 20 marks. You have been hired as a consultant by Crichton Office Supplies to write a business report to the owners. In your report, discuss holding stock in greater quantities for this business, compare the use of an award to an enterprise agreement for Crichton Office Supplies, and recommend human resource strategies to improve the maintenance of staff. CRICHTON OFFICE SUPPLIES BUSINESS REPORT EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Crichton Office Supplies imports office products for small business customers from its Western Sydney warehouse. Limited stock delays orders, while minimum award wages coincide with low satisfaction and rising staff turnover. This report assesses the benefits and costs of holding greater quantities, compares the award with an enterprise agreement, and recommends one human resource strategy, a balanced rewards system. Performance management will support staff consultation and review of the rewards. These actions aim to improve customer availability and retention while keeping costs sustainable. 1. HOLDING STOCK IN GREATER QUANTITIES Crichton should hold greater quantities selectively using just in case inventory management, which keeps stock available in anticipation of demand. Holding greater quantities can make products available to meet customer demand, reduce customer lead times, lower unit costs through bulk buying and provide alternatives if one item is out of stock. For Crichton, holding more of frequently ordered stationery, paper and toner would allow small business customers’ orders to be dispatched sooner instead of waiting for imported products. Availability improves speed and dependability, supports customer satisfaction and repeat orders, and avoids losing an immediate sale when a product is unavailable. Larger orders may also secure bulk buying savings and reduce the unit purchase cost. However, excess inventory has holding costs, including warehouse space, insurance, security and handling. It ties up working capital that could be used elsewhere and risks theft, damage or obsolescence. A blanket increase could crowd the Western Sydney warehouse and divert cash from wages or other operations. Crichton should therefore use sales records and supplier lead times to set reorder points and safety stock for fast moving products, while keeping lower quantities of slow movers. Management should monitor stockouts, customer lead times, inventory turnover and carrying costs. This targeted increase delivers the stated benefits without stockpiling every product. 2. AWARD COMPARED WITH ENTERPRISE AGREEMENT An award is an industry or occupation specific set of minimum wages and conditions established by the Fair Work Commission. It is a safety net that applies by default, giving Crichton a clear legal baseline and relatively simple administration. Keeping pay at the award minimum may help control immediate wage costs, but an award is not tailored to this warehouse or its employees. In this scenario, low worker satisfaction and increasing turnover show that meeting the minimum has not been enough to maintain staff. An enterprise agreement is negotiated collectively at a specific workplace between the employer and employees, often with union involvement. Unlike the standardised award, it can tailor pay and conditions to Crichton, such as higher wages, predictable rosters or training arrangements. It must pass the Better Off Overall Test, meaning employees must be better off overall than under the relevant award, and it cannot remove National Employment Standards. Negotiating with employees gives them a voice in conditions and can improve acceptance, satisfaction and commitment. Better conditions may reduce resignations and therefore lower repeated recruitment, induction and training costs. The trade off is that higher pay and bargaining require money and management time. Overall, the award is simpler and may cost less immediately, while an affordable, compliant enterprise agreement is more responsive to Crichton’s retention problem and may reduce longer term replacement costs. 3. RECOMMENDATION: REWARDS Crichton should introduce one balanced rewards strategy because the maintenance stage of the HR cycle aims to keep existing employees motivated, loyal and retained. The reward package should combine fair remuneration with recognition of team performance, rather than relying on minimum pay alone. A team bonus could recognise accurate order picking, dependable dispatch and positive customer feedback, since warehouse employees rely on one another to complete orders. Crichton should also offer non monetary rewards such as public recognition, greater job variety or flexible working hours, as employees value different benefits. Performance management should support this single rewards strategy: managers and employees can agree clear, fair criteria, discuss progress regularly and use two way feedback to learn which rewards employees value. This prevents speed targets from encouraging rushed errors and allows managers to recognise good work or address concerns early. The business can review satisfaction, turnover, absenteeism, order errors and customer delays to assess whether the reward system is working. A relevant and affordable package can improve satisfaction and loyalty, retain experienced staff and reduce recruitment and training costs. It also links employee effort to the service reliability Crichton’s customers need. CONCLUSION Crichton should increase stock selectively to improve availability, meet demand, reduce lead times and capture bulk buying savings, while controlling holding costs. An enterprise agreement is more adaptable than relying only on an award if it is affordable and passes the required test. The single recommended HR strategy is a balanced rewards system, supported by performance management to make it fair and assess its effect on retention. Question 27: Essay Prompt: Assess how influences on marketing impact the marketing process. Question 27 is selected. RESPONSE Marketing influences have a substantial impact on the marketing process because they shape what a business researches, which customers it targets, the objectives it sets and the strategies it implements. The process moves through situational analysis, market research, establishing objectives, identifying target markets, developing marketing strategies, and implementation, monitoring and control. Apple demonstrates that consumer choice, economic conditions, competition, government regulation and ethical expectations can redirect these stages. Their effects are not limited to one advertisement or product, because evidence at each stage informs the next. These influences create opportunities when Apple adapts, but can also cause lost sales, penalties and damage to trust when decisions miss customer expectations or legal requirements. Consumer choice has a significant impact on Apple’s market research and identification of target markets because customer preferences determine what the business needs to know before committing to products and promotion. Psychological factors such as perception and quality expectations, as well as sociocultural trends such as social media, gaming and streaming, shape what customers value in a phone. Apple uses post purchase feedback surveys, including monthly country by country surveys, to identify purchase drivers, popular features, demographics and customer satisfaction, giving it current primary information rather than depending only on broad reports. This research can influence product development and targeting. For example, Apple released larger iPhones in 2014 in response to customer demand, while its marketing promotes camera, screen and processing features valued by customers using social media and streaming. Marketing then carries this evidence forward, allowing Apple to refine objectives and adapt its offer for the customers it has identified. However, the iPhone 5c shows that consumer choice can be misread, as colour options did not outweigh stronger quality expectations. Therefore, research into changing preferences has a substantial effect, but Apple must continually test assumptions rather than rely on one feature or an established image. Economic and competitive influences have a substantial impact on Apple’s situational analysis, objectives and marketing strategies because they alter customers’ ability to spend and the alternatives available to them. A recession can reduce disposable income and confidence, making customers more price sensitive, while strong competition forces Apple to explain why its premium products are worth their price. A SWOT analysis can identify Apple’s brand reputation as a strength, its high prices as a weakness, and lower priced Asian competitors such as Xiaomi and OPPO as threats. These findings guide objectives such as defending market share without abandoning premium positioning, while helping Apple choose which customer segments to prioritize and how to balance premium devices with more accessible options. The vault’s case study records declining iPhone sales during the Global Financial Crisis, followed by Apple offering the lower priced iPhone 5c and continuing to sell older models. During the COVID 19 period, Apple introduced the iPhone SE and Mini versions for price sensitive buyers. These decisions can widen Apple’s target market and support sales, but too much emphasis on lower prices could weaken premium positioning and margins. Economic and competitive pressures therefore materially shape Apple’s objectives and product and pricing decisions, although each response must be checked against its long term brand strategy. Government, legal and ethical influences have a decisive impact on Apple’s implementation, monitoring and control because they set boundaries for product claims, consumer rights, privacy and market access. Apple’s iPhone 6 launch in China was delayed amid privacy concerns, demonstrating that a marketing plan cannot simply be applied identically in every country. Regulation also affected Apple’s expansion in India, while government incentives for local smartphone manufacturing created an opportunity to adjust market entry and production plans. In Australia, Apple received a 9 million dollar penalty over misrepresentations about consumer rights and gave an undertaking to improve its consumer guarantee policies and practices. This shows that misleading claims about repairs or guarantees can turn marketing into legal and reputational risk, forcing changes to promotion and after sales communication. Apple must therefore monitor customer feedback, verify claims and adapt distribution and promotion to local rules. Its monitoring should compare complaints and sales with objectives so that corrective action follows changes in customer or legal expectations. These influences constrain Apple’s choices and add compliance costs, but ignoring them is more damaging because penalties and lost trust undermine loyalty and sales. Overall, influences affect every stage of Apple’s marketing process, but consumer choice and economic and competitive conditions have the greatest ongoing effect because they determine what customers value and whether Apple’s offer remains attractive. Government, legal and ethical requirements may not create customer preferences, yet they can decisively limit launches and promotional claims. Apple’s surveys, product adjustments and policy changes show that the process works best as a continuous cycle of research, action and control. Apple can protect its market position only when it adapts to customers and competitors while maintaining truthful, lawful marketing, which preserves trust and supports repeat purchases. title: Finance 1 · Role of Financial Management
text: 💰 Finance 1 · Role of Financial Management Finance · ① Role ← you are here · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Finance module is examinable. This file covers the Role of financial management dot points only. Definition : Financial management deals with the analysis, interpretation and evaluation of all financial records. It is the financial manager's responsibility to source finance that enables the business to achieve its strategic goals. 1. Strategic Role of Financial Management The process of setting objectives throughout the business and deciding what resources are needed to achieve them Developing a strategic plan as part of financial management ensures the business survives and grows in a competitive world Financial management provides a framework for all other business activities — it does not follow the lead of other managers ⚠️ Exam trap : A common multiple-choice question asks what the strategic role of finance is. The answer is "provides a framework for all other business activities" — not "sets short-term goals" (that's tactical/operational). 2. Objectives of Financial Management Five objectives, split by time horizon. Horizon Objective Definition Short term (within 12 months) Liquidity The ability to pay back current liabilities with current assets Short term Profitability The ability of the business to maximise profits Short term Efficiency The ability to manage costs and the collection of money from customers Long term (2–5 years) Growth The ability of the business to grow and expand Long term Solvency How the business is financed (debt vs equity) — the ability to meet long-term financial commitments Long-term goal of the business is to increase the wealth of the owners . Long-term goals depend on profitability in the short term resulting from increased operating efficiency. ⭐ Each objective has its own strategy family — that mapping is in ④ Strategies and is the spine of most extended-response questions. 3. Interdependence with Other Key Business Functions Interdependence = the mutual reliance between finance and the other key business functions. Function Relationship with Finance Operations Finance provides funding and budgets so products can be made profitably. Operations produces quality products with minimal expense, generating higher revenue margins that flow back to finance Marketing Finance sets the marketing budget. Marketing generates the sales revenue that finance then allocates, monitors and reinvests Human Resources Wages and training are major budget items. Finance sets salary budgets; HR must justify expenditure through productivity gains. Commission and incentive schemes are a joint HR–finance decision Model "Explain" answer (scaffold from class) Define — Financial management is interdependent with operations because of the relationship between business revenue and expenditure. Relationship — Finance provides funding and budgets so the product can be produced profitably, while operations produces quality products with minimal expense to generate a higher revenue margin. Implications — Both functions supply each other with information and resources that drive growth and profit maximisation. Link — Hence the business grows in the marketplace and increases revenue margins, leading to increased profitability. ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Liquidity vs Solvency Liquidity = short -term, can we pay bills due now (current ratio). Solvency = long -term, can we meet commitments over years (gearing ratio). Both are about paying debts — the difference is purely the time frame Profitability vs Efficiency Profitability = how much profit we make. Efficiency = how well we manage costs and collect money Strategic vs tactical role Strategic = provides the framework for all other business activities . Tactical = short-term goal setting Profit vs cash flow A profitable business can still fail from poor liquidity. Profit is accounting; cash flow is money actually in the account 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Financial management The analysis, interpretation and evaluation of all financial records Strategic role of finance Providing a framework for all other business activities Liquidity The ability to pay current liabilities with current assets Solvency The ability to meet long-term financial commitments Profitability The ability of the business to maximise profits Efficiency The ability to manage costs and the collection of money from customers Growth The ability of the business to grow and expand Interdependence The mutual reliance between finance and the other key business functions Next: ② Influences on Financial Management · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Finance 2 · Influences on Financial Management
text: 🏦 Finance 2 · Influences on Financial Management Finance · ① Role · ② Influences ← you are here · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Finance module is examinable. This file covers the Influences on financial management dot points only — which in this module means sources of finance , institutions, government and global markets. 1. Internal Sources of Finance Internal sources are recorded under equity in the balance sheet. The money comes from the owners or from the business's own activities. Source Definition Owner's equity Funds contributed by owners or partners to establish and build the business Retained profits Net profit that has been reinvested in the business. Added as equity — increases the owner's claim Owner's Equity section of the Balance Sheet = Capital + Retained Profits 2. External Sources of Finance Financed from external organisations — either debt or equity . Debt = any money that has been borrowed . Short-term debt is repayable within 12 months; long-term is over 12 months. Equity = attached to the ownership of shares in an incorporated business — the owner's financial claim on the assets. 2.1 Debt Finance — Short Term Source Detail Overdraft Flexibility to borrow from a bank at short notice through a cheque/current account. Interest must be paid. Used for working capital and claimable as a tax deduction. More flexible than a bank loan; assists with short-term liquidity issues Commercial bill A written order for a loan amount guaranteed by the business's bank . Borrowed from businesses with surplus funds. Normally 30–180 days , usually for amounts over $100,000 Factoring Selling accounts receivable to a specialist factoring firm to create cash inflow. The factoring company takes over management and collection of the unpaid accounts and pays the seller the value minus a commission . Business receives up to 90% within 48 hours . The riskiest source because of unpaid debts — that risk is borne by the debt collection agency 2.2 Debt Finance — Long Term Source Detail Mortgage A loan repaid over a set number of years with interest, used to purchase land or property . The property becomes the security . If the business defaults, the bank takes and sells the property Debenture Long-term debt acquired by offering a prospectus to the general public on the securities exchange. Set interest rate for a fixed time. More risky to the lender than a mortgage — not tied to specific property, so there is no security. Unlike shares, the level of profit does not affect the interest rate Unsecured notes Usually issued by finance companies to gain funds. Higher interest rates reflecting greater risk. Also called bonds Leasing Leasing non-current assets (cars, equipment) for payments to the owner. Reduces the cost of acquiring assets as full value need not be paid instantly. Lease payments are tax deductible — they appear under Expenses in the Profit and Loss Statement, reducing net profit and therefore company tax Two types of lease: Operating lease — short periods, normally shorter than the life of the asset. The owner carries out maintenance. Financial lease — the lessor purchases the asset on behalf of the lessee. Runs for the lifetime of the asset . Why lease rather than buy? Lease costs are tax deductible; flexibility if the asset is only needed for a short period; distributes the cost over time, which is better for cash flow . 2.3 Equity Financing Equity financing comes from the owners . Equity reflects the owner's financial claim on the assets of the business. Legal structure Term used Sole trader / Partnership Owners' Equity Public / Private companies Shareholders' Funds Private equity — current owners invite people or organisations to invest. Normally proprietary companies (Pty Ltd). Shareholders do not necessarily have control, and there is no guarantee of dividends. Public equity — companies listed on the ASX ; anyone can invest. Type Definition Ordinary shares Issued on the ASX, with or without voting rights at the AGM New share issues Shares sold for the first time on the public market — either an IPO (initial public offering) or a new offering if more finance is needed Rights issue The company offers existing shareholders the chance to buy more shares Placements Additional shares offered to specific institutions (venture capitalists) and specific investors Share purchase plans An offer to existing shareholders to purchase more shares without brokerage fees , normally below normal prices. Requires ASIC permission Equity — Advantages Equity — Disadvantages No debt servicing costs such as interest Takes time If the business makes a loss, no dividend needs to be paid (though this may worry shareholders into selling) Dilutes ownership 2.4 Financial Grants Financial gifts from government to help businesses establish. Strict criteria: location, personal characteristics of the owner, type of industry, type of goods/services. Criteria commonly include Indigenous people, regional businesses, the IT industry, and businesses providing innovative or essential services. The government is not paid back and gets no ownership . Its return comes through increased employment, growth and taxes . 3. Financial Institutions Institution Role Banks Accept deposits and provide loans; the largest source of funds for business Investment banks Trade in money, securities and financial futures; arrange long-term finance for expansion; advise on foreign exchange cover , mergers (two businesses agree to combine, e.g. Westpac and St George) and takeovers (one business buys another, which ceases to exist); operate unit trusts ; arrange overseas finance at cheaper interest rates. Example: Macquarie Bank Finance and life insurance companies Non-bank financial intermediaries specialising in smaller commercial finance . Provide secured and unsecured loans. Policyholders pay a premium , which is lent to businesses; the company earns income from interest Superannuation funds Provide funds to the corporate sector through investment of superannuation contributions Unit trusts (mutual funds) Take funds from a large number of small investors and invest them in specific types of financial assets Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) Market operator, clearing house and payment system facilitator. Oversees compliance with operating rules and promotes corporate governance among listed companies 3.1 Primary vs Secondary Market — a guaranteed exam distinction Primary market Secondary market What is traded New shares, issued for the first time Pre-owned (existing) securities Who gets the money The company receives the proceeds The selling shareholder — the company receives nothing Purpose Raise new capital Provide liquidity so investors can buy and sell easily Because the secondary market provides liquidity, it makes investing in the primary market more attractive. 4. Influence of Government Influence Detail Monetary policy The RBA assists the federal government to achieve low inflation and economic growth. Securities and loans are bought and sold to put pressure on interest rates and alter the economic cycle. This impacts debt servicing costs — if interest rates rise, loan repayment costs rise ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission) Enforces and administers the Corporations Act ; protects consumers in investments, life and general insurance, superannuation and banking (except lending). Aims to reduce fraud and unfair practices . Ensures companies adhere to the law, collects company information and makes it public Company taxation Companies pay company tax on profits , paid before dividends are distributed to shareholders Why company tax matters to financial management : Tax reduces net profit available for distribution and reinvestment. It also makes debt more attractive than equity , because interest payments are generally tax-deductible expenses while dividends are not. 5. Global Market Influences Financial risks in global markets are greater than domestic ones, but such risk is necessary for business strategy. Influence Definition Interest rates Comparison of domestic interest rates to rates in other countries Availability of funds The ease with which a business can access funds on the international financial market Global economic outlook The projected changes to the level of economic growth throughout the world Why are these "uncontrollable"? They are external macro-environmental factors existing independently of any one business. A single firm cannot change global interest rates or economic trends — it can only develop internal strategies to mitigate their impact. Negative global outlook → funding : When the outlook is negative, lenders become risk-averse and restrict lending because they fear non-repayment. Finance becomes harder to obtain, and where available, carries a higher interest rate . ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Debenture vs mortgage A mortgage is secured against property . A debenture has no security — which is why it is riskier to the lender Primary vs secondary market Primary = new shares, the company gets the money. Secondary = existing shares, the company gets nothing Overdraft vs bank loan Overdraft is flexible short-term borrowing on a current account. A loan is a fixed amount for a fixed term Operating vs financial lease Operating = short , owner maintains it. Financial = runs for the asset's whole life Factoring vs leasing Factoring sells your receivables for cash. Leasing rents an asset Merger vs takeover Merger = both agree to combine. Takeover = one buys the other, which ceases to exist ASIC vs ACCC ASIC = companies, the Corporations Act, financial services. ACCC = competition and consumers Debt vs equity Debt must be repaid and interest is tax deductible . Equity dilutes ownership and dividends are not deductible 📝 Exam habit Recommending a source of finance? Apply the matching principle (in ③ Processes ). Short-term need → short-term source. Long-term asset → long-term source. Recommending an overdraft to buy premises loses the mark. 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Retained profits Net profit reinvested in the business rather than distributed Overdraft Flexible short-notice borrowing through a cheque or current account Commercial bill A loan guaranteed by a bank, 30–180 days, usually over $100,000 Factoring Selling accounts receivable to a specialist firm for immediate cash, less a commission Mortgage A long-term loan secured against land or property Debenture Long-term debt offered to the public via prospectus, with no security Leasing Paying to use a non-current asset owned by another party IPO Initial public offering — shares sold publicly for the first time Rights issue An offer to existing shareholders to purchase additional shares ASIC The body enforcing the Corporations Act and reducing fraud and unfair practices Monetary policy RBA use of interest rates to influence the economy Next: ③ Processes of Financial Management · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Finance 3 · Processes of Financial Management
text: 📊 Finance 3 · Processes of Financial Management Finance · ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes ← you are here · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Finance module is examinable. This file covers the Processes of financial management dot points only. ⭐ This is the section the calculations come from. The three statements and the seven ratios are directly examinable. 1. Planning and Implementing Financial planning is responsible for both short-term and long-term planning. It includes: Determining the viability of projects Making decisions and projections for future liquidity and performance Setting financial goals , and determining and implementing strategies to achieve them Financial needs : A new business must determine establishment costs and how to finance them (debt and/or equity). An existing business must determine the financing required for future plans . 1.1 Budgets Budgets show the cash required for planned outlays for a particular period, and the cost of capital expenditure and associated expenses. Budgets are used as: A plan for achieving set outcomes A means of establishing standards for monitoring Budgets sit in both the planning process (giving departments and cost centres a plan to follow) and the implementation process (identifying variances and flagging areas to investigate). Type of budget Covers Operating budgets Main activities — sales, production, raw materials, labour Project budgets Capital expenditure and research and development Financial budgets Funds required to pay for inputs and anticipated inflows from future sales 1.2 Record Systems Systems that ensure data recorded and information provided is accurate, reliable, efficient and accessible . Minimising errors is important to fulfil the legal requirement to provide information to shareholders and the ATO . Most errors in computerised accounting systems occur through human error at data entry. All public companies are legally required to have an audit every year. Auditors are qualified, independent, external people who check the records to ensure the accounts show a true and fair view . 1.3 Financial Risks The risk that a business is unable to pay its debts as they fall due . Factors include: Theft of goods Not meeting sales targets Non-payment of accounts by accounts receivable Interest rate rises Risk and borrowing : There is a direct relationship between borrowing and risk. Higher debt (gearing) increases fixed interest costs, reduces financial flexibility, and raises the risk of insolvency if sales targets are not met. 1.4 Financial Controls Controls ensuring financial plans are implemented effectively and achieving set goals: Monitoring and controlling budgets — ongoing throughout the year Monitoring finances through the preparation of the cash flow statement, income statement and balance sheet — for most businesses, monthly Use of financial ratios to monitor performance 2. Debt vs Equity Financing Debt Equity Repayment Must be repaid No repayment obligation Cost Interest — tax deductible Dividends — not tax deductible Ownership Ownership retained Dilutes ownership Risk to business Higher — fixed commitments regardless of profit Lower — no payment required if a loss is made Effect on gearing Increases gearing Decreases gearing Speed Generally faster Slower — takes time 3. The Matching Principle Matching the term and source of finance to the use of finance. Short-term finance (overdraft, commercial bill, factoring) should fund short-term needs — working capital, inventory, wages Long-term finance (mortgage, debenture, shares, leasing) should fund long-term assets — property, plant, equipment Why it matters : Using an overdraft to buy a factory means the debt falls due long before the asset generates a return, creating a liquidity crisis . Using a 20-year mortgage to buy stock means paying interest for two decades on inventory sold in a month. Note — a second meaning. "Matching principle" is also an accounting term (see §6): revenue must be matched to the expenses incurred in earning it, in the same accounting period. Read the question carefully to see which is being asked. 4. The Three Financial Statements Memorise these three structures — they are examinable directly. 4.1 Cash Flow Statement Opening Cash Balance + Cash Receipts (inflows) − Cash Payments (outflows) = Closing Cash Balance Records actual cash movements over a period. A cash flow budget , by contrast, is a forecast of expected future cash flows used to identify shortfalls in advance. 4.2 Income Statement (Revenue Statement / Profit and Loss) Sales Less: Sales Returns = NET SALES Less: Cost of Goods Sold = GROSS PROFIT Less: Expenses (selling + administrative + financial) = NET PROFIT The whole statement is two subtractions. Sales − COGS = Gross Profit . Gross Profit − Expenses = Net Profit . Cost of Goods Sold is itself a calculation: COGS = Opening Stock + Purchases − Closing Stock Why closing stock is subtracted: stock still sitting in the warehouse wasn't sold, so it isn't a cost of goods sold . It carries forward as next period's opening stock. The three expense categories — you may be asked to classify these: Category What goes in it Selling Advertising, sales staff wages and commission, delivery to customers Administrative Office wages, rent, electricity, insurance, stationery, depreciation Financial Interest on loans, bank fees, discounts given, bad debts Worked example — building a revenue statement from scratch Given : Sales $620,000 | Sales returns $20,000 | Opening stock $60,000 | Purchases $310,000 | Closing stock $70,000 | Selling expenses $55,000 | Administrative expenses $50,000 | Financial expenses $15,000 Step Working Result Net Sales 620,000 − 20,000 $600,000 COGS 60,000 + 310,000 − 70,000 $300,000 Gross Profit 600,000 − 300,000 $300,000 Total Expenses 55,000 + 50,000 + 15,000 $120,000 Net Profit 300,000 − 120,000 $180,000 Then the ratios follow straight off it: Gross Profit Ratio = (300,000 ÷ 600,000) × 100 = 50% Net Profit Ratio = (180,000 ÷ 600,000) × 100 = 30% Expense Ratio = (120,000 ÷ 600,000) × 100 = 20% Check: Gross Profit Ratio − Expense Ratio = Net Profit Ratio. 50 − 20 = 30 ✅ Use this to catch arithmetic errors in the exam in about five seconds. Four traps in these calculations Trap The fix Using Sales instead of Net Sales as the denominator If the question gives sales returns, you must deduct them first. Every ratio then uses net sales Adding closing stock in COGS It's minus . Opening plus , closing minus Dividing profit ratios by Gross Profit The denominator for gross profit ratio, net profit ratio and expense ratio is always sales Forgetting × 100 and the % sign These three are percentages. Current ratio and gearing are ratios written 2:1 — no percentage Net Profit vs Return on Owners' Equity. Both use net profit on top. Net profit ratio divides by sales (how efficiently the business converts revenue into profit). ROE divides by owners' equity (what the owners get back on what they put in). Different question, same numerator. 4.3 Balance Sheet Owners' Equity = Assets (Current + Non-Current) − Liabilities (Current + Non-Current) Shows the financial position at a point in time — a snapshot. The income statement, by contrast, shows performance over a period . Current Non-Current Assets Cash, accounts receivable, inventory Property, plant, equipment, vehicles, intangibles (goodwill, patents) Liabilities Overdraft, accounts payable, short-term loans Mortgage, debentures, long-term loans Worked example — building a balance sheet A business has: Cash $20,000 | Accounts Receivable $40,000 | Inventory $50,000 | Equipment $200,000 | Accounts Payable $30,000 | Overdraft $20,000 | Mortgage $150,000 Current Assets = 20,000 + 40,000 + 50,000 = $110,000 Non-Current Assets = $200,000 → Total Assets = $310,000 Current Liabilities = 30,000 + 20,000 = $50,000 Non-Current Liabilities = $150,000 → Total Liabilities = $200,000 Owners' Equity = 310,000 − 200,000 = $110,000 5. Financial Ratios These are the ratios your course requires, with the formulas and benchmarks as taught. Learn these exact forms. # Ratio Formula Objective Benchmark 1 Current Ratio Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities Liquidity 2:1 2 Gearing Ratio Total Liabilities ÷ Owners' Equity Solvency 0.5:1 to 1:1 (i.e. up to 100%) 3 Gross Profit Ratio (Gross Profit ÷ Sales) × 100 Profitability No ideal — compare to previous periods and industry average 4 Net Profit Ratio (Net Profit ÷ Sales) × 100 Profitability No ideal — compare to previous periods and industry average 5 Return on Owners' Equity (Net Profit ÷ Owners' Equity) × 100 Profitability No ideal — compare to previous periods and industry average 6 Expense Ratio (Total Expenses ÷ Sales) × 100 Efficiency Lowest possible 7 Accounts Receivable Turnover Step 1: Sales ÷ Accounts Receivable → Step 2: 365 ÷ Step 1 answer Efficiency 30 days ⚠️ Common error — the gearing formula. Gearing is Total Liabilities ÷ Owners' Equity , not non-current liabilities over total assets. Some textbooks use other variants; use the one above for this course. 📎 The syllabus wording is "total equity" where your teacher's sheet says "owners' equity" — same figure, use your teacher's wording. 5.0 Comparative Ratio Analysis — the named dot point ✅ Syllabus dot point: "comparative ratio analysis — over different time periods, against standards, with similar businesses." This is a named part of the course , not just good technique. A ratio on its own earns the calculation mark; the comparison earns the analysis marks. Three comparisons, and the question usually tells you which to use: Compare against When What it shows Different time periods The stimulus gives two or more years Trend — is it improving or deteriorating, and how fast Standards / benchmarks The stimulus gives an industry average, or you use the ideal (2:1, 0.5–1:1, 30 days) Whether performance is acceptable Similar businesses The stimulus names a competitor Relative competitive position ⚠️ If the stimulus prints an industry average, that is the standard — it overrides the generic ideal. Knox 21(a) gave a debt-to-equity industry average of 0.3:1 ; you used the generic 0.5–1:1 range and lost the mark. QTC's 0.99:1 is inside the generic range but more than three times the industry figure. 5.1 What each ratio tells you (say this in the exam, don't just calculate) Ratio Plain-English meaning Current Ratio For every $1 of current liabilities, how many $ of current assets the business has Gearing Ratio For every $1 of equity, how much debt the business has Gross Profit Ratio For every $1 of sales, how much is left after paying COGS Net Profit Ratio For every $1 of sales, how much is left after paying all expenses Return on Owners' Equity How much return owners get back from their investment Expense Ratio For every $1 of sales, how much is spent on expenses Accounts Receivable Turnover How many days it takes to collect money from customers 5.2 Worked Ratio Example — full set Given : Sales $500,000 | COGS $300,000 | Total Expenses $120,000 | Current Assets $150,000 | Current Liabilities $75,000 | Total Liabilities $200,000 | Owners' Equity $250,000 | Accounts Receivable $41,000 Ratio Working Result Interpretation Gross Profit 500,000 − 300,000 $200,000 — Net Profit 200,000 − 120,000 $80,000 — Current Ratio 150,000 ÷ 75,000 2:1 Meets the 2:1 benchmark — sound liquidity Gearing 200,000 ÷ 250,000 0.8:1 Within the 0.5–1:1 range — acceptable solvency Gross Profit Ratio (200,000 ÷ 500,000) × 100 40% 40c in every sales dollar remains after COGS Net Profit Ratio (80,000 ÷ 500,000) × 100 16% 16c in every sales dollar is net profit Return on Owners' Equity (80,000 ÷ 250,000) × 100 32% Owners earn 32c per dollar invested Expense Ratio (120,000 ÷ 500,000) × 100 24% 24c of every sales dollar goes to expenses AR Turnover Step 1: 500,000 ÷ 41,000 = 12.2 → Step 2: 365 ÷ 12.2 ≈ 30 days Meets the 30-day benchmark 6. Limitations of Financial Reports Financial reports can be complicated to understand without a financial background and may not give a clear picture of the performance and position of the business. 6.1 Normalised Earnings Earnings adjusted for the cyclical ups and downs of the economy. On the Profit and Loss Statement and Retained Profits on the Balance Sheet, earnings are adjusted to remove unusual or one-off influences . Example : the sale of land or property where the business made a capital gain. Normalised earnings show a true reflection of earnings from operations . 6.2 Capitalising Expenses The purchase price of a non-current asset is added to the cost of setting it up, and that total is used as the value of the asset in the balance sheet . The value is then written off as an expense in the income statement over the asset's useful life — this is depreciation . Worked example — capitalising expenses Purchased new equipment for $1,000,000: Item Amount Purchase price $1,000,000 Delivery costs $500 Installation costs $1,500 Training costs $5,000 Value of asset in Balance Sheet $1,007,000 (historical cost) These costs would normally appear as expenses in the P&L, except where they relate to purchasing a non-current asset — then they are included in the asset's value on the Balance Sheet. The abuse : Taking ordinary expenses and inappropriately capitalising them is illegal. It lowers reported expenses, inflates profit, and misleads stakeholders. 6.3 Valuing Assets Businesses normally follow the historical cost concept — recording assets at purchase price. But real values change: Appreciation — inflation and market forces mean land and property tend to rise in value, so the business should revalue to show a true reflection Wear and tear — equipment loses value, so it should be devalued through depreciation Increasing asset values : To increase the value of assets such as land and property, a business needs at least two independent valuations as evidence. Worked example — straight-line depreciation Historical cost $1,000,000 | Useful lifetime 10 years | Disposal value $1,000 Straight-line depreciation = (Historical cost − Disposal value) ÷ Useful lifetime = (1,000,000 − 1,000) ÷ 10 = 999,000 ÷ 10 = $99,900 per year Income Statement (Expenses) Balance Sheet (Non-Current Assets) Year 1 Depreciation $99,900 1,000,000 − 99,900 accumulated = $900,100 Year 2 Depreciation $99,900 1,000,000 − 199,800 accumulated = $800,200 Intangibles : Goodwill, trademarks, licences and patents are impossible to value accurately , which is itself a limitation. 6.4 Timing Issues Financial reports cover a period , usually one year. If the business experiences seasonal fluctuations , the position may not be a true representation — and businesses may exploit this to appear more profitable. The matching principle (accounting sense) : Each transaction should be recorded at the time it actually occurs . Revenue must be matched to all expenses incurred in earning that revenue in a particular accounting period — even if cash has not been paid or received . By recording some transactions outside the current financial year, they will not appear on the current reports. 6.5 Debt Repayments Reports do not disclose specific information about some debt repayments. Example : money owed to workers for annual leave or sick leave. It is difficult to predict when workers will take leave, so the business cannot recognise exactly when the debt will be paid. 6.6 Notes to the Financial Statements The details and additional information left out of the main reporting documents (balance sheet, income statement). These normally appear in the appendices of Annual Reports and/or a Prospectus. Limitation : Notes are not regulated by law as strictly as the financial report itself, so notes may in fact be used to mislead . 7. Ethical Issues in Financial Reporting Accountants must display: Integrity Objectivity Confidentiality A high level of professional and technical ability Financial managers and accountants therefore cannot be "creative" when recording transactions and preparing reports in order to make the business appear more profitable. Standards : IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) and AAS (Australian Accounting Standards). AAS selects the appropriate IFRS standards to adapt to the Australian market and adds specific requirements. Business accounts must be audited and monitored by independent organisations such as ASIC , which checks accounts and procedures to ensure a true and fair representation . 7.1 Unethical Financial Practices Practice Definition Audits (misuse of) Audits are independent examinations of financial information — internal or external. External auditors are independent ; compromising that independence is unethical Cut-off periods Financial reporting timed to give a misleading impression of current performance Inappropriate use of funds Company officials using company assets for personal gain; false invoices issued for more than inputs are worth Corporate raiding Buying an undervalued company and increasing profit or selling off the assets . The owner's personal wealth increases at the cost of employees who lose their jobs Misuse of business credit cards Managers and employees using business credit cards and money for personal use Other issues: fictitious revenues, hidden liabilities and expenses, improper disclosures or omissions, and fraudulent asset valuations . 7.2 Six Named Ethical Examples Issue Explanation and example Window dressing Using legal techniques to show a better financial position than actually exists. Example : at year end, offering a valued customer bulk stock at a discount. This shows improved cash flow and low stock on the Balance Sheet. Ethically it may not show a true and fair position — it hides whether stock was sold below cost, or would have sold at all at full price Income smoothing (timing) Reducing taxation by reducing net profit. Example : XYZ pays $10,000 insurance in advance in January 2022 for the year, and records all of it as an expense in June for FY2021/22. Only 6 months was incurred, so $5,000 belongs in FY2021/22 and $5,000 in FY2022/23. Profit falls, so less tax is paid Continuous disclosure Legally a business need not inform shareholders if it is likely to make a loss after previously indicating profit. Ethically it should, so shareholders can make informed decisions. Disclosure requirements are also reduced during takeovers Valuing intangible assets Hard to value. Example : Facebook bought WhatsApp for $19 billion despite it never making a profit, but with over 45 million users. Should it be valued at purchase price or potential future value? Valuing assets Legally a business needs an independent valuation — but it can obtain several and choose the one that suits the position it wants to show. Legal, but may not be the most accurate Debt repayments A business must provide for annual leave and long service leave. Annual leave is easy to estimate. Long service leave vests after 10 years, so the business must assess the probability of employees staying that long and when they will take it — raising the ethical question of how to value that future liability ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Gearing vs leverage The same thing . Highly geared = highly leveraged = heavy reliance on borrowed funds Cash flow statement vs cash flow budget Statement = record of what happened. Budget = forecast of what will Income statement vs balance sheet Income statement = performance over a period . Balance sheet = position at a point in time Normalised earnings vs window dressing Normalised earnings removes one-offs for clarity (legitimate). Window dressing is deliberately flattering (legal but misleading) Window dressing vs fraud Window dressing is legal . Fraud is not Capitalising vs expensing Capitalising puts the cost on the balance sheet as an asset. Expensing puts it on the P&L immediately Matching principle — two meanings (a) match the finance term to the use ; (b) match revenue to expenses in a period .
