Read the question Appreciation vs depreciation Assets: appreciation = rises in value, depreciation = falls . Also used for currency — same words, different context 📝 Exam habits that have cost you marks Use the benchmark printed in the stimulus. In your Knox trial, 21(a) gave an industry average of 0.3:1 for gearing and you used the generic 0.5–1:1 range. If the paper supplies a benchmark, that benchmark wins. A ratio without a comparison is a number, not analysis. Compare to last year, to the industry, or to the benchmark — then say whether it is good or bad and why. 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Budget A statement of the cash required for planned outlays in a particular period Audit An independent examination of financial information Matching principle Matching the term and source of finance to its use; in accounting, matching revenue to the expenses incurred in earning it Working capital Current Assets − Current Liabilities Normalised earnings Earnings adjusted to remove unusual or one-off influences Capitalising expenses Adding set-up costs to an asset's balance-sheet value Historical cost Recording assets at their original purchase price Depreciation The systematic write-off of an asset's cost over its useful life Window dressing Using legal techniques to present a better financial position than actually exists Income smoothing Shifting expenses between periods to reduce net profit and therefore tax Next: ④ Financial Management Strategies · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Finance 4 · Financial Management Strategies
text: 🎯 Finance 4 · Financial Management Strategies Finance · ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies ← you are here · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Finance module is examinable. This file covers the Financial management strategies dot points only. 1. The Objective → Strategy Map ⭐ Each objective has its own strategy family. This mapping is the spine of most extended-response questions. If the question names an objective, this table tells you which strategies to write about. Objective Strategy family Profitability Cost controls (fixed and variable, cost centres, expense minimisation); revenue controls (marketing objectives) Liquidity Working capital management — control of current assets and current liabilities; leasing; sale and lease-back Efficiency Cash flow management — cash flow statements, distribution of payments, discounts for early payment, factoring Solvency Choosing the best source of finance for the situation (debt vs equity) 2. Cash Flow Management Cash flow statements record inflows and outflows. Strategies: Strategy How it works Distribution of payments Spreading payments through the month/year so large outflows do not coincide, avoiding a cash shortfall Discounts for early payment Offering customers a discount (e.g. 2/10 net 30) to pay sooner — reduces debtor days and accelerates inflow Factoring Selling accounts receivable for immediate cash (at a cost) Other ways to increase inflows : tighten credit terms, increase sales revenue, sell unused non-current assets, lease rather than purchase. Other ways to decrease outflows : negotiate longer supplier payment terms, reduce inventory (JIT), cut discretionary expenses, refinance at lower rates, delay non-essential capital expenditure. Cash flow cycle : Cash → Inventory → Production → Sales → Debtors → Cash. The longer the cycle, the more working capital is needed. Businesses aim to shorten it. 3. Working Capital Management Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities 3.1 Control of Current Assets Asset Management focus Cash Maintain adequate levels — not so much that it sits idle, not so little that bills cannot be paid Receivables Minimise collection time; check creditworthiness; offer early payment discounts; enforce credit policies Inventories Balance too much (storage costs, obsolescence) against too little (stockouts, lost sales) 3.2 Control of Current Liabilities Liability Management focus Payables Maximise payment time without damaging supplier relationships or credit terms Loans Seek the lowest-cost finance; monitor charges and interest Overdrafts Use for genuine short-term shortfalls; minimise interest paid 3.3 Named Working Capital Strategies Strategy Effect Leasing Frees cash that would be tied up in purchasing assets outright; payments are tax deductible Sale and lease-back Selling an asset the business owns and leasing it straight back . Generates an immediate large cash inflow while retaining the use of the asset 4. Profitability Management 4.1 Cost Controls Control Detail Fixed and variable costs Fixed costs do not change with output (rent, insurance, salaries). Variable costs change directly with output (raw materials, wages per unit). Managing the mix affects break-even Cost centres A cost centre is a department or area of the business to which costs can be directly attributed, so performance can be measured and controlled. Direct cost centres relate to production; indirect cost centres (HR, IT) support the whole business Expense minimisation Systematically reducing expenses — bulk buying, global sourcing, outsourcing, reducing overheads, automation 4.2 Revenue Controls Setting marketing objectives and using the marketing mix to drive sales revenue: product differentiation, market development, product development, diversification, pricing strategies, improved promotion. Profit formula Profit = Total Revenue − Total Costs Profit = (Price × Quantity Sold) − (Fixed Costs + Variable Costs) To improve profit: increase revenue (price or quantity) OR decrease costs (fixed or variable). 4.3 Break-Even Analysis Concept Formula Break-Even Point (units) Fixed Costs ÷ (Selling Price per unit − Variable Cost per unit) Break-Even Point ($) Break-even units × Selling Price per unit Contribution per unit Selling Price per unit − Variable Cost per unit Margin of Safety Actual (or expected) sales − Break-even sales Target Profit (units) (Fixed Costs + Target Profit) ÷ Contribution per unit Worked example A café has fixed costs of $60,000/year . Each coffee sells for $5 with a variable cost of $2 . Calculation Working Result Contribution per unit 5 − 2 $3 Break-even (units) 60,000 ÷ 3 20,000 coffees Break-even ($) 20,000 × 5 $100,000 Margin of safety (selling 25,000) 25,000 − 20,000 5,000 coffees Units for $15,000 target profit (60,000 + 15,000) ÷ 3 25,000 coffees Change Effect on Break-Even Point ↑ Selling price Decreases (fewer units needed) ↑ Variable costs Increases ↑ Fixed costs Increases ↓ Selling price Increases ↓ Variable costs Decreases ↓ Fixed costs Decreases 5. Global Financial Management Four additional factors/risks when operating globally: exchange rates, interest rates, methods of international payment, hedging and derivatives . 5.1 Exchange Rates Exchange rate = the value of a country's money calculated using another country's money. Appreciation = the AUD rises in value against another currency. Depreciation = the AUD falls in value against another currency. Scenario Effect on the Australian business Business imports from China and the AUD depreciates against the Yuan Costs more Business has borrowed from the US and the AUD appreciates against the USD Pays less Business has lent money to a UK business and the AUD depreciates against the pound Receives less Business exports to France and the AUD appreciates against the Euro Costs the Australian business less ⭐ Memory hook : A strong (appreciating) AUD makes imports cheaper and exports dearer (less competitive overseas). A weak (depreciating) AUD makes imports dearer and exports cheaper (more competitive overseas). 5.2 Interest Rates It is important to find the lowest interest rates, as exchange rate fluctuations can make repayments more costly. Advantages of borrowing overseas: The interest rate can be cheaper There are fewer restrictions Finance may be acquired more quickly and easily The risk : If the AUD depreciates , the foreign loan becomes much more expensive to repay. If global interest rates rise, repayments increase beyond what was planned. 5.3 Methods of International Payment Method How it works Risk Payment in advance Exporter receives payment, then sends the goods No risk for the exporter ; risk sits with the importer (goods may never arrive). Few importers accept this Letter of credit A document issued by a bank to the seller, with instructions from the buyer authorising the seller to draw a specified amount from the buyer's bank account under certain conditions. The bank ensures the exporter gets paid Existing risk for the importer Bill of exchange A written order from the seller requesting the buyer pay a specified amount at a specified time. The bank ensures the importer receives goods and the exporter is paid Existing risk for the exporter Clean payment Goods are shipped before payment is received Significant risk for the exporter — used only with trusted long-standing partners 5.4 Hedging Hedging = any strategy used by a business to reduce financial risks . It is like buying insurance to protect property — protection against unforeseen risks. Businesses hedge when uncertain of the future , to reduce foreign exchange and interest rate risks. Natural hedging occurs when a business: Sets up subsidiaries in other countries and uses them to pay for expenses and goods purchased from that country Sets up bank accounts in a country where it buys or sells goods, and uses funds from that account to pay expenses in that country 5.5 Derivatives A derivative is a special contract between global businesses and suppliers. Three main types: Type How it works Forward exchange contract An agreement with a FOREX business guaranteeing a certain exchange rate on a certain day Currency options contract The business has the option (no obligation) to buy or sell foreign currency when the exchange rate movement is to its advantage. Allows use of the spot rate Swap contract A written contract allowing an Australian business to pay an overseas supplier in another currency at a spot rate Spot rate = the exchange rate at a specific time on a specific day. Forward exchange contract — the trade-off: Advantage : If the spot rate turns out less favourable (e.g. the AUD has depreciated), the contracted rate is cheaper for the business. Example : contracted at AUD$1:USD$0.72, spot in 6 months is AUD$1:USD$0.63 → the contract is better. Disadvantage : If the spot rate turns out more favourable (e.g. the AUD has appreciated), the contracted rate is more expensive . Example : spot in 6 months is AUD$1:USD$0.95 → the contract is worse than the spot rate. Why choose an options contract over a forward contract? Options protect against unfavourable movements while retaining the opportunity to gain if movements are favourable — you simply don't exercise the option. The trade-off is that options cost a premium. Swap contract example : An Australian business has excess USD and needs to pay a Chinese company for materials. The Chinese company may agree to accept USD, because it can then use those USD to pay an American supplier of its own. ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Hedging vs derivative Hedging is any strategy to reduce financial risk. A derivative is one specific type of hedging contract Spot rate vs forward rate Spot = the rate today . Forward = locked in for a future date Forward contract vs options contract A forward obliges you to transact at the agreed rate. An option gives you the right but not the obligation Letter of credit vs bill of exchange Letter of credit is issued by the buyer's bank . Bill of exchange is a written order from the seller Appreciation vs depreciation (currency) Strong AUD: imports cheaper , exports dearer . Weak AUD: the reverse Cost centre vs profit centre A cost centre only incurs costs. A profit centre also generates revenue Fixed vs variable costs Fixed don't change with output (rent). Variable change directly with output (raw materials) Leasing vs sale and lease-back Leasing = you never owned it. Sale and lease-back = you sold something you owned and rented it back Break-even units vs break-even dollars Units = FC ÷ contribution. Dollars = units × selling price . Read which the question wants 📝 Exam habits Break-even: check whether the question wants units or dollars. They are different answers from the same calculation. Sale and lease-back is a liquidity strategy , not a solvency one. It generates immediate cash. Your notes list it under liquidity for exactly this reason. Top-band tip : Integrate strategies from other topics (e.g. JIT from Operations) and link them back to the finance impact. 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Working capital Current Assets − Current Liabilities Sale and lease-back Selling an asset the business owns and immediately leasing it back Cost centre An area of a business to which costs can be directly attributed Break-even point The level of sales at which total revenue equals total costs Margin of safety Actual or expected sales minus break-even sales Exchange rate The value of one country's currency expressed in another's Hedging Any strategy used by a business to reduce financial risk Derivative A contract used to hedge — a forward, option or swap Spot rate The exchange rate at a specific time on a specific day Letter of credit A bank document guaranteeing payment to the exporter Bill of exchange A written order from the seller requesting payment at a specified time Back to: ① Role · 📕 Full note · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · MOC

title: Finance — Full Module Note
text: 📕 Finance — Full Module Note The whole module in one file. Split versions: ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies Scope: the full HSC Finance module is examinable. 🔧 Maintenance note: sections 1–4 below are mirrored in the four split files. If one is corrected, correct both. Sections 5–8 exist only here. 1. Role of Financial Management Definition : Financial management deals with the analysis, interpretation and evaluation of all financial records. It is the financial manager's responsibility to source finance that enables the business to achieve its strategic goals. 1.1 Strategic Role of Financial Management The process of setting objectives throughout the business and deciding what resources are needed to achieve them Developing a strategic plan as part of financial management ensures the business survives and grows in a competitive world Financial management provides a framework for all other business activities — it does not follow the lead of other managers Exam trap : A common multiple-choice question asks what the strategic role of finance is. The answer is "provides a framework for all other business activities" — not "sets short-term goals" (that's tactical/operational). 1.2 Objectives of Financial Management Five objectives, split by time horizon. Horizon Objective Definition Short term (within 12 months) Liquidity The ability to pay back current liabilities with current assets Short term Profitability The ability of the business to maximise profits Short term Efficiency The ability to manage costs and the collection of money from customers Long term (2–5 years) Growth The ability of the business to grow and expand Long term Solvency How the business is financed (debt vs equity) — the ability to meet long-term financial commitments Confusing pair — Liquidity vs Solvency Liquidity = short -term. Can we pay bills due now with assets we can convert to cash now ? Measured by the current ratio . Solvency = long -term. Can we meet commitments over years ? Measured by the gearing ratio . Both are about paying debts — the difference is purely the time frame . Long-term goal of the business is to increase the wealth of the owners . Long-term goals depend on profitability in the short term resulting from increased operating efficiency. 1.3 Interdependence with Other Key Business Functions Interdependence = the mutual reliance between finance and the other key business functions. Function Relationship with Finance Operations Finance provides funding and budgets so products can be made profitably. Operations produces quality products with minimal expense, generating higher revenue margins that flow back to finance Marketing Finance sets the marketing budget. Marketing generates the sales revenue that finance then allocates, monitors and reinvests Human Resources Wages and training are major budget items. Finance sets salary budgets; HR must justify expenditure through productivity gains. Commission and incentive schemes are a joint HR–finance decision Model "Explain" answer (scaffold from class) Define — Financial management is interdependent with operations because of the relationship between business revenue and expenditure. Relationship — Finance provides funding and budgets so the product can be produced profitably, while operations produces quality products with minimal expense to generate a higher revenue margin. Implications — Both functions supply each other with information and resources that drive growth and profit maximisation. Link — Hence the business grows in the marketplace and increases revenue margins, leading to increased profitability. 2. Influences on Financial Management 2.1 Internal Sources of Finance Internal sources are recorded under equity in the balance sheet. The money comes from the owners or from the business's own activities. Source Definition Owner's equity Funds contributed by owners or partners to establish and build the business Retained profits Net profit that has been reinvested in the business. Added as equity — increases the owner's claim Owner's Equity section of the Balance Sheet = Capital + Retained Profits 2.2 External Sources of Finance Financed from external organisations — either debt or equity . Debt = any money that has been borrowed . Short-term debt is repayable within 12 months; long-term is over 12 months. Equity = attached to the ownership of shares in an incorporated business — the owner's financial claim on the assets. Debt Finance — Short Term Source Detail Overdraft Flexibility to borrow from a bank at short notice through a cheque/current account. Interest must be paid. Used for working capital and claimable as a tax deduction. More flexible than a bank loan; assists with short-term liquidity issues Commercial bill A written order for a loan amount guaranteed by the business's bank . Borrowed from businesses with surplus funds. Normally 30–180 days , usually for amounts over $100,000 Factoring Selling accounts receivable to a specialist factoring firm to create cash inflow. The factoring company takes over management and collection of the unpaid accounts and pays the seller the value minus a commission . Business receives up to 90% within 48 hours . The riskiest source because of unpaid debts — that risk is borne by the debt collection agency Debt Finance — Long Term Source Detail Mortgage A loan repaid over a set number of years with interest, used to purchase land or property . The property becomes the security . If the business defaults, the bank takes and sells the property Debenture Long-term debt acquired by offering a prospectus to the general public on the securities exchange. Set interest rate for a fixed time. More risky to the lender than a mortgage — not tied to specific property, so there is no security. Unlike shares, the level of profit does not affect the interest rate Unsecured notes Usually issued by finance companies to gain funds. Higher interest rates reflecting greater risk. Also called bonds Leasing Leasing non-current assets (cars, equipment) for payments to the owner. Reduces the cost of acquiring assets as full value need not be paid instantly. Lease payments are tax deductible — they appear under Expenses in the Profit and Loss Statement, reducing net profit and therefore company tax Two types of lease: Operating lease — short periods, normally shorter than the life of the asset. The owner carries out maintenance. Financial lease — the lessor purchases the asset on behalf of the lessee. Runs for the lifetime of the asset . Why lease rather than buy? Lease costs are tax deductible; flexibility if the asset is only needed for a short period; distributes the cost over time, which is better for cash flow . Equity Financing Equity financing comes from the owners . Equity reflects the owner's financial claim on the assets of the business. Legal structure Term used Sole trader / Partnership Owners' Equity Public / Private companies Shareholders' Funds Private equity — current owners invite people or organisations to invest. Normally proprietary companies (Pty Ltd). Shareholders do not necessarily have control, and there is no guarantee of dividends. Public equity — companies listed on the ASX ; anyone can invest. Type Definition Ordinary shares Issued on the ASX, with or without voting rights at the AGM New share issues Shares sold for the first time on the public market — either an IPO (initial public offering) or a new offering if more finance is needed Rights issue The company offers existing shareholders the chance to buy more shares Placements Additional shares offered to specific institutions (venture capitalists) and specific investors Share purchase plans An offer to existing shareholders to purchase more shares without brokerage fees , normally below normal prices. Requires ASIC permission Equity — Advantages Equity — Disadvantages No debt servicing costs such as interest Takes time If the business makes a loss, no dividend needs to be paid (though this may worry shareholders into selling) Dilutes ownership Financial Grants Financial gifts from government to help businesses establish. Strict criteria: location, personal characteristics of the owner, type of industry, type of goods/services. Criteria commonly include Indigenous people, regional businesses, the IT industry, and businesses providing innovative or essential services. The government is not paid back and gets no ownership . Its return comes through increased employment, growth and taxes . 2.3 Financial Institutions Institution Role Banks Accept deposits and provide loans; the largest source of funds for business Investment banks Trade in money, securities and financial futures; arrange long-term finance for expansion; advise on foreign exchange cover , mergers (two businesses agree to combine, e.g. Westpac and St George) and takeovers (one business buys another, which ceases to exist); operate unit trusts ; arrange overseas finance at cheaper interest rates. Example: Macquarie Bank Finance and life insurance companies Non-bank financial intermediaries specialising in smaller commercial finance . Provide secured and unsecured loans. Policyholders pay a premium , which is lent to businesses; the company earns income from interest Superannuation funds Provide funds to the corporate sector through investment of superannuation contributions Unit trusts (mutual funds) Take funds from a large number of small investors and invest them in specific types of financial assets Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) Market operator, clearing house and payment system facilitator. Oversees compliance with operating rules and promotes corporate governance among listed companies Primary vs Secondary Market — a guaranteed exam distinction Primary market Secondary market What is traded New shares, issued for the first time Pre-owned (existing) securities Who gets the money The company receives the proceeds The selling shareholder — the company receives nothing Purpose Raise new capital Provide liquidity so investors can buy and sell easily Because the secondary market provides liquidity, it makes investing in the primary market more attractive. 2.4 Influence of Government Influence Detail Monetary policy The RBA assists the federal government to achieve low inflation and economic growth. Securities and loans are bought and sold to put pressure on interest rates and alter the economic cycle. This impacts debt servicing costs — if interest rates rise, loan repayment costs rise ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission) Enforces and administers the Corporations Act ; protects consumers in investments, life and general insurance, superannuation and banking (except lending). Aims to reduce fraud and unfair practices . Ensures companies adhere to the law, collects company information and makes it public Company taxation Companies pay company tax on profits , paid before dividends are distributed to shareholders Why company tax matters to financial management : Tax reduces net profit available for distribution and reinvestment. It also makes debt more attractive than equity , because interest payments are generally tax-deductible expenses while dividends are not. 2.5 Global Market Influences Financial risks in global markets are greater than domestic ones, but such risk is necessary for business strategy. Influence Definition Interest rates Comparison of domestic interest rates to rates in other countries Availability of funds The ease with which a business can access funds on the international financial market Global economic outlook The projected changes to the level of economic growth throughout the world Why are these "uncontrollable"? They are external macro-environmental factors existing independently of any one business. A single firm cannot change global interest rates or economic trends — it can only develop internal strategies to mitigate their impact. Negative global outlook → funding : When the outlook is negative, lenders become risk-averse and restrict lending because they fear non-repayment. Finance becomes harder to obtain, and where available, carries a higher interest rate . 3. Processes of Financial Management 3.1 Planning and Implementing Financial planning is responsible for both short-term and long-term planning. It includes: Determining the viability of projects Making decisions and projections for future liquidity and performance Setting financial goals , and determining and implementing strategies to achieve them Financial needs : A new business must determine establishment costs and how to finance them (debt and/or equity). An existing business must determine the financing required for future plans . Budgets Budgets show the cash required for planned outlays for a particular period, and the cost of capital expenditure and associated expenses. Budgets are used as: A plan for achieving set outcomes A means of establishing standards for monitoring Budgets sit in both the planning process (giving departments and cost centres a plan to follow) and the implementation process (identifying variances and flagging areas to investigate). Type of budget Covers Operating budgets Main activities — sales, production, raw materials, labour Project budgets Capital expenditure and research and development Financial budgets Funds required to pay for inputs and anticipated inflows from future sales Record Systems Systems that ensure data recorded and information provided is accurate, reliable, efficient and accessible . Minimising errors is important to fulfil the legal requirement to provide information to shareholders and the ATO . Most errors in computerised accounting systems occur through human error at data entry. All public companies are legally required to have an audit every year. Auditors are qualified, independent, external people who check the records to ensure the accounts show a true and fair view . Financial Risks The risk that a business is unable to pay its debts as they fall due . Factors include: Theft of goods Not meeting sales targets Non-payment of accounts by accounts receivable Interest rate rises Risk and borrowing : There is a direct relationship between borrowing and risk. Higher debt (gearing) increases fixed interest costs, reduces financial flexibility, and raises the risk of insolvency if sales targets are not met. Financial Controls Controls ensuring financial plans are implemented effectively and achieving set goals: Monitoring and controlling budgets — ongoing throughout the year Monitoring finances through the preparation of the cash flow statement, income statement and balance sheet — for most businesses, monthly Use of financial ratios to monitor performance 3.2 Debt vs Equity Financing Debt Equity Repayment Must be repaid No repayment obligation Cost Interest — tax deductible Dividends — not tax deductible Ownership Ownership retained Dilutes ownership Risk to business Higher — fixed commitments regardless of profit Lower — no payment required if a loss is made Effect on gearing Increases gearing Decreases gearing Speed Generally faster Slower — takes time 3.3 The Matching Principle Matching the term and source of finance to the use of finance. Short-term finance (overdraft, commercial bill, factoring) should fund short-term needs — working capital, inventory, wages Long-term finance (mortgage, debenture, shares, leasing) should fund long-term assets — property, plant, equipment Why it matters : Using an overdraft to buy a factory means the debt falls due long before the asset generates a return, creating a liquidity crisis . Using a 20-year mortgage to buy stock means paying interest for two decades on inventory sold in a month. Note — a second meaning. "Matching principle" is also an accounting term (see §3.6): revenue must be matched to the expenses incurred in earning it, in the same accounting period. Read the question carefully to see which is being asked. 3.4 The Three Financial Statements Memorise these three structures — they are examinable directly. Cash Flow Statement Opening Cash Balance + Cash Receipts (inflows) − Cash Payments (outflows) = Closing Cash Balance Records actual cash movements over a period. A cash flow budget , by contrast, is a forecast of expected future cash flows used to identify shortfalls in advance. Income Statement (Revenue Statement / Profit and Loss) Sales Less: Sales Returns = NET SALES Less: Cost of Goods Sold = GROSS PROFIT Less: Expenses (selling + administrative + financial) = NET PROFIT The whole statement is two subtractions. Sales − COGS = Gross Profit . Gross Profit − Expenses = Net Profit . Cost of Goods Sold is itself a calculation: COGS = Opening Stock + Purchases − Closing Stock Why closing stock is subtracted: stock still sitting in the warehouse wasn't sold, so it isn't a cost of goods sold . It carries forward as next period's opening stock. The three expense categories — you may be asked to classify these: Category What goes in it Selling Advertising, sales staff wages and commission, delivery to customers Administrative Office wages, rent, electricity, insurance, stationery, depreciation Financial Interest on loans, bank fees, discounts given, bad debts Worked example — building a revenue statement from scratch Given : Sales $620,000 | Sales returns $20,000 | Opening stock $60,000 | Purchases $310,000 | Closing stock $70,000 | Selling expenses $55,000 | Administrative expenses $50,000 | Financial expenses $15,000 Step Working Result Net Sales 620,000 − 20,000 $600,000 COGS 60,000 + 310,000 − 70,000 $300,000 Gross Profit 600,000 − 300,000 $300,000 Total Expenses 55,000 + 50,000 + 15,000 $120,000 Net Profit 300,000 − 120,000 $180,000 Then the ratios follow straight off it: Gross Profit Ratio = (300,000 ÷ 600,000) × 100 = 50% Net Profit Ratio = (180,000 ÷ 600,000) × 100 = 30% Expense Ratio = (120,000 ÷ 600,000) × 100 = 20% Check: Gross Profit Ratio − Expense Ratio = Net Profit Ratio. 50 − 20 = 30 ✅ Use this to catch arithmetic errors in the exam in about five seconds. Four traps in these calculations Trap The fix Using Sales instead of Net Sales as the denominator If the question gives sales returns, you must deduct them first. Every ratio then uses net sales Adding closing stock in COGS It's minus . Opening plus , closing minus Dividing profit ratios by Gross Profit The denominator for gross profit ratio, net profit ratio and expense ratio is always sales Forgetting × 100 and the % sign These three are percentages. Current ratio and gearing are ratios written 2:1 — no percentage Net Profit vs Return on Owners' Equity. Both use net profit on top. Net profit ratio divides by sales (how efficiently the business converts revenue into profit). ROE divides by owners' equity (what the owners get back on what they put in). Different question, same numerator. Balance Sheet Owners' Equity = Assets (Current + Non-Current) − Liabilities (Current + Non-Current) Shows the financial position at a point in time — a snapshot. The income statement, by contrast, shows performance over a period . Current Non-Current Assets Cash, accounts receivable, inventory Property, plant, equipment, vehicles, intangibles (goodwill, patents) Liabilities Overdraft, accounts payable, short-term loans Mortgage, debentures, long-term loans Worked example — building a balance sheet A business has: Cash $20,000 | Accounts Receivable $40,000 | Inventory $50,000 | Equipment $200,000 | Accounts Payable $30,000 | Overdraft $20,000 | Mortgage $150,000 Current Assets = 20,000 + 40,000 + 50,000 = $110,000 Non-Current Assets = $200,000 → Total Assets = $310,000 Current Liabilities = 30,000 + 20,000 = $50,000 Non-Current Liabilities = $150,000 → Total Liabilities = $200,000 Owners' Equity = 310,000 − 200,000 = $110,000 3.5 Financial Ratios These are the ratios your course requires, with the formulas and benchmarks as taught. Learn these exact forms. # Ratio Formula Objective Benchmark 1 Current Ratio Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities Liquidity 2:1 2 Gearing Ratio Total Liabilities ÷ Owners' Equity Solvency 0.5:1 to 1:1 (i.e. up to 100%) 3 Gross Profit Ratio (Gross Profit ÷ Sales) × 100 Profitability No ideal — compare to previous periods and industry average 4 Net Profit Ratio (Net Profit ÷ Sales) × 100 Profitability No ideal — compare to previous periods and industry average 5 Return on Owners' Equity (Net Profit ÷ Owners' Equity) × 100 Profitability No ideal — compare to previous periods and industry average 6 Expense Ratio (Total Expenses ÷ Sales) × 100 Efficiency Lowest possible 7 Accounts Receivable Turnover Step 1: Sales ÷ Accounts Receivable → Step 2: 365 ÷ Step 1 answer Efficiency 30 days Common error — the gearing formula. Gearing is Total Liabilities ÷ Owners' Equity , not non-current liabilities over total assets. Some textbooks use other variants; use the one above for this course. Confusing pair — Gearing vs Leverage. They describe the same idea: the proportion of the business funded by debt rather than equity . "Highly geared" = "highly leveraged" = heavy reliance on borrowed funds → higher financial risk but potentially higher return to owners. What each ratio tells you (say this in the exam, don't just calculate) Ratio Plain-English meaning Current Ratio For every $1 of current liabilities, how many $ of current assets the business has Gearing Ratio For every $1 of equity, how much debt the business has Gross Profit Ratio For every $1 of sales, how much is left after paying COGS Net Profit Ratio For every $1 of sales, how much is left after paying all expenses Return on Owners' Equity How much return owners get back from their investment Expense Ratio For every $1 of sales, how much is spent on expenses Accounts Receivable Turnover How many days it takes to collect money from customers Worked Ratio Example — full set Given : Sales $500,000 | COGS $300,000 | Total Expenses $120,000 | Current Assets $150,000 | Current Liabilities $75,000 | Total Liabilities $200,000 | Owners' Equity $250,000 | Accounts Receivable $41,000 Ratio Working Result Interpretation Gross Profit 500,000 − 300,000 $200,000 — Net Profit 200,000 − 120,000 $80,000 — Current Ratio 150,000 ÷ 75,000 2:1 Meets the 2:1 benchmark — sound liquidity Gearing 200,000 ÷ 250,000 0.8:1 Within the 0.5–1:1 range — acceptable solvency Gross Profit Ratio (200,000 ÷ 500,000) × 100 40% 40c in every sales dollar remains after COGS Net Profit Ratio (80,000 ÷ 500,000) × 100 16% 16c in every sales dollar is net profit Return on Owners' Equity (80,000 ÷ 250,000) × 100 32% Owners earn 32c per dollar invested Expense Ratio (120,000 ÷ 500,000) × 100 24% 24c of every sales dollar goes to expenses AR Turnover Step 1: 500,000 ÷ 41,000 = 12.2 → Step 2: 365 ÷ 12.2 ≈ 30 days Meets the 30-day benchmark 3.6 Limitations of Financial Reports Financial reports can be complicated to understand without a financial background and may not give a clear picture of the performance and position of the business. Normalised Earnings Earnings adjusted for the cyclical ups and downs of the economy. On the Profit and Loss Statement and Retained Profits on the Balance Sheet, earnings are adjusted to remove unusual or one-off influences . Example : the sale of land or property where the business made a capital gain. Normalised earnings show a true reflection of earnings from operations . Capitalising Expenses The purchase price of a non-current asset is added to the cost of setting it up, and that total is used as the value of the asset in the balance sheet . The value is then written off as an expense in the income statement over the asset's useful life — this is depreciation . Worked example — capitalising expenses Purchased new equipment for $1,000,000: Item Amount Purchase price $1,000,000 Delivery costs $500 Installation costs $1,500 Training costs $5,000 Value of asset in Balance Sheet $1,007,000 (historical cost) These costs would normally appear as expenses in the P&L, except where they relate to purchasing a non-current asset — then they are included in the asset's value on the Balance Sheet. The abuse : Taking ordinary expenses and inappropriately capitalising them is illegal. It lowers reported expenses, inflates profit, and misleads stakeholders. Valuing Assets Businesses normally follow the historical cost concept — recording assets at purchase price. But real values change: Appreciation — inflation and market forces mean land and property tend to rise in value, so the business should revalue to show a true reflection Wear and tear — equipment loses value, so it should be devalued through depreciation Increasing asset values : To increase the value of assets such as land and property, a business needs at least two independent valuations as evidence. Worked example — straight-line depreciation Historical cost $1,000,000 | Useful lifetime 10 years | Disposal value $1,000 Straight-line depreciation = (Historical cost − Disposal value) ÷ Useful lifetime = (1,000,000 − 1,000) ÷ 10 = 999,000 ÷ 10 = $99,900 per year Income Statement (Expenses) Balance Sheet (Non-Current Assets) Year 1 Depreciation $99,900 1,000,000 − 99,900 accumulated = $900,100 Year 2 Depreciation $99,900 1,000,000 − 199,800 accumulated = $800,200 Intangibles : Goodwill, trademarks, licences and patents are impossible to value accurately , which is itself a limitation. Timing Issues Financial reports cover a period , usually one year. If the business experiences seasonal fluctuations , the position may not be a true representation — and businesses may exploit this to appear more profitable. The matching principle (accounting sense) : Each transaction should be recorded at the time it actually occurs . Revenue must be matched to all expenses incurred in earning that revenue in a particular accounting period — even if cash has not been paid or received . By recording some transactions outside the current financial year, they will not appear on the current reports. Debt Repayments Reports do not disclose specific information about some debt repayments. Example : money owed to workers for annual leave or sick leave. It is difficult to predict when workers will take leave, so the business cannot recognise exactly when the debt will be paid. Notes to the Financial Statements The details and additional information left out of the main reporting documents (balance sheet, income statement). These normally appear in the appendices of Annual Reports and/or a Prospectus. Limitation : Notes are not regulated by law as strictly as the financial report itself, so notes may in fact be used to mislead . 3.7 Ethical Issues in Financial Reporting Accountants must display: Integrity Objectivity Confidentiality A high level of professional and technical ability Financial managers and accountants therefore cannot be "creative" when recording transactions and preparing reports in order to make the business appear more profitable. Standards : IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) and AAS (Australian Accounting Standards). AAS selects the appropriate IFRS standards to adapt to the Australian market and adds specific requirements. Business accounts must be audited and monitored by independent organisations such as ASIC , which checks accounts and procedures to ensure a true and fair representation . Unethical Financial Practices Practice Definition Audits (misuse of) Audits are independent examinations of financial information — internal or external. External auditors are independent ; compromising that independence is unethical Cut-off periods Financial reporting timed to give a misleading impression of current performance Inappropriate use of funds Company officials using company assets for personal gain; false invoices issued for more than inputs are worth Corporate raiding Buying an undervalued company and increasing profit or selling off the assets . The owner's personal wealth increases at the cost of employees who lose their jobs Misuse of business credit cards Managers and employees using business credit cards and money for personal use Other issues: fictitious revenues, hidden liabilities and expenses, improper disclosures or omissions, and fraudulent asset valuations . Six Named Ethical Examples Issue Explanation and example Window dressing Using legal techniques to show a better financial position than actually exists. Example : at year end, offering a valued customer bulk stock at a discount. This shows improved cash flow and low stock on the Balance Sheet. Ethically it may not show a true and fair position — it hides whether stock was sold below cost, or would have sold at all at full price Income smoothing (timing) Reducing taxation by reducing net profit. Example : XYZ pays $10,000 insurance in advance in January 2022 for the year, and records all of it as an expense in June for FY2021/22. Only 6 months was incurred, so $5,000 belongs in FY2021/22 and $5,000 in FY2022/23. Profit falls, so less tax is paid Continuous disclosure Legally a business need not inform shareholders if it is likely to make a loss after previously indicating profit. Ethically it should, so shareholders can make informed decisions. Disclosure requirements are also reduced during takeovers Valuing intangible assets Hard to value. Example : Facebook bought WhatsApp for $19 billion despite it never making a profit, but with over 45 million users. Should it be valued at purchase price or potential future value? Valuing assets Legally a business needs an independent valuation — but it can obtain several and choose the one that suits the position it wants to show. Legal, but may not be the most accurate Debt repayments A business must provide for annual leave and long service leave. Annual leave is easy to estimate. Long service leave vests after 10 years, so the business must assess the probability of employees staying that long and when they will take it — raising the ethical question of how to value that future liability 4. Financial Management Strategies Each objective has its own strategy family. This mapping is the spine of most extended-response questions. Objective Strategy family Profitability Cost controls (fixed and variable, cost centres, expense minimisation); revenue controls (marketing objectives) Liquidity Working capital management — control of current assets and current liabilities; leasing; sale and lease-back Efficiency Cash flow management — cash flow statements, distribution of payments, discounts for early payment, factoring Solvency Choosing the best source of finance for the situation (debt vs equity) 4.1 Cash Flow Management Cash flow statements record inflows and outflows. Strategies: Strategy How it works Distribution of payments Spreading payments through the month/year so large outflows do not coincide, avoiding a cash shortfall Discounts for early payment Offering customers a discount (e.g. 2/10 net 30) to pay sooner — reduces debtor days and accelerates inflow Factoring Selling accounts receivable for immediate cash (at a cost) Other ways to increase inflows : tighten credit terms, increase sales revenue, sell unused non-current assets, lease rather than purchase. Other ways to decrease outflows : negotiate longer supplier payment terms, reduce inventory (JIT), cut discretionary expenses, refinance at lower rates, delay non-essential capital expenditure. Cash flow cycle : Cash → Inventory → Production → Sales → Debtors → Cash. The longer the cycle, the more working capital is needed. Businesses aim to shorten it. 4.2 Working Capital Management Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities Control of Current Assets Asset Management focus Cash Maintain adequate levels — not so much that it sits idle, not so little that bills cannot be paid Receivables Minimise collection time; check creditworthiness; offer early payment discounts; enforce credit policies Inventories Balance too much (storage costs, obsolescence) against too little (stockouts, lost sales) Control of Current Liabilities Liability Management focus Payables Maximise payment time without damaging supplier relationships or credit terms Loans Seek the lowest-cost finance; monitor charges and interest Overdrafts Use for genuine short-term shortfalls; minimise interest paid Named Working Capital Strategies Strategy Effect Leasing Frees cash that would be tied up in purchasing assets outright; payments are tax deductible Sale and lease-back Selling an asset the business owns and leasing it straight back . Generates an immediate large cash inflow while retaining the use of the asset 4.3 Profitability Management Cost Controls Control Detail Fixed and variable costs Fixed costs do not change with output (rent, insurance, salaries). Variable costs change directly with output (raw materials, wages per unit). Managing the mix affects break-even Cost centres A cost centre is a department or area of the business to which costs can be directly attributed, so performance can be measured and controlled. Direct cost centres relate to production; indirect cost centres (HR, IT) support the whole business Expense minimisation Systematically reducing expenses — bulk buying, global sourcing, outsourcing, reducing overheads, automation Revenue Controls Setting marketing objectives and using the marketing mix to drive sales revenue: product differentiation, market development, product development, diversification, pricing strategies, improved promotion. Profit formula Profit = Total Revenue − Total Costs Profit = (Price × Quantity Sold) − (Fixed Costs + Variable Costs) To improve profit: increase revenue (price or quantity) OR decrease costs (fixed or variable). Break-Even Analysis Concept Formula Break-Even Point (units) Fixed Costs ÷ (Selling Price per unit − Variable Cost per unit) Break-Even Point ($) Break-even units × Selling Price per unit Contribution per unit Selling Price per unit − Variable Cost per unit Margin of Safety Actual (or expected) sales − Break-even sales Target Profit (units) (Fixed Costs + Target Profit) ÷ Contribution per unit Worked example A café has fixed costs of $60,000/year . Each coffee sells for $5 with a variable cost of $2 . Calculation Working Result Contribution per unit 5 − 2 $3 Break-even (units) 60,000 ÷ 3 20,000 coffees Break-even ($) 20,000 × 5 $100,000 Margin of safety (selling 25,000) 25,000 − 20,000 5,000 coffees Units for $15,000 target profit (60,000 + 15,000) ÷ 3 25,000 coffees Change Effect on Break-Even Point ↑ Selling price Decreases (fewer units needed) ↑ Variable costs Increases ↑ Fixed costs Increases ↓ Selling price Increases ↓ Variable costs Decreases ↓ Fixed costs Decreases 4.4 Global Financial Management Four additional factors/risks when operating globally: exchange rates, interest rates, methods of international payment, hedging and derivatives . Exchange Rates Exchange rate = the value of a country's money calculated using another country's money. Appreciation = the AUD rises in value against another currency. Depreciation = the AUD falls in value against another currency. Scenario Effect on the Australian business Business imports from China and the AUD depreciates against the Yuan Costs more Business has borrowed from the US and the AUD appreciates against the USD Pays less Business has lent money to a UK business and the AUD depreciates against the pound Receives less Business exports to France and the AUD appreciates against the Euro Costs the Australian business less Memory hook : A strong (appreciating) AUD makes imports cheaper and exports dearer (less competitive overseas). A weak (depreciating) AUD makes imports dearer and exports cheaper (more competitive overseas). Interest Rates It is important to find the lowest interest rates, as exchange rate fluctuations can make repayments more costly. Advantages of borrowing overseas: The interest rate can be cheaper There are fewer restrictions Finance may be acquired more quickly and easily The risk : If the AUD depreciates , the foreign loan becomes much more expensive to repay. If global interest rates rise, repayments increase beyond what was planned. Methods of International Payment Method How it works Risk Payment in advance Exporter receives payment, then sends the goods No risk for the exporter ; risk sits with the importer (goods may never arrive). Few importers accept this Letter of credit A document issued by a bank to the seller, with instructions from the buyer authorising the seller to draw a specified amount from the buyer's bank account under certain conditions. The bank ensures the exporter gets paid Existing risk for the importer Bill of exchange A written order from the seller requesting the buyer pay a specified amount at a specified time. The bank ensures the importer receives goods and the exporter is paid Existing risk for the exporter Clean payment Goods are shipped before payment is received Significant risk for the exporter — used only with trusted long-standing partners Hedging Hedging = any strategy used by a business to reduce financial risks . It is like buying insurance to protect property — protection against unforeseen risks. Businesses hedge when uncertain of the future , to reduce foreign exchange and interest rate risks. Natural hedging occurs when a business: Sets up subsidiaries in other countries and uses them to pay for expenses and goods purchased from that country Sets up bank accounts in a country where it buys or sells goods, and uses funds from that account to pay expenses in that country Derivatives A derivative is a special contract between global businesses and suppliers. Three main types: Type How it works Forward exchange contract An agreement with a FOREX business guaranteeing a certain exchange rate on a certain day Currency options contract The business has the option (no obligation) to buy or sell foreign currency when the exchange rate movement is to its advantage. Allows use of the spot rate Swap contract A written contract allowing an Australian business to pay an overseas supplier in another currency at a spot rate Spot rate = the exchange rate at a specific time on a specific day. Forward exchange contract — the trade-off: Advantage : If the spot rate turns out less favourable (e.g. the AUD has depreciated), the contracted rate is cheaper for the business. Example : contracted at AUD$1:USD$0.72, spot in 6 months is AUD$1:USD$0.63 → the contract is better. Disadvantage : If the spot rate turns out more favourable (e.g. the AUD has appreciated), the contracted rate is more expensive . Example : spot in 6 months is AUD$1:USD$0.95 → the contract is worse than the spot rate. Why choose an options contract over a forward contract? Options protect against unfavourable movements while retaining the opportunity to gain if movements are favourable — you simply don't exercise the option. The trade-off is that options cost a premium. Swap contract example : An Australian business has excess USD and needs to pay a Chinese company for materials. The Chinese company may agree to accept USD, because it can then use those USD to pay an American supplier of its own. 5. Section IV Essay Structures Assess / Evaluate (Judgement-Based) Introduction : Start with a judgement sentence → state what you are evaluating (use syllabus dot points) → include your case studies. Body Paragraph Purpose 1 Answer the question — judgement with brief overview. Define key concepts. Include case study 2 Advantages — prove they are advantages by linking to a financial objective . Use figures 3 Disadvantages — prove they are disadvantages by linking to a financial objective 4 Re-state judgement, link to long-term business goals Conclusion : 1–2 summary sentences per body paragraph, including case study. Analyse / Explain How (Cause-and-Effect) Introduction : Link two ideas (cause and effect) → state what you are analysing → include case studies. Body Paragraph Purpose 1 Cause/effect #1 — how is the business impacted, and why? Case study 2 Cause/effect #2 — same structure, linked to #1 3 Positive implications (long term) — link to strategic role and business goals 4 Negative implications — point out an issue The "Explain" Scaffold (used in class) A. Define — What is it? B. Cause/s — How does the issue impact the business? C. Effects — What does this lead to? D. Link — What does this mean for the business? Assessing Financial Performance — Ratio Scaffold Intro : Brief intro about the business; state which ratios you are analysing Current Ratio : Cause → How → Effect → Judgement (link to liquidity ) Gearing Ratio : Same structure (link to solvency ) Net Profit Ratio : Same structure (link to profitability ) Top-band tip : Integrate strategies from other topics (e.g. JIT from Operations) and link them back to the finance impact. Financial strategies scenario — PEEL example Scenario: XYZ Retail has high inventory, low cash, high receivables. P : JIT inventory management can control high inventory levels E : High inventory increases storage costs and the risk of obsolescence E : JIT reduces storage costs, minimises expenses and improves profitability. Risk: may not have enough stock to meet demand L : By reducing inventory costs, XYZ Retail maximises profit for reinvestment and business growth 6. Common Exam Pitfalls Don't just calculate — interpret. A ratio means nothing without a comment on whether it is good or bad, and why. Compare ratios over time or to industry benchmarks. Use specific numbers from the stimulus — don't be vague. Link everything back to the business in the question. Profit ≠ cash flow. A profitable business can still fail from poor liquidity. Liquidity ≠ solvency. Current ratio = short term. Gearing = long term. Break-even : check whether the question wants units or dollars . Inventory MANAGEMENT vs VALUATION : management = JIT/JIC; valuation = FIFO/LIFO. Variance : favourable on costs means spending was below budget; adverse on revenue means sales were below budget. Gearing formula : Total Liabilities ÷ Owners' Equity. 7. Glossary — Terms Students Mix Up Term Plain meaning Don't confuse with Liquidity Short-term ability to pay debts Solvency (long-term) Solvency Long-term ability to meet commitments Liquidity (short-term) Gearing / Leverage Proportion of funding from debt vs equity These two are the same thing Debenture Long-term debt sold to the public via prospectus; no security Mortgage (secured against property) Unsecured note Higher-interest bond issued by finance companies Debenture (also unsecured but company-issued) Factoring Selling receivables for immediate cash Leasing (renting an asset) Primary market New shares — company gets the money Secondary market — company gets nothing Overdraft Flexible short-term borrowing on a current account Bank loan (fixed amount and term) Operating lease Short-term; owner maintains the asset Financial lease — runs for the asset's life Appreciation Asset (or currency) rises in value Depreciation — falls in value Depreciation Systematic write-off of an asset's cost over its life Currency depreciation (AUD falling) — same word, different context Capitalising an expense Recording a cost as an asset on the Balance Sheet Expensing it immediately on the P&L Normalised earnings Earnings with one-off events removed Window dressing (deliberately misleading) Window dressing Legal techniques making the position look better Fraud (illegal) Income smoothing Shifting expenses between years to reduce tax Normalised earnings (removes one-offs for clarity) Matching principle (a) Match finance term to use; (b) match revenue to expenses in a period Two distinct meanings — read the question Hedging Any strategy to reduce financial risk Derivative — a specific type of hedging contract Spot rate Exchange rate today Forward rate — locked in for a future date Cash flow statement Record of past cash movements Cash flow budget — forecast of future cash Income statement Performance over a period Balance sheet — position at a point in time Cost centre Area of the business costs are attributed to Profit centre (also generates revenue) Merger Two businesses agree to combine Takeover — one buys the other, which ceases to exist 8. Key Definitions Quick Reference Term One-Line Definition Financial management Analysis, interpretation and evaluation of all financial records Strategic role of finance Provides a framework for all other business activities Liquidity Ability to pay current liabilities with current assets Solvency Ability to meet long-term financial commitments Profitability Ability of the business to maximise profits Efficiency Ability to manage costs and collection of money from customers Growth Ability of the business to grow and expand Owner's equity Funds contributed by owners to establish and build the business Retained profits Net profit reinvested in the business Overdraft Flexible short-notice borrowing on a current account Commercial bill Loan guaranteed by a bank, 30–180 days, usually over $100,000 Factoring Selling accounts receivable to a specialist firm for immediate cash Mortgage Long-term loan secured against land or property Debenture Long-term debt offered to the public via prospectus, no security Leasing Paying to use a non-current asset owned by another party Sale and lease-back Selling an owned asset and leasing it straight back IPO Initial public offering — shares sold publicly for the first time Rights issue Offer to existing shareholders to buy more shares Placement Additional shares offered to specific institutions/investors ASX Market operator, clearing house and payment system facilitator ASIC Enforces the Corporations Act; reduces fraud and unfair practices Monetary policy RBA use of interest rates to influence the economy Company tax Tax on company profits, paid before dividends Working capital Current Assets − Current Liabilities Cost centre Area of a business to which costs are directly attributed Break-even point Level of sales where total revenue equals total costs Normalised earnings Earnings adjusted to remove unusual or one-off influences Capitalising expenses Adding set-up costs to an asset's balance-sheet value Historical cost Recording assets at their original purchase price Depreciation Systematic write-off of an asset's cost over its useful life Matching principle Revenue matched to expenses incurred in earning it Notes to financial statements Additional detail in the appendices of annual reports Window dressing Legal techniques making the financial position look better Income smoothing Reducing net profit to reduce tax payable Audit Independent examination of financial information IFRS / AAS International / Australian accounting standards Exchange rate Value of one currency expressed in another Hedging Any strategy used to reduce financial risk Derivative A contract used to hedge — forward, option or swap Spot rate The exchange rate on a particular day Letter of credit Bank document guaranteeing payment to the exporter Bill of exchange Written order from seller requesting payment at a specified time See also: Marketing | Operations | Human Resources | Case Studies | MOC

title: Finance Syllabus Summary
text: Finance - Syllabus Summary 1. Role of Financial Management Strategic role: provide the financial framework for business activities and strategic goals Objectives: Short term: liquidity, profitability and efficiency Long term: growth and solvency Long-term goal: increase owners' wealth through sustainable profitability, growth and efficiency Interdependence: Operations needs budgets and funding; cost control and output affect profit Marketing uses finance budgets and generates sales revenue HR wages, training and rewards require budgeting and productivity review 2. Influences on Financial Management Internal finance: owner's equity and retained profits External debt finance: Short term: overdraft, commercial bill and factoring Long term: mortgage, debenture, unsecured notes/bonds and leasing External equity finance: Private equity and public share issues IPOs, rights issues, placements and share purchase plans Financial grants: government funding subject to eligibility criteria Financial institutions: banks, investment banks, finance/insurance companies, superannuation funds, unit trusts and ASX Primary market: new securities; proceeds go to the issuing business Secondary market: existing securities; proceeds go to the selling investor Government and regulation: RBA monetary policy and interest rates affect borrowing costs ASIC, Corporations Act compliance, disclosure and investor protection Company tax affects distributable and reinvested profit Interest deductibility can make debt more attractive than equity Global influences: international interest rates, availability of funds and global economic outlook Finance selection considerations: cost, term, risk, control, gearing and purpose of funds 3. Processes of Financial Management Planning and implementation: Assess project viability and future funding needs Set goals and projections for liquidity and performance Use operating, project and financial budgets Maintain accurate records, controls and independent audits Financial risk: sales shortfalls, unpaid receivables, theft and interest-rate rises Financial controls: budget variance monitoring, financial statements and ratio analysis Financing choices: debt vs equity; match the term of finance to the use of funds Cash flow statement: Opening cash balance + receipts − payments = closing cash balance Actual cash movements; distinguish from a forecast cash-flow budget Income statement: Net sales = sales − sales returns COGS = opening stock + purchases − closing stock Gross profit = net sales − COGS Net profit = gross profit − other expenses COGS is deducted once to calculate gross profit; do not subtract it again from gross profit Balance sheet: assets = liabilities + owners' equity; current and non-current categories Financial ratios: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; liquidity benchmark 2:1 Gearing = total liabilities ÷ owners' equity; course benchmark 0.5:1 to 1:1 Gross profit ratio = gross profit ÷ net sales × 100 Net profit ratio = net profit ÷ net sales × 100 Return on owners' equity = net profit ÷ owners' equity × 100 Expense ratio = total expenses ÷ net sales × 100 Accounts receivable turnover: sales ÷ accounts receivable, then 365 ÷ result; benchmark 30 days Ratio analysis: interpret results, compare across periods and against the industry benchmark; use net sales where returns are provided Limitations: normalised earnings, capitalised expenses, asset valuations, timing/cut-off, debt repayments and notes to financial statements Ethics: integrity, objectivity and confidentiality; accurate disclosure, independent audits and true-and-fair reporting Unethical practices: window dressing, income smoothing, hidden liabilities, fictitious revenue, misuse of funds and misleading asset valuations 4. Financial Management Strategies Cash flow management: Spread payments to avoid cash shortfalls Offer early-payment discounts and enforce credit terms Factor receivables; increase inflows and control discretionary outflows Shorten the cash-flow cycle Working capital management: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities Control cash, receivables and inventory Manage payables, loans and overdrafts Leasing and sale-and-lease-back to release cash Profitability management: Fixed and variable cost controls; cost centres; expense minimisation Revenue growth through marketing objectives and the marketing mix Profit = total revenue − total costs Break-even analysis: Contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit Break-even dollars = break-even units × selling price Margin of safety = actual/expected sales − break-even sales Target-profit units = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution per unit Global financial management: Manage exchange-rate and interest-rate exposure Select international payment methods: payment in advance, letter of credit, bill of exchange and clean payment Hedge risks naturally or through derivatives Forward exchange contracts lock a rate; options provide a choice; swaps enable payment in another currency See also: Finance FULL | Finance 1 Role | Finance 2 Influences | Finance 3 Processes | Finance 4 Strategies | MOC

title: Human Resources 1 · Role of Human Resource Management
text: 👥 Human Resources 1 · Role of Human Resource Management Human Resources · ① Role ← you are here · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note ✅ HSC SCOPE — everything is examinable. The trial (5 Aug 2026) excluded HR Strategies and Effectiveness Indicators. That exclusion has expired. The HSC on Monday 26 October covers the full module. Definition : Human resource management is the management of people to achieve business objectives. It is one of the four key business functions. 1. Strategic Role of Human Resources HRM aligns the workforce with the strategic direction of the business Attracts, develops and retains talented employees Creates a positive corporate culture Manages employee relations and legal compliance Employees are treated as an asset to be developed , not a cost to be minimised ⭐ Link to performance : Skilled, motivated employees → higher productivity → better operations, more effective marketing, and lower costs to finance. This is the argument to make in every extended response. 2. Interdependence with Other Key Business Functions Function Relationship with HR Operations HR recruits and trains production staff. Operations determines skill needs and staffing levels. Productivity depends on workforce quality Marketing HR recruits the marketing team. Marketing effectiveness depends on staff creativity and skills. Customer-facing staff need service training Finance Wages and training are major budget items. Finance sets salary budgets; HR must justify expenditure through productivity gains Exam tip : Always show how HR connects to the other three functions — interdependence is a guaranteed exam concept. 3. Outsourcing HR Functions Businesses increasingly outsource HR activities to external providers. Type Detail Human resource functions Recruitment, payroll, training, and specialist advice contracted to external firms Using contractors Engaging workers who are not employees . Provides flexibility and avoids on-costs Domestic contractors Located within Australia Global contractors Located overseas — lower cost, but risks in quality, communication, time zones and legal jurisdiction ⚠️ Stakeholders are not part of the Role section. The syllabus lists "stakeholders — employers, employees, employer associations, unions, government organisations, society" as the first dot point under HR key influences → Human Resources 2 Influences §1. ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Employee vs contractor An employee works under a contract of service — the business controls how, when and where, and owes leave, super and award conditions. A contractor works under a contract for service — they control their own methods, invoice for a result, and handle their own tax and insurance. Misclassifying an employee as a contractor is sham contracting and is illegal Unions vs employer associations Unions represent employees . Employer associations represent employers . Both are stakeholders, opposite sides Outsourcing vs using contractors Outsourcing hands an entire function to an external firm. Using contractors engages individual workers who are not employees 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Human resource management The management of people to achieve business objectives Contractor A worker engaged under a contract for service Sham contracting Illegally treating an employee as if they were a contractor Corporate culture The shared values, attitudes and behaviours of the organisation Outsourcing (HR) Contracting HR functions to external providers Next: ② Influences on Human Resources · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Human Resources 2 · Influences on Human Resources
text: ⚖️ Human Resources 2 · Influences on Human Resources Human Resources · ① Role · ② Influences ← you are here · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note ✅ HSC SCOPE — everything is examinable. The HSC on Monday 26 October covers the full module. 1. Stakeholders ✅ Syllabus dot point: "stakeholders — employers, employees, employer associations, unions, government organisations, society" — the first of the HR key influences. Stakeholder Interest Employers Productivity, profitability, flexibility, retaining skilled staff Employees Fair pay, safe conditions, job security, career development, work–life balance Employer associations Represent and advise employers in negotiations and disputes Unions Represent employees; negotiate pay and conditions; protect rights Government organisations Fair Work Commission, Fair Work Ombudsman, WHS regulators, Australian Human Rights Commission — set and enforce the legal framework Society Expects ethical treatment, safe workplaces, diversity, and fair employment practices Stakeholders often have conflicting interests: employers want cost flexibility, employees want security. Good HRM manages that tension — that sentence is the judgement most stakeholder questions want. 2. All Six Influences at a Glance Influence Impact Stakeholders Competing demands from employers, employees, unions, government and society shape HR policy — see §1 Legal Fair Work Act 2009, WHS Act, anti-discrimination law, awards, the NES — set minimum standards Economic In a boom : low unemployment, skills shortages, wage pressure, harder to recruit. In a downturn : higher unemployment, easier recruitment, pressure for redundancies Technological Remote work, automation of HR processes (HRIS), AI recruitment, video interviews. Changes the skills required and can displace roles Social Changing work patterns, an ageing workforce, increased workforce participation of women, greater cultural diversity, demand for work–life balance Ethics and CSR Fair pay, diversity and inclusion, bullying and harassment prevention, whistleblower protection, safe working conditions throughout the supply chain 3. The Legal Framework 3.1 The Employment Contract The employment contract is a legally binding agreement between employer and employee. It may be created through: Instrument Detail Common law contract The individual agreement between employer and employee. Both parties have common law obligations — the employer must pay wages and provide a safe workplace; the employee must obey lawful instructions and act in good faith Awards Industry- or occupation-specific minimum pay and conditions set by the Fair Work Commission. A safety net Enterprise agreements Collective agreements negotiated at the workplace between employer and employees (often with a union). Must pass the Better Off Overall Test (BOOT) — employees must be better off than under the relevant award National Employment Standards (NES) The legislated minimum entitlements that apply to all employees regardless of any award or agreement 3.2 Key Legislation Law Purpose Fair Work Act 2009 The national workplace relations system — minimum wages, the NES, unfair dismissal, enterprise bargaining, the Fair Work Commission Work Health and Safety Act Employer duty of care ; hazard identification, risk assessment and control; consultation with workers Anti-discrimination legislation Prohibits discrimination on grounds including sex, race, age, disability, marital status, religion, sexual orientation Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) Requires that employment decisions are based on merit and that barriers for disadvantaged groups are removed Employment Protection Act 1982 (NSW) Provides a minimum scale for severance payments for permanent employees under NSW awards, for employers with more than 15 employees 3.3 Work Health and Safety and Workers Compensation WHS : The employer has a duty of care to provide a safe workplace — safe equipment, training, supervision, and consultation. Workers compensation : A no-fault insurance scheme providing income and medical costs to workers injured at work. Employers must hold a policy. Cost of failure : injury, absenteeism, workers compensation premiums, legal penalties, damaged reputation, low morale. 3.4 Termination and Unfair Dismissal Type Definition Unfair dismissal Dismissal that is harsh, unjust or unreasonable — claimable through the Fair Work Commission Unlawful termination Dismissal for a prohibited reason — e.g. pregnancy, race, union membership, temporary absence due to illness Constructive dismissal The employee resigns because the employer's conduct made continued employment intolerable Summary dismissal Immediate dismissal for serious misconduct (theft, violence, fraud) Worked process — dismissing for poor performance without triggering an unfair dismissal claim An employer cannot dismiss instantly for poor performance. A documented process must be followed, and it must be written into the employment contract : Step Action 1. Verbal warning Recorded on the staff file. The employer must offer assistance and training ; all support given must be documented 2. First written warning If no improvement in the given time despite assistance, a written warning is filed. A set time to improve is given, with further support documented 3. Second written warning If still no improvement, a further written warning is issued with a final set time to improve 4. Termination If the employee has still not improved, employment can be terminated This process takes a long time and requires accurate documentation , in case the employee sues for unfair dismissal. Failing to follow it exposes the business to a claim. ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Award vs enterprise agreement An award is an industry-wide safety net set by the Fair Work Commission and applies by default. An enterprise agreement is negotiated at a specific workplace and must leave employees better off overall . Awards are the floor; agreements build above it Unfair dismissal vs unlawful termination Unfair = harsh, unjust or unreasonable . Unlawful = for a prohibited reason (pregnancy, race, union membership) Summary dismissal vs unfair dismissal Summary = immediate, for serious misconduct — and it is lawful. Unfair dismissal is the claim brought against a dismissal Constructive dismissal vs resignation Constructive = the employee resigned because the employer made staying intolerable . It counts as a dismissal EEO vs anti-discrimination law EEO requires decisions based on merit and barriers removed (proactive). Anti-discrimination law prohibits conduct (reactive) NES vs awards The NES are 11 legislated minimums for everyone . Awards are industry-specific and sit on top 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Award Industry- or occupation-specific minimum pay and conditions set by the Fair Work Commission Enterprise agreement A workplace-negotiated collective agreement that must pass the Better Off Overall Test NES The National Employment Standards — legislated minimum entitlements for all employees Common law contract The individual agreement between employer and employee Duty of care The employer's WHS obligation to provide a safe workplace EEO Employment decisions based on merit, with barriers for disadvantaged groups removed Unfair dismissal A dismissal that is harsh, unjust or unreasonable Summary dismissal Immediate dismissal for serious misconduct Next: ③ Processes of Human Resource Management · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Human Resources 3 · Processes — The HR Cycle
text: 🔄 Human Resources 3 · Processes — The HR Cycle Human Resources · ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes ← you are here · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note ✅ HSC SCOPE — everything is examinable. The HSC on Monday 26 October covers the full module. ⭐ The HR cycle is the spine of this topic. Many questions are structured around one stage. Learn the four in order. ACQUISITION → DEVELOPMENT → MAINTENANCE → SEPARATION (get them) (grow them) (keep them) (exit them) ↑ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘ (cycle repeats) 1. Acquisition The stage that involves identifying staff needs, recruitment and selection . Identifying needs : If there is a missing skill, or more work than current workers can do in a timely manner, the business may need to recruit. Once the need is established, the business must write: Document Definition Job description Describes the tasks and responsibilities of the employee Job specification Defines the skills, knowledge and abilities required for the job 1.1 Recruitment Recruitment = where the business accumulates a pool of potential candidates for a job. Method Detail Internal Moving or promoting existing people External Outsourcing to private employment agencies; interviews on university campuses; trainee positions through cadetships Internal External Advantages Cheaper, faster, motivates staff, known performance, shorter induction Fresh ideas, larger talent pool, new perspectives, brings in scarce skills Disadvantages Limited pool, creates another vacancy, risk of "inbreeding" of ideas Expensive, unknown performance, longer adjustment and induction 1.2 Selection Selection = a screening process in staff acquisition. Information gathered about applicants is reviewed and the most appropriate applicant is chosen. Information is gathered through: Interviews — one-to-one or panel Application forms Referee checks Written references Written / computer tests Case study — Apple's recruitment What Apple looks for : cross-collaboration, flexibility and adaptability to new things, problem solving and thinking outside the box, ability to keep up with a fast pace of work. Apple's selection process : typically 2–3 interviews and potentially up to 7. Candidates are observed from the start for personality and behaviour; there are introductions and small conversations, candidates are split into sections and placed in scenarios to demonstrate their responses, and asked questions throughout. 1.3 Induction Training Induction is the transition from acquisition to development in the HR cycle. It is the procedure where a new employee is introduced to the business and becomes familiar with how it works.
