What induction must include: Shown all policies and procedures Introduced to co-workers and allocated a mentor Understanding of work health and safety procedures, including emergency procedures Shown where facilities are Entitlements — how breaks work, how long and how often Why induction is necessary for all new employees, even experienced ones : Policies and procedures differ between businesses . Even an experienced worker needs to know this business's rules, be introduced to co-workers and a mentor, know what to do in an emergency, know where everything is, and understand their entitlements. It gets employees to a work-ready state faster and saves them the time of finding everything out themselves. 2. Development Businesses must develop the skills and capabilities of staff to maintain competitive advantage . Development involves preparing employees for future responsibilities due to a change in the business's strategies or growth in its size or market share. Effective development results in increased motivation , greater business flexibility , and improved use of technology and innovation . Development includes training and performance appraisals . 2.1 Training Training = any activity aimed at improving an employee's present and future performance in the workforce. Method Examples On the job Apprenticeships, mentoring, coaching, job rotation, shadowing Off the job External conferences, TAFE courses, university, workshops Benefits of training and development: For the employee For the business Enhanced skills More efficient More marketable More productive Better job satisfaction For the economy For the customer More competitive Gets a better service/product More productive On the job vs off the job: Advantages Disadvantages On the job Generally the most cost effective; employees remain productive; opportunity to learn whilst doing; training alongside real colleagues Quality depends on the trainer's ability and available time; bad habits may be passed on ; learning environment may not be conducive; potential disruption to operations Off the job A wider range of skills or qualifications can be obtained; can learn from outside specialists and experts; employees more confident when starting a job More expensive; lost working time and output; employees with new qualifications may leave for better jobs 2.2 Performance Appraisal Performance appraisal = a formal assessment of how well a person is working . It identifies: The person's strengths Areas that need further development Areas the employee would like further professional development in The professional goals of the employee This forms the basis for promotions and pay rises . Why it must be managed constructively : A poorly handled appraisal demotivates, damages trust and increases turnover. A constructive one clarifies expectations, identifies development needs and motivates. Why appraisals help employers assess HR effectiveness : Aggregated appraisal data reveals whether training is working, where skill gaps remain, and whether recruitment is selecting the right people. Other performance management methods : KPIs, 360-degree feedback (supervisor, peers, subordinates, self), balanced scorecard (financial, customer, internal processes, learning and growth). 3. Maintenance Maintenance is the stage where owners and managers ensure existing staff are: Kept motivated Remain loyal Retained Staff are maintained by providing working conditions and a work environment that motivate them to be increasingly productive and gain satisfaction from their work. 3.1 Benefits Used to Maintain Staff Type Examples Monetary benefits — paid on top of usual entitlements, forming part of the remuneration package Commission; piece rate based on output; bonuses for meeting targets; shared ownership schemes; fringe benefits (e.g. a company car) Non-monetary benefits Greater job variety; more flexible working hours; increased status in the job or community; autonomy in work; access to a subsidised cafeteria Intrinsic rewards A reward that comes from within the person — in employment, the feeling of satisfaction that comes with doing a job well 3.2 Other Maintenance Strategies Strategy Benefit to employer Benefit to employee Employee participation Better decisions, higher commitment, lower turnover Sense of ownership, voice in decisions, higher satisfaction Team work Improved problem solving, flexibility, peer support Social belonging, shared load, skill sharing Flexible working conditions Wider talent pool, reduced absenteeism, lower office costs Work–life balance, reduced stress, retention of carers Training and rewards Higher productivity, skilled workforce, competitive advantage Career progression, marketability, recognition Flexible work practices : part-time, job sharing (two employees share one full-time role), telecommuting, flextime (flexible start/finish with core hours), compressed working week (full hours in fewer days). Family-friendly programs : parental leave, carer's leave, on-site childcare, flexible hours. Likely benefits to the employer : improved retention of experienced staff, reduced absenteeism, stronger employer brand, wider recruitment pool. Workplace diversity Benefits : wider talent pool, better decision-making, improved creativity, better understanding of diverse customers, enhanced reputation Challenges : communication barriers, potential bias, differing work styles, training costs, resistance to change The cost of sexual harassment and bullying : legal liability and compensation, WHS breaches, absenteeism and stress leave, high turnover, low morale and productivity, reputational damage, difficulty recruiting. 4. Separation Separation is the ending of the employment relationship . It may be initiated by either the employee or the employer, and is either voluntary or involuntary . Type Forms Voluntary Retirement ; resignation ; voluntary redundancy — where a job is no longer required, or the firm is restructuring or has been taken over Involuntary — management decides employees are no longer required Involuntary redundancy — due to firms closing down or new technology (the Employment Protection Act 1982 (NSW) provides a minimum scale for severance payments for permanent employees under NSW awards, for employers with more than 15 employees); instant dismissal for employees who breach the law; summary dismissal for poor work performance Why involuntary separation must be managed carefully : risk of unfair dismissal claims, damage to the morale of remaining staff ("survivor syndrome"), reputational damage, loss of corporate knowledge, and legal obligations around notice, consultation and severance. Entitlements on redundancy : notice period (or payment in lieu), redundancy/severance pay based on years of service, accrued annual leave, accrued long service leave where applicable. Role of the Fair Work Commission in unfair dismissal : receives and conciliates claims, determines whether the dismissal was harsh, unjust or unreasonable, and can order reinstatement or compensation . Case study — NAB NAB announced plans to downsize its workforce by 12% to cut operating costs as more processes became automated. The bank planned to shed 6,000 roles while adding 2,000 technology jobs over three years, including specialists in software engineering, data and security. Hiring more tech professionals brings its own challenge because they are highly sought after . Use this for : technology as an influence on HR; involuntary redundancy; the changing nature of skills; the tension between cost control (finance) and workforce capability (HR). ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Job description vs job specification Description describes the JOB . Specification specifies the PERSON . Mnemonic: de S cription = the po S ition; spec ification = the spec ial qualities of the person Recruitment vs selection Recruitment accumulates the pool . Selection chooses from it Induction vs training Induction introduces them to this business . Training improves job performance Training vs development Training is about now (current role). Development is about next (future responsibilities) Maintenance vs development Maintenance keeps them. Development grows them Redundancy vs dismissal Redundancy = the JOB no longer exists (restructuring, technology, closure) — not about performance, and it attracts severance pay. Dismissal = the PERSON is removed (misconduct or poor performance); the job usually still exists Monetary / non-monetary / intrinsic Monetary = money or money's worth, paid by the business. Non-monetary = a benefit that isn't cash. Intrinsic = comes from inside the person — the business can create conditions for it but cannot hand it over Piece rate vs commission Piece rate is based on output produced . Commission is based on sales made Voluntary vs involuntary separation Voluntary = the employee chose . Involuntary = management decided . Note redundancy can be either 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition HR cycle Acquisition → Development → Maintenance → Separation Acquisition Identifying staff needs, recruitment and selection Job description A document describing the tasks and responsibilities of the employee Job specification A document defining the skills, knowledge and abilities required for the job Recruitment Accumulating a pool of potential candidates for a job Selection A screening process in which the most appropriate applicant is chosen Induction The procedure introducing a new employee to the business and how it works Training Any activity aimed at improving an employee's present and future performance Development Preparing employees for future responsibilities Performance appraisal A formal assessment of how well a person is working Maintenance Keeping existing staff motivated, loyal and retained Intrinsic reward A reward that comes from within the person Separation The ending of the employment relationship Redundancy Where a job is no longer required by the business Next: ④ Human Resource Strategies · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Human Resources 4 · Strategies and Effectiveness Indicators
text: 🎯 Human Resources 4 · Strategies and Effectiveness Indicators Human Resources · ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies ← you are here · 📕 Full note ✅ HSC SCOPE — everything is examinable. The trial (5 Aug 2026) excluded HR Strategies and Effectiveness Indicators. That exclusion has expired. The HSC on Monday 26 October covers the full module. This file was rewritten from the three teacher documents added 2 September 2026 : Document Feeds HR Strategies — Leadership Style, Job Design, Recruitment §1–3 HR Strategies — Training and Development, Performance Management, Workplace Disputes and Global HR §4–8 Strategies and Indicators Summary §11.2 — the strategy → indicator map ⚠️ Your teacher defines administrative vs developmental performance management differently from the standard textbook. See §5. Use your teacher's version. 1. Leadership Style Leadership style is the manner and approach in which leaders of a business interact with staff. Leaders make decisions, develop strategies for the development of the business, and interact with employees. Built on three factors: 1. Providing staff with DIRECTION 2. Implementing plans and ORGANISING staff 3. MOTIVATING staff The eight styles: Style How it works Key feature Authoritarian (transactional / autocratic) Managers are responsible for telling employees what they want done and how to accomplish the task Employees cannot contribute to decision-making · decisions made quickly Participative / democratic The leader includes one or more employees in the decision-making process Employees consulted on what to do and how ; encouraged to become empowered . The final decision is still the leader's Delegative / laissez-faire The leader allows employees to make decisions Requires employees with the relevant knowledge and skills , and a manager who trusts their ability Pacesetting The leader sets an example of high performance, high pace and high quality; the team is expected to follow Values results above all. Good for short-term results, but detrimental to engagement and motivation long term Affiliative Puts people first — creating a harmonious environment and building emotional bonds Requires empathy and the ability to build relationships across communication styles Coaching Characterised by collaboration, support and guidance Focused on bringing out the best in the team by guiding them through goals and obstacles Coercive A command and control style Relies on forcing people to do what they are told, whether they want it or not Transformational Works with followers beyond their immediate self-interest to identify needed change Creates a vision , guides change through influence and inspiration , and executes it alongside committed members 2. Job Design Job design is where managers develop and specify the work activities of individuals or groups. It is the process of determining the types of tasks an employee needs to complete, and of identifying the skills, knowledge, personal traits, duties and responsibilities required to perform a position. Effective job design seeks to meet the needs of both the business and the employee — the task must allow the employee to work toward the objectives. Job design involves: Creating a job description Personal specifications Strategies that improve employee motivation and productivity Concept Definition Job satisfaction The extent to which employees are satisfied working in their current position Job enrichment The extent a business develops tasks with the abilities of existing staff in mind — reducing the boredom associated with many types of work The six job design strategies: 1. Job rotation 4. Semi-autonomous work groups 2. Job enlargement 5. Team structures 3. Job enrichment 6. Flexible work structures General vs specific job design: general design gives employees a variety of tasks, increasing motivation and flexibility. Specific design gives a narrow, repetitive set, increasing efficiency and speed but risking boredom and turnover — which is why specialised job design often reduces job satisfaction . 3. Recruitment An effective recruitment strategy ensures the right people are hired to do the right job. The seven consequences of a poor selection process: 1. Increased training costs 2. Increased job dissatisfaction 3. Lower performance 4. Increased labour turnover 5. Increased absenteeism, if the staff member feels inadequate for the job 6. Increased accidents / defect rates 7. Increased claims of discrimination ⭐ That list is the answer to "What is the likely outcome of a poor recruitment decision?" and to "How does selecting the wrong employee increase costs and reduce productivity?" Internal vs external: the choice depends on the type of skills and qualifications needed , whether current staff already have them, and whether recruiting is cheaper than training an existing employee . General skills Specific skills What Skills, attitudes and behaviours that are a good cultural fit Skills required for particular jobs Includes Flexibility and versatility · social confidence · positive attitude · motivation · ability to work in a team or independently · leadership and decision-making · willingness to learn · ability to work under pressure Technical and role-specific capability Why businesses target them Cultural fit and adaptability Skill shortages — filling identified gaps 4. Training and Development Crucial to ensuring staff stay motivated, performance goals are met, the possibility of accidents decreases, skill shortages are filled, and staff retention increases. When deciding between developing staff and recruiting, a business considers: Option Invest further in in-house training and development Retain experts who retire , on a part-time basis Recruit staff for specific skills Retain women through flexible work structures Share staff with other firms Outsource functions to specialist firms Sponsor overseas migrants Build networks or alliances with firms holding specialist skills 5. Performance Management The process of recognising the efforts and contributions of employees to their work. It is an ongoing process of communication between the direct manager and the employee. It involves: 1. Clarification of expectations 2. Setting employee workplace objectives 3. Providing feedback 4. Evaluating employee performance The three stages of the cycle: Stage What happens 1. Planning Expectations and goals developed by both the employer and the employee 2. Checking in Managers regularly observe performance to provide feedback 3. Assessment Measuring performance against the objectives Why it is ongoing: after assessment, new goals are established, beginning the cycle again. Performance needs to be continuously monitored, reviewed and improved. The four benefits: The employee has an improved understanding of their role and what needs to be done The employer can identify problems earlier Reviews make the employee aware of their personal goals Identifies areas of development either needed or requested by the employee ⚠️ 5.1 Administrative vs Developmental — use your teacher's definition Administrative Developmental Your teacher's document HR completes skills audits of all staff and identifies training needs . Assists with HR planning . Information kept in an employee database HR plans and implements training for staff — both on the job and off the job The generic textbook version Evaluating output to decide pay, promotion, retention, termination Feedback used to build skills Use your teacher's version. It's what your school marks against, and it also fits the exam answers better — the Knox trial's Q10 (a business keeping data on time spent online, meetings and client feedback) is administrative precisely because it is data collection for HR planning. The tell: administrative records and audits ; developmental plans and delivers . 6. Rewards Used to motivate employees and encourage them to work together as a team to achieve common goals. Two axes: MONETARY or NON-MONETARY INDIVIDUAL or GROUP Designing a reward program — for the business: Consideration Business strategy Economic conditions Organisational objectives of rewards Rewards and benefits offered by competitors Relevant awards and agreements , minimum employment standards Union power Profitability / viability of the business Designing a reward program — for the individual (often called performance pay : remuneration distributed according to individual employee performance) Basis What it covers Performance related Incentive plans for performance above standards or criteria , bonuses, production-related criteria Job related Role and level of responsibility , scope of supervision, base pay, interpersonal skills, knowledge and skills, experience, value to company Other Group incentives Individual or team performance pay? Both, depending on the nature of the work. Team-based pay encourages cooperation and communication toward common objectives; individual pay recognises outstanding contribution. Using both prevents excessive competition while still rewarding individual effort. Why provide both monetary and non-monetary rewards? Because employees are motivated by different factors. Monetary rewards — bonuses, commissions, pay increases — provide financial motivation. Non-monetary rewards — recognition, promotion, flexible working, career development — improve job satisfaction and loyalty . McDonald's provides rewards and recognition programs, discounted meals and retail discounts, plus flexible working and career development opportunities. 7. Global HR Strategies Globalisation, technological development and HR applications have increased the complexity of managing HR. High labour costs and skill shortages in Australia have led businesses to operate globally. Seven factors to consider before outsourcing globally: 1. Labour costs 5. Political stability 2. Service / product quality 6. Language and cultural differences 3. Infrastructure requirements 7. Skills and supply of labour overseas 4. Overseas labour market regulations The China example: countries such as China have factories producing goods at a competitive price, so Australian companies have moved production there because it is cheaper. Impact ✅ Reduced costs for the business ❌ Loss of jobs and factory closures in Australia Australia's skills shortage is major and will increase. Two strategies used to overcome it: The Temporary Skills Shortage Visa , allowing businesses to bring people from overseas to fill the shortage Outsourcing functions overseas to access people with those skills 8. Workplace Disputes Disputes occur between employers and employees where their interests are in conflict. Every business should have a grievance procedure to guide employees, employers and unions in resolving one. A grievance procedure policy: Provides a clear outline of the issues Illustrates the correct and appropriate processes when raising a complaint Provides a mechanism for quick resolution The four resolution steps, in order: # Method Who decides 1 Negotiation — discussion between both parties to resolve the dispute. Unions and employer associations may be involved The parties 2 Mediation — an independent party with no ties to either side assists the parties to reach a settlement The parties 3 Conciliation — Fair Work Australia acts as a mediator and offers suggestions to resolve the problem The parties 4 Arbitration — the final stage. A commissioner hears both cases and makes a decision that is legally binding on both parties The commissioner Overt vs covert industrial action: overt action is visible and deliberate — strikes, work bans, work-to-rule (refusing tasks outside normal duties), lockouts, picket lines. Covert action is concealed — absenteeism , high turnover, sabotage, deliberate under-performance. Absenteeism appearing as an indicator in §11 and as covert action here is the same phenomenon read two ways. 9. Organisational Structures 📎 Not a syllabus dot point. Organisational structure is Preliminary (Year 11) content. Useful background for leadership and job design answers, but don't spend HSC revision time here — §1–§8 and §11 are what's examined. Structure Description Pros Cons Flat Few management layers, wide span of control Faster communication, empowerment Manager overload, unclear reporting Tall Many management layers, narrow span of control Clear career path, close supervision Slow communication, bureaucracy Centralised Decisions made at the top Consistency, control Slow response, disempowerment Decentralised Decisions pushed to lower levels Faster response, empowerment Inconsistency, coordination challenges Functional Grouped by function Specialisation, efficiency Silos, poor cross-functional communication Matrix Dual reporting (function + project) Flexible, cross-functional Conflicting priorities, complex reporting Span of control = the number of employees a manager directly supervises. Flat structures have a wide span; tall structures a narrow one. 10. Motivation Theories 📎 Not syllabus dot points. Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor and Locke & Latham do not appear anywhere in the HSC Business Studies syllabus. They are textbook extension. Worth knowing anyway , because they explain why rewards and job design work — a sentence of Herzberg inside a rewards answer reads as sophistication. But learn them last , after §1–§8 and §11. 10.1 Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs Self-Actualisation (reach full potential) ──────────────────── Esteem Needs (recognition, status) ──────────────────── Social/Belonging Needs (teamwork, friendship) ──────────────────── Safety Needs (job security, safe workplace) ──────────────────── Physiological Needs (salary, basic conditions) Application : Lower-level needs must be met before higher-level rewards will motivate. Pay and safety first, then belonging, then recognition, then growth opportunities. 10.2 Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory Factor Description Examples Hygiene factors Cause dissatisfaction if absent, but do not motivate when present Salary, working conditions, job security, company policy, supervision Motivators Actually motivate and satisfy Achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement, personal growth Application : Fix hygiene factors to prevent dissatisfaction, then use motivators to engage employees. Raising pay alone removes dissatisfaction but does not create motivation. 10.3 McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y Theory X (authoritarian) Theory Y (participative) Workers are lazy and avoid work Workers are self-motivated and enjoy work Need close supervision and control Need autonomy and responsibility Motivated by punishment and reward Motivated by intrinsic factors Management style: command and control Management style: empowerment and trust 10.4 Locke and Latham's Goal Setting Theory Motivation increases when goals are specific , challenging but achievable , accepted by the employee , and accompanied by feedback on progress. 11. Effectiveness Indicators of Human Resource Management ✅ This is its own syllabus heading — a FIFTH section, not part of strategies. The HR topic runs: role → key influences → processes → strategies → effectiveness of human resource management . It's kept in this file because §11.2 maps each strategy to the indicators that measure it, and you can't evaluate a strategy without them. The syllabus lists exactly seven indicators: corporate culture, benchmarking key variables, changes in staff turnover, absenteeism, accidents, levels of disputation, worker satisfaction. An effective HR function is one where management and employees work well together in their efforts to achieve the goals of the business. The effectiveness of that relationship is examined through seven indicators. 11.1 The Seven Indicators Indicator Definition What a poor result signals Corporate culture The culture within an organisation — the values and beliefs within a business. An effective culture is one that is believed, demonstrated and acted upon by both management and employees A positive culture produces happier workers → lower turnover, higher productivity, better customer service, lower absenteeism. A negative culture produces less satisfied workers Benchmarking key variables The process of measuring an employee's performance against established standards If employees repeatedly fail to meet performance goals, management must examine why. Employees are more likely to meet goals where there are effective appraisal systems, training and development, and reward systems Changes in staff turnover The rate at which employees leave a business A high level caused by voluntary separation — mainly resignations — indicates poor employment relations Absenteeism Employees being unable to attend work for reasons such as illness or family responsibilities Costly, because the work isn't done — it places additional demands on remaining staff and can cause greater hostility . A sharp rise over a short period signals unhappy, unsatisfied workers Level of disputation The number and severity of disputes in a workplace The more disputes, the less effective management is at the employment relations function. Employers must examine why and rectify the practices causing them Accidents The number of accidents per year Increases may be due to lack of training , or poor workplace health and safety procedures and policies Worker satisfaction Whether employees are happy and contented and fulfilling their desires and needs at work Satisfied employees work more efficiently and value the organisation they work for Turnover isn't automatically bad — some brings in fresh skills and removes poor performers. What matters is who is leaving, and whether the separation was voluntary . Losing high performers voluntarily is the warning sign. 11.2 Which Indicator Measures Which Strategy ⭐ Straight from your teacher's Strategies and Indicators Summary . This is the table that answers "evaluate the effectiveness of [strategy]" — it tells you which evidence to cite. Strategy Indicators used to measure it Leadership style Corporate culture · Benchmarks · Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Worker satisfaction Job design Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Number of accidents · Worker satisfaction Recruitment Corporate culture · Benchmarks · Staff turnover · Absenteeism Training and development Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Number of accidents · Corporate culture · Worker satisfaction Performance management Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Number of accidents · Worker satisfaction Rewards Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Number of accidents · Worker satisfaction Workplace disputes Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Worker satisfaction The patterns worth noticing: Staff turnover and absenteeism measure everything. If you can only remember two, remember these — they appear against all seven strategies. Accidents attach to the strategies that change how work is done — job design, training, performance management, rewards. Not to recruitment or leadership. Corporate culture and benchmarks attach to the strategies that shape who is in the business and how they are led — leadership, recruitment, training. Workplace disputes is the narrowest — three indicators, and notably not accidents or benchmarks. How to use it in an answer: "The effectiveness of the training and development strategy can be measured through changes in staff turnover and the number of accidents . A reduction in both would indicate the strategy has improved employee capability and workplace safety…" ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Authoritarian vs coercive Authoritarian = the leader decides and directs ; employees don't participate but aren't compelled. Coercive = the leader forces compliance , "whether they want it or not." Autocratic is about who decides ; coercive is about how compliance is obtained Pacesetting vs transformational Pacesetting models high performance and expects imitation — values results more than anything , and burns people out. Transformational creates a shared vision . One drives through people, the other with them Rotation vs enlargement vs enrichment Rotation = moving between jobs (variety across time). Enlargement = more tasks at the same level (horizontal). Enrichment = more responsibility and autonomy (vertical). Rotation changes where , enlargement how many , enrichment how demanding Training vs development Training = perform the current role better. Development = prepare for future responsibilities. Now vs next Administrative vs developmental performance management Teacher's version : administrative records and audits (skills audits, employee database). Developmental plans and delivers training Mediation / conciliation / arbitration Mediation — the third party facilitates only , no suggestions. Conciliation — the third party suggests solutions ; the parties still decide. Arbitration — the third party imposes a binding decision . Escalating: facilitates → suggests → decides Overt vs covert industrial action Overt = visible (strikes, bans, lockouts, pickets). Covert = concealed (absenteeism, turnover, sabotage, deliberate under-performance) Strike vs lockout Strike = employees stop work. Lockout = employer shuts them out Hygiene factors vs motivators Hygiene prevents dissatisfaction but doesn't motivate. Motivators actively create satisfaction Turnover vs absenteeism Turnover = the rate staff leave and are replaced . Absenteeism = unplanned days off Flat vs tall structure Flat = few layers, wide span of control. Tall = many layers, narrow span 📝 Exam habits Don't just list strategies — link each to an effectiveness indicator. The difference between a mid-band and top-band HR answer is almost always §11. Quantify where you can: "staff turnover fell from 22% to 14%." 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Leadership style The manner and approach in which leaders of a business interact with staff Job design The process by which managers develop and specify the work activities of individuals or groups Job satisfaction The extent to which employees are satisfied working in their current position Job enrichment Developing tasks with the abilities of existing staff in mind, reducing boredom Performance management The ongoing process of recognising the efforts and contributions of employees to their work Performance pay Remuneration distributed according to individual employee performance Grievance procedure A policy guiding employees, employers and unions in resolving a dispute Mediation A third party facilitates discussion without imposing a decision Conciliation A third party suggests solutions; the parties decide Arbitration A third party imposes a binding decision Span of control The number of employees a manager directly supervises Benchmarking The process of measuring an employee's performance against established standards Staff turnover The rate at which employees leave a business Absenteeism Employees being unable to attend work Back to: ① Role · 📕 Full note · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · MOC

title: Human Resources — Full Module Note
text: 📕 Human Resources — Full Module Note The whole module in one file. Split versions: ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies ✅ HSC SCOPE — everything is examinable. The trial (5 Aug 2026) excluded HR Strategies and Effectiveness Indicators. That exclusion has expired. The HSC on Monday 26 October covers the full module. §4 and §6 are now back in scope , and both were rewritten from the three teacher documents added on 2 September: Document Feeds HR Strategies — Leadership Style, Job Design, Recruitment §4.1–4.3 HR Strategies — Training and Development, Performance Management, Workplace Disputes and Global HR §4.4–4.8 Strategies and Indicators Summary §6.2 — the strategy → indicator map ⚠️ Your teacher defines administrative vs developmental performance management differently from the standard textbook. See §4.5. Use your teacher's version — see Confusing Pairs . 🔧 Maintenance note: sections 1–6 below are mirrored in the four split files. If one is corrected, correct both. Sections 7–10 exist only here. 1. Role of Human Resource Management Definition : Human resource management is the management of people to achieve business objectives. It is one of the four key business functions. 1.1 Strategic Role of Human Resources HRM aligns the workforce with the strategic direction of the business Attracts, develops and retains talented employees Creates a positive corporate culture Manages employee relations and legal compliance Employees are treated as an asset to be developed , not a cost to be minimised Link to performance : Skilled, motivated employees → higher productivity → better operations, more effective marketing, and lower costs to finance. This is the argument to make in every extended response. 1.2 Interdependence with Other Key Business Functions Function Relationship with HR Operations HR recruits and trains production staff. Operations determines skill needs and staffing levels. Productivity depends on workforce quality Marketing HR recruits the marketing team. Marketing effectiveness depends on staff creativity and skills. Customer-facing staff need service training Finance Wages and training are major budget items. Finance sets salary budgets; HR must justify expenditure through productivity gains Exam tip : Always show how HR connects to the other three functions — interdependence is a guaranteed exam concept. 1.3 Outsourcing HR Functions Businesses increasingly outsource HR activities to external providers. Type Detail Human resource functions Recruitment, payroll, training, and specialist advice contracted to external firms Using contractors Engaging workers who are not employees . Provides flexibility and avoids on-costs Domestic contractors Located within Australia Global contractors Located overseas — lower cost, but risks in quality, communication, time zones and legal jurisdiction Confusing pair — Employee vs Contractor An employee works under a contract of service — the business controls how, when and where they work, and owes them leave, superannuation and award conditions. A contractor works under a contract for service — they control their own methods, invoice for a result, and are responsible for their own tax and insurance. Misclassifying an employee as a contractor (" sham contracting ") is illegal. 1.4 Stakeholders in Human Resources ⚠️ Syllabus placement: stakeholders are the first dot point under HR key influences (§2), not under the role of HRM. Grouped here for teaching; answer stakeholder questions as an influence . Stakeholder Interest Employers Productivity, profitability, flexibility, retaining skilled staff Employees Fair pay, safe conditions, job security, career development, work–life balance Employer associations Represent and advise employers in negotiations and disputes Unions Represent employees; negotiate pay and conditions; protect rights Government organisations Fair Work Commission, Fair Work Ombudsman, WHS regulators, Australian Human Rights Commission — set and enforce the legal framework Society Expects ethical treatment, safe workplaces, diversity, and fair employment practices Stakeholders often have conflicting interests: employers want cost flexibility, employees want security. Good HRM manages that tension. 2. Influences on Human Resources Influence Impact Stakeholders Competing demands from employers, employees, unions, government and society shape HR policy Legal Fair Work Act 2009, WHS Act, anti-discrimination law, awards, the NES — set minimum standards Economic In a boom : low unemployment, skills shortages, wage pressure, harder to recruit. In a downturn : higher unemployment, easier recruitment, pressure for redundancies Technological Remote work, automation of HR processes (HRIS), AI recruitment, video interviews. Changes the skills required and can displace roles Social Changing work patterns, an ageing workforce, increased workforce participation of women, greater cultural diversity, demand for work–life balance Ethics and CSR Fair pay, diversity and inclusion, bullying and harassment prevention, whistleblower protection, safe working conditions throughout the supply chain 2.1 The Legal Framework The Employment Contract The employment contract is a legally binding agreement between employer and employee. It may be created through: Instrument Detail Common law contract The individual agreement between employer and employee. Both parties have common law obligations — the employer must pay wages and provide a safe workplace; the employee must obey lawful instructions and act in good faith Awards Industry- or occupation-specific minimum pay and conditions set by the Fair Work Commission. A safety net Enterprise agreements Collective agreements negotiated at the workplace between employer and employees (often with a union). Must pass the Better Off Overall Test (BOOT) — employees must be better off than under the relevant award National Employment Standards (NES) The legislated minimum entitlements that apply to all employees regardless of any award or agreement Confusing pair — Award vs Enterprise Agreement An award is an industry-wide safety net set by the Fair Work Commission — it applies by default. An enterprise agreement is negotiated at a specific workplace and must leave employees better off overall than the award. Awards are the floor; agreements build above it. Key Legislation Law Purpose Fair Work Act 2009 The national workplace relations system — minimum wages, the NES, unfair dismissal, enterprise bargaining, the Fair Work Commission Work Health and Safety Act Employer duty of care ; hazard identification, risk assessment and control; consultation with workers Anti-discrimination legislation Prohibits discrimination on grounds including sex, race, age, disability, marital status, religion, sexual orientation Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) Requires that employment decisions are based on merit and that barriers for disadvantaged groups are removed Employment Protection Act 1982 (NSW) Provides a minimum scale for severance payments for permanent employees under NSW awards, for employers with more than 15 employees Work Health and Safety and Workers Compensation WHS : The employer has a duty of care to provide a safe workplace — safe equipment, training, supervision, and consultation. Workers compensation : A no-fault insurance scheme providing income and medical costs to workers injured at work. Employers must hold a policy. Cost of failure : injury, absenteeism, workers compensation premiums, legal penalties, damaged reputation, low morale. Termination and Unfair Dismissal Type Definition Unfair dismissal Dismissal that is harsh, unjust or unreasonable — claimable through the Fair Work Commission Unlawful termination Dismissal for a prohibited reason — e.g. pregnancy, race, union membership, temporary absence due to illness Constructive dismissal The employee resigns because the employer's conduct made continued employment intolerable Summary dismissal Immediate dismissal for serious misconduct (theft, violence, fraud) Worked process — dismissing for poor performance without triggering an unfair dismissal claim An employer cannot dismiss instantly for poor performance. A documented process must be followed, and it must be written into the employment contract : Step Action 1. Verbal warning Recorded on the staff file. The employer must offer assistance and training ; all support given must be documented 2. First written warning If no improvement in the given time despite assistance, a written warning is filed. A set time to improve is given, with further support documented 3. Second written warning If still no improvement, a further written warning is issued with a final set time to improve 4. Termination If the employee has still not improved, employment can be terminated This process takes a long time and requires accurate documentation , in case the employee sues for unfair dismissal. Failing to follow it exposes the business to a claim. 3. Processes of Human Resource Management — The HR Cycle The HR cycle is the spine of this topic. Four stages, in order: ACQUISITION → DEVELOPMENT → MAINTENANCE → SEPARATION (get them) (grow them) (keep them) (exit them) ↑ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘ (cycle repeats) 3.1 Acquisition The stage that involves identifying staff needs, recruitment and selection . Identifying needs : If there is a missing skill, or more work than current workers can do in a timely manner, the business may need to recruit. Once the need is established, the business must write: Document Definition Job description Describes the tasks and responsibilities of the employee Job specification Defines the skills, knowledge and abilities required for the job Confusing pair — Job description vs Job specification Description describes the JOB (what the role does). Specification specifies the PERSON (what they need to have). Mnemonic: de S cription = the po S ition; spec ification = the spec ial qualities of the person. Recruitment Recruitment = where the business accumulates a pool of potential candidates for a job. Method Detail Internal Moving or promoting existing people External Outsourcing to private employment agencies; interviews on university campuses; trainee positions through cadetships Internal External Advantages Cheaper, faster, motivates staff, known performance, shorter induction Fresh ideas, larger talent pool, new perspectives, brings in scarce skills Disadvantages Limited pool, creates another vacancy, risk of "inbreeding" of ideas Expensive, unknown performance, longer adjustment and induction Selection Selection = a screening process in staff acquisition. Information gathered about applicants is reviewed and the most appropriate applicant is chosen. Information is gathered through: Interviews — one-to-one or panel Application forms Referee checks Written references Written / computer tests Case study — Apple's recruitment What Apple looks for : cross-collaboration, flexibility and adaptability to new things, problem solving and thinking outside the box, ability to keep up with a fast pace of work. Apple's selection process : typically 2–3 interviews and potentially up to 7. Candidates are observed from the start for personality and behaviour; there are introductions and small conversations, candidates are split into sections and placed in scenarios to demonstrate their responses, and asked questions throughout. Induction Training Induction is the transition from acquisition to development in the HR cycle. It is the procedure where a new employee is introduced to the business and becomes familiar with how it works. What induction must include: Shown all policies and procedures Introduced to co-workers and allocated a mentor Understanding of work health and safety procedures, including emergency procedures Shown where facilities are Entitlements — how breaks work, how long and how often Why induction is necessary for all new employees, even experienced ones : Policies and procedures differ between businesses . Even an experienced worker needs to know this business's rules, be introduced to co-workers and a mentor, know what to do in an emergency, know where everything is, and understand their entitlements. It gets employees to a work-ready state faster and saves them the time of finding everything out themselves. 3.2 Development Businesses must develop the skills and capabilities of staff to maintain competitive advantage . Development involves preparing employees for future responsibilities due to a change in the business's strategies or growth in its size or market share. Effective development results in increased motivation , greater business flexibility , and improved use of technology and innovation . Development includes training and performance appraisals . Training Training = any activity aimed at improving an employee's present and future performance in the workforce. Method Examples On the job Apprenticeships, mentoring, coaching, job rotation, shadowing Off the job External conferences, TAFE courses, university, workshops Benefits of training and development: For the employee For the business Enhanced skills More efficient More marketable More productive Better job satisfaction For the economy For the customer More competitive Gets a better service/product More productive On the job vs off the job: Advantages Disadvantages On the job Generally the most cost effective; employees remain productive; opportunity to learn whilst doing; training alongside real colleagues Quality depends on the trainer's ability and available time; bad habits may be passed on ; learning environment may not be conducive; potential disruption to operations Off the job A wider range of skills or qualifications can be obtained; can learn from outside specialists and experts; employees more confident when starting a job More expensive; lost working time and output; employees with new qualifications may leave for better jobs Performance Appraisal Performance appraisal = a formal assessment of how well a person is working . It identifies: The person's strengths Areas that need further development Areas the employee would like further professional development in The professional goals of the employee This forms the basis for promotions and pay rises . Why it must be managed constructively : A poorly handled appraisal demotivates, damages trust and increases turnover. A constructive one clarifies expectations, identifies development needs and motivates. Why appraisals help employers assess HR effectiveness : Aggregated appraisal data reveals whether training is working, where skill gaps remain, and whether recruitment is selecting the right people. Other performance management methods : KPIs, 360-degree feedback (supervisor, peers, subordinates, self), balanced scorecard (financial, customer, internal processes, learning and growth). 3.3 Maintenance Maintenance is the stage where owners and managers ensure existing staff are: Kept motivated Remain loyal Retained Staff are maintained by providing working conditions and a work environment that motivate them to be increasingly productive and gain satisfaction from their work. Benefits Used to Maintain Staff Type Examples Monetary benefits — paid on top of usual entitlements, forming part of the remuneration package Commission; piece rate based on output; bonuses for meeting targets; shared ownership schemes; fringe benefits (e.g. a company car) Non-monetary benefits Greater job variety; more flexible working hours; increased status in the job or community; autonomy in work; access to a subsidised cafeteria Intrinsic rewards A reward that comes from within the person — in employment, the feeling of satisfaction that comes with doing a job well Confusing trio — Monetary / Non-monetary / Intrinsic Monetary = money or money's worth, paid by the business. Non-monetary = a benefit the business provides that isn't cash. Intrinsic = comes from inside the person — the business can create conditions for it but cannot hand it over. Other Maintenance Strategies Strategy Benefit to employer Benefit to employee Employee participation Better decisions, higher commitment, lower turnover Sense of ownership, voice in decisions, higher satisfaction Team work Improved problem solving, flexibility, peer support Social belonging, shared load, skill sharing Flexible working conditions Wider talent pool, reduced absenteeism, lower office costs Work–life balance, reduced stress, retention of carers Training and rewards Higher productivity, skilled workforce, competitive advantage Career progression, marketability, recognition Flexible work practices : part-time, job sharing (two employees share one full-time role), telecommuting, flextime (flexible start/finish with core hours), compressed working week (full hours in fewer days). Family-friendly programs : parental leave, carer's leave, on-site childcare, flexible hours. Likely benefits to the employer : improved retention of experienced staff, reduced absenteeism, stronger employer brand, wider recruitment pool. Workplace diversity Benefits : wider talent pool, better decision-making, improved creativity, better understanding of diverse customers, enhanced reputation Challenges : communication barriers, potential bias, differing work styles, training costs, resistance to change The cost of sexual harassment and bullying : legal liability and compensation, WHS breaches, absenteeism and stress leave, high turnover, low morale and productivity, reputational damage, difficulty recruiting. 3.4 Separation Separation is the ending of the employment relationship . It may be initiated by either the employee or the employer, and is either voluntary or involuntary . Type Forms Voluntary Retirement ; resignation ; voluntary redundancy — where a job is no longer required, or the firm is restructuring or has been taken over Involuntary — management decides employees are no longer required Involuntary redundancy — due to firms closing down or new technology (the Employment Protection Act 1982 (NSW) provides a minimum scale for severance payments for permanent employees under NSW awards, for employers with more than 15 employees); instant dismissal for employees who breach the law; summary dismissal for poor work performance Confusing pair — Redundancy vs Dismissal Redundancy = the JOB no longer exists (restructuring, technology, closure). It is not about the person's performance. Dismissal = the PERSON is removed (misconduct or poor performance). The job usually still exists. This distinction matters legally: redundancy attracts severance pay; dismissal for misconduct generally does not. Why involuntary separation must be managed carefully : risk of unfair dismissal claims, damage to the morale of remaining staff ("survivor syndrome"), reputational damage, loss of corporate knowledge, and legal obligations around notice, consultation and severance. Entitlements on redundancy : notice period (or payment in lieu), redundancy/severance pay based on years of service, accrued annual leave, accrued long service leave where applicable. Role of the Fair Work Commission in unfair dismissal : receives and conciliates claims, determines whether the dismissal was harsh, unjust or unreasonable, and can order reinstatement or compensation . Case study — NAB NAB announced plans to downsize its workforce by 12% to cut operating costs as more processes became automated. The bank planned to shed 6,000 roles while adding 2,000 technology jobs over three years, including specialists in software engineering, data and security. Hiring more tech professionals brings its own challenge because they are highly sought after . Use this for : technology as an influence on HR; involuntary redundancy; the changing nature of skills; the tension between cost control (finance) and workforce capability (HR). 4. Human Resource Strategies Rewritten from your teacher's two HR Strategies documents (2 Sept 2026). Each strategy is paired with the indicators that measure it in §6.2 . 4.1 Leadership Style Leadership style is the manner and approach in which leaders of a business interact with staff. Leaders make decisions, develop strategies for the development of the business, and interact with employees. Built on three factors: 1. Providing staff with DIRECTION 2. Implementing plans and ORGANISING staff 3. MOTIVATING staff The eight styles: Style How it works Key feature Authoritarian (transactional / autocratic) Managers are responsible for telling employees what they want done and how to accomplish the task Employees cannot contribute to decision-making · decisions made quickly Participative / democratic The leader includes one or more employees in the decision-making process Employees consulted on what to do and how ; encouraged to become empowered . The final decision is still the leader's Delegative / laissez-faire The leader allows employees to make decisions Requires employees with the relevant knowledge and skills , and a manager who trusts their ability Pacesetting The leader sets an example of high performance, high pace and high quality; the team is expected to follow Values results above all. Good for short-term results, but detrimental to engagement and motivation long term Affiliative Puts people first — creating a harmonious environment and building emotional bonds Requires empathy and the ability to build relationships across communication styles Coaching Characterised by collaboration, support and guidance Focused on bringing out the best in the team by guiding them through goals and obstacles Coercive A command and control style Relies on forcing people to do what they are told, whether they want it or not Transformational Works with followers beyond their immediate self-interest to identify needed change Creates a vision , guides change through influence and inspiration , and executes it alongside committed members Confusing pair — Authoritarian vs Coercive Authoritarian = the leader decides and directs . Employees don't participate, but they aren't compelled. Coercive = the leader forces compliance , "whether they want it or not." Autocratic is about who decides . Coercive is about how compliance is obtained . Confusing pair — Pacesetting vs Transformational Pacesetting models high performance and expects imitation — values results more than anything , and burns people out. Transformational creates a shared vision and moves people beyond self-interest. Both are demanding. One drives through people, the other with them. 4.2 Job Design Job design is where managers develop and specify the work activities of individuals or groups. It is the process of determining the types of tasks an employee needs to complete, and of identifying the skills, knowledge, personal traits, duties and responsibilities required to perform a position. Effective job design seeks to meet the needs of both the business and the employee — the task must allow the employee to work toward the objectives. Job design involves: Creating a job description Personal specifications Strategies that improve employee motivation and productivity Concept Definition Job satisfaction The extent to which employees are satisfied working in their current position Job enrichment The extent a business develops tasks with the abilities of existing staff in mind — reducing the boredom associated with many types of work The six job design strategies: 1. Job rotation 4. Semi-autonomous work groups 2. Job enlargement 5. Team structures 3. Job enrichment 6. Flexible work structures Confusing trio — Rotation vs Enlargement vs Enrichment Rotation — moving between different jobs. Variety across time. Enlargement — more tasks at the same level . Horizontal expansion. Enrichment — more responsibility and autonomy . Vertical expansion, matched to ability. Rotation changes where , enlargement changes how many , enrichment changes how demanding . General vs specific job design: general design gives employees a variety of tasks, increasing motivation and flexibility. Specific design gives a narrow, repetitive set, increasing efficiency and speed but risking boredom and turnover — which is why specialised job design often reduces job satisfaction . 4.3 Recruitment An effective recruitment strategy ensures the right people are hired to do the right job. The seven consequences of a poor selection process: 1. Increased training costs 2. Increased job dissatisfaction 3. Lower performance 4. Increased labour turnover 5. Increased absenteeism, if the staff member feels inadequate for the job 6. Increased accidents / defect rates 7. Increased claims of discrimination That list is the answer to "What is the likely outcome of a poor recruitment decision?" and to "How does selecting the wrong employee increase costs and reduce productivity?" Internal vs external: the choice depends on the type of skills and qualifications needed , whether current staff already have them, and whether recruiting is cheaper than training an existing employee . General skills Specific skills What Skills, attitudes and behaviours that are a good cultural fit Skills required for particular jobs Includes Flexibility and versatility · social confidence · positive attitude · motivation · ability to work in a team or independently · leadership and decision-making · willingness to learn · ability to work under pressure Technical and role-specific capability Why businesses target them Cultural fit and adaptability Skill shortages — filling identified gaps 4.4 Training and Development Crucial to ensuring staff stay motivated, performance goals are met, the possibility of accidents decreases, skill shortages are filled, and staff retention increases. When deciding between developing staff and recruiting, a business considers: Option Invest further in in-house training and development Retain experts who retire , on a part-time basis Recruit staff for specific skills Retain women through flexible work structures Share staff with other firms Outsource functions to specialist firms Sponsor overseas migrants Build networks or alliances with firms holding specialist skills Confusing pair — Training vs Development Training allows employees to perform their current roles more effectively. Development prepares them for future responsibilities and promotion . Training is about now; development is about next. 4.5 Performance Management The process of recognising the efforts and contributions of employees to their work. It is an ongoing process of communication between the direct manager and the employee. It involves: 1. Clarification of expectations 2. Setting employee workplace objectives 3. Providing feedback 4. Evaluating employee performance The three stages of the cycle: Stage What happens 1. Planning Expectations and goals developed by both the employer and the employee 2. Checking in Managers regularly observe performance to provide feedback 3. Assessment Measuring performance against the objectives Why it is ongoing: after assessment, new goals are established, beginning the cycle again. Performance needs to be continuously monitored, reviewed and improved. The four benefits: The employee has an improved understanding of their role and what needs to be done The employer can identify problems earlier Reviews make the employee aware of their personal goals Identifies areas of development either needed or requested by the employee ⚠️ Administrative vs Developmental — use your teacher's definition Administrative Developmental Your teacher's document HR completes skills audits of all staff and identifies training needs . Assists with HR planning . Information kept in an employee database HR plans and implements training for staff — both on the job and off the job The generic textbook version Evaluating output to decide pay, promotion, retention, termination Feedback used to build skills Use your teacher's version. It's what your school marks against, and it also fits the exam answers better — the Knox trial's Q10 (a business keeping data on time spent online, meetings and client feedback) is administrative precisely because it is data collection for HR planning. The tell: administrative records and audits ; developmental plans and delivers . 4.6 Rewards Used to motivate employees and encourage them to work together as a team to achieve common goals. Two axes: MONETARY or NON-MONETARY INDIVIDUAL or GROUP Designing a reward program — for the business: Consideration Business strategy Economic conditions Organisational objectives of rewards Rewards and benefits offered by competitors Relevant awards and agreements , minimum employment standards Union power Profitability / viability of the business Designing a reward program — for the individual (often called performance pay : remuneration distributed according to individual employee performance) Basis What it covers Performance related Incentive plans for performance above standards or criteria , bonuses, production-related criteria Job related Role and level of responsibility , scope of supervision, base pay, interpersonal skills, knowledge and skills, experience, value to company Other Group incentives Individual or team performance pay? Both, depending on the nature of the work. Team-based pay encourages cooperation and communication toward common objectives; individual pay recognises outstanding contribution. Using both prevents excessive competition while still rewarding individual effort. Why provide both monetary and non-monetary rewards? Because employees are motivated by different factors. Monetary rewards — bonuses, commissions, pay increases — provide financial motivation. Non-monetary rewards — recognition, promotion, flexible working, career development — improve job satisfaction and loyalty . McDonald's provides rewards and recognition programs, discounted meals and retail discounts, plus flexible working and career development opportunities. 4.7 Global HR Strategies Globalisation, technological development and HR applications have increased the complexity of managing HR. High labour costs and skill shortages in Australia have led businesses to operate globally. Seven factors to consider before outsourcing globally: 1. Labour costs 5. Political stability 2. Service / product quality 6. Language and cultural differences 3. Infrastructure requirements 7. Skills and supply of labour overseas 4. Overseas labour market regulations The China example: countries such as China have factories producing goods at a competitive price, so Australian companies have moved production there because it is cheaper. Impact ✅ Reduced costs for the business ❌ Loss of jobs and factory closures in Australia Australia's skills shortage is major and will increase. Two strategies used to overcome it: The Temporary Skills Shortage Visa , allowing businesses to bring people from overseas to fill the shortage Outsourcing functions overseas to access people with those skills 4.8 Workplace Disputes Disputes occur between employers and employees where their interests are in conflict. Every business should have a grievance procedure to guide employees, employers and unions in resolving one. A grievance procedure policy: Provides a clear outline of the issues Illustrates the correct and appropriate processes when raising a complaint Provides a mechanism for quick resolution The four resolution steps, in order: # Method Who decides 1 Negotiation — discussion between both parties to resolve the dispute. Unions and employer associations may be involved The parties 2 Mediation — an independent party with no ties to either side assists the parties to reach a settlement The parties 3 Conciliation — Fair Work Australia acts as a mediator and offers suggestions to resolve the problem The parties 4 Arbitration — the final stage. A commissioner hears both cases and makes a decision that is legally binding on both parties The commissioner Confusing trio — Mediation vs Conciliation vs Arbitration Mediation — the third party facilitates only . No suggestions. Conciliation — the third party suggests solutions . The parties still decide. Arbitration — the third party imposes a binding decision . Escalating intervention: facilitates → suggests → decides. Overt vs covert industrial action: overt action is visible and deliberate — strikes, work bans, work-to-rule (refusing tasks outside normal duties), lockouts, picket lines. Covert action is concealed — absenteeism , high turnover, sabotage, deliberate under-performance. Absenteeism appearing as an indicator in §6 and as covert action here is the same phenomenon read two ways. 4.9 Organisational Structures Structure Description Pros Cons Flat Few management layers, wide span of control Faster communication, empowerment Manager overload, unclear reporting Tall Many management layers, narrow span of control Clear career path, close supervision Slow communication, bureaucracy Centralised Decisions made at the top Consistency, control Slow response, disempowerment Decentralised Decisions pushed to lower levels Faster response, empowerment Inconsistency, coordination challenges Functional Grouped by function Specialisation, efficiency Silos, poor cross-functional communication Matrix Dual reporting (function + project) Flexible, cross-functional Conflicting priorities, complex reporting Span of control = the number of employees a manager directly supervises. Flat structures have a wide span; tall structures a narrow one. 5. Motivation Theories Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs Self-Actualisation (reach full potential) ──────────────────── Esteem Needs (recognition, status) ──────────────────── Social/Belonging Needs (teamwork, friendship) ──────────────────── Safety Needs (job security, safe workplace) ──────────────────── Physiological Needs (salary, basic conditions) Application : Lower-level needs must be met before higher-level rewards will motivate. Pay and safety first, then belonging, then recognition, then growth opportunities. Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory Factor Description Examples Hygiene factors Cause dissatisfaction if absent, but do not motivate when present Salary, working conditions, job security, company policy, supervision Motivators Actually motivate and satisfy Achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement, personal growth Application : Fix hygiene factors to prevent dissatisfaction, then use motivators to engage employees. Raising pay alone removes dissatisfaction but does not create motivation. McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y Theory X (authoritarian) Theory Y (participative) Workers are lazy and avoid work Workers are self-motivated and enjoy work Need close supervision and control Need autonomy and responsibility Motivated by punishment and reward Motivated by intrinsic factors Management style: command and control Management style: empowerment and trust Locke and Latham's Goal Setting Theory Motivation increases when goals are specific , challenging but achievable , accepted by the employee , and accompanied by feedback on progress. 6. Effectiveness Indicators of Human Resource Management An effective HR function is one where management and employees work well together in their efforts to achieve the goals of the business. The effectiveness of that relationship is examined through seven indicators. 6.1 The Seven Indicators Indicator Definition What a poor result signals Corporate culture The culture within an organisation — the values and beliefs within a business. An effective culture is one that is believed, demonstrated and acted upon by both management and employees A positive culture produces happier workers → lower turnover, higher productivity, better customer service, lower absenteeism. A negative culture produces less satisfied workers Benchmarking key variables The process of measuring an employee's performance against established standards If employees repeatedly fail to meet performance goals, management must examine why. Employees are more likely to meet goals where there are effective appraisal systems, training and development, and reward systems Changes in staff turnover The rate at which employees leave a business A high level caused by voluntary separation — mainly resignations — indicates poor employment relations Absenteeism Employees being unable to attend work for reasons such as illness or family responsibilities Costly, because the work isn't done — it places additional demands on remaining staff and can cause greater hostility . A sharp rise over a short period signals unhappy, unsatisfied workers Level of disputation The number and severity of disputes in a workplace The more disputes, the less effective management is at the employment relations function. Employers must examine why and rectify the practices causing them Accidents The number of accidents per year Increases may be due to lack of training , or poor workplace health and safety procedures and policies Worker satisfaction Whether employees are happy and contented and fulfilling their desires and needs at work Satisfied employees work more efficiently and value the organisation they work for Turnover isn't automatically bad — some brings in fresh skills and removes poor performers. What matters is who is leaving, and whether the separation was voluntary . Losing high performers voluntarily is the warning sign. 6.2 Which Indicator Measures Which Strategy Straight from your teacher's Strategies and Indicators Summary . This is the table that answers "evaluate the effectiveness of [strategy]" — it tells you which evidence to cite. Strategy Indicators used to measure it Leadership style Corporate culture · Benchmarks · Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Worker satisfaction Job design Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Number of accidents · Worker satisfaction Recruitment Corporate culture · Benchmarks · Staff turnover · Absenteeism Training and development Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Number of accidents · Corporate culture · Worker satisfaction Performance management Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Number of accidents · Worker satisfaction Rewards Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Number of accidents · Worker satisfaction Workplace disputes Staff turnover · Absenteeism · Worker satisfaction The patterns worth noticing: Staff turnover and absenteeism measure everything. If you can only remember two, remember these — they appear against all seven strategies. Accidents attach to the strategies that change how work is done — job design, training, performance management, rewards. Not to recruitment or leadership. Corporate culture and benchmarks attach to the strategies that shape who is in the business and how they are led — leadership, recruitment, training. Workplace disputes is the narrowest — three indicators, and notably not accidents or benchmarks. How to use it in an answer: "The effectiveness of the training and development strategy can be measured through changes in staff turnover and the number of accidents . A reduction in both would indicate the strategy has improved employee capability and workplace safety…" 7. Section IV & Short Answer Structures HR Strategy Answer Structure (4–6 marks) Define the strategy — "Recruitment is the process of accumulating a pool of potential candidates…" Explain how it works — describe the steps or methods Apply to the business — link to a specific case study Evaluate effectiveness — discuss advantages and disadvantages, impact on business performance Recommendation Structure (8 marks) Recommend — "It is recommended that [business] implement [strategy]" Define — explain what the strategy involves Reason 1 — how it addresses the identified problem Reason 2 — an additional benefit Link — restate the recommendation with justification, tied to a business goal Assess / Evaluate the Effectiveness of HR Strategies Intro: Judgement + define HRM + name the strategies and case study Body 1: Strategy 1 → how it works → effect → EFFECTIVENESS INDICATOR (e.g. reduced staff turnover) → link to business goal Body 2: Strategy 2 → same structure → different indicator Body 3: Limitation / cost / counter-argument Conclusion: Restate judgement, link to long-term goals Top-band tip : The difference between a mid-band and top-band HR answer is almost always the effectiveness indicators (§6). Quantify where you can: "staff turnover fell from 22% to 14%." HSC Verb Frameworks Verb What to do Marks guide Identify Name or state a concept 1–2 Outline Sketch in general terms 2–3 Describe Give features and characteristics 2–3 Distinguish State the differences between two things 3–4 Explain How and why, with an example 3–4 Analyse Break down, show relationships and implications 4–6 Discuss Present multiple perspectives, then judge 5–6 Assess / Evaluate Make a judgement with supporting evidence 7–8 Recommend Provide a course of action with justification 7–8 8. Common Exam Pitfalls Learn the HR cycle in order — acquisition, development, maintenance, separation. Many questions are structured around one stage. Job description (the job) vs job specification (the person). Redundancy (the job goes) vs dismissal (the person goes). Voluntary vs involuntary separation — and note that redundancy can be either. Award (industry safety net) vs enterprise agreement (workplace-negotiated, must pass BOOT). Don't just list strategies — link them to an effectiveness indicator . Induction is part of acquisition , and is the bridge into development. Mediation / conciliation / arbitration differ by how much power the third party has. Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction. They are not the same. Always show interdependence with operations, marketing and finance. 9. Glossary — Terms Students Mix Up Term Plain meaning Don't confuse with Job description Describes the job's tasks and responsibilities Job specification — the person's required skills Job specification The skills, knowledge and abilities required Job description — the duties Recruitment Accumulating a pool of candidates Selection — choosing from the pool Selection Screening and choosing the best applicant Recruitment — attracting them Induction Introducing a new employee to the business Training — improving job performance Training Improving present and future job performance Development — preparing for future roles Development Preparing employees for future responsibilities Training — current role focus Maintenance Keeping staff motivated, loyal and retained Development — growing their skills Redundancy The job no longer exists Dismissal — the person is removed Summary dismissal Immediate dismissal for serious misconduct Unfair dismissal — harsh, unjust or unreasonable Unfair dismissal Harsh, unjust or unreasonable dismissal Unlawful termination — for a prohibited reason Constructive dismissal Employee resigns due to employer's conduct Voluntary resignation Award Industry-wide minimum safety net Enterprise agreement — workplace-negotiated Enterprise agreement Workplace agreement passing the BOOT Common law contract — individual NES 11 legislated minimum entitlements for all employees Awards (industry-specific) Employee Contract of service; entitled to leave and super Contractor — contract for service Monetary benefit Cash or cash-equivalent from the business Non-monetary — a non-cash benefit Intrinsic reward Satisfaction from within the person Extrinsic rewards given by the business Fringe benefit Non-cash benefit forming part of remuneration (company car) Intrinsic reward Piece rate Pay based on output produced Commission (pay based on sales ) Mediation Third party facilitates ; parties decide Arbitration — third party decides Conciliation Third party suggests solutions Mediation — only facilitates Arbitration Third party imposes a binding decision Mediation and conciliation (non-binding) Strike Employees stop work Lockout — employer shuts them out Span of control Number of employees a manager supervises Chain of command (reporting lines) Turnover Rate at which staff leave and are replaced Absenteeism — unplanned days off Hygiene factors Prevent dissatisfaction; don't motivate Motivators — actively create satisfaction EEO Decisions based on merit; barriers removed Anti-discrimination law (prohibits conduct) Sham contracting Illegally treating an employee as a contractor Legitimate use of contractors 10. Key Definitions Quick Reference Term One-Line Definition Human resource management The management of people to achieve business objectives HR cycle Acquisition → Development → Maintenance → Separation Acquisition Identifying staff needs, recruitment and selection Job description Describes the tasks and responsibilities of the employee Job specification Defines the skills, knowledge and abilities required for the job Recruitment Accumulating a pool of potential candidates for a job Selection A screening process where the most appropriate applicant is chosen Cadetship A trainee position used as an external recruitment method Induction Introducing a new employee to the business and how it works Development Preparing employees for future responsibilities Training Any activity aimed at improving present and future performance On the job training Learning while working — apprenticeships, mentoring Off the job training External courses, conferences, TAFE Performance appraisal Formal assessment of how well a person is working 360-degree feedback Feedback from supervisor, peers, subordinates and self Maintenance Keeping existing staff motivated, loyal and retained Monetary benefits Benefits paid on top of usual entitlements as part of remuneration Non-monetary benefits Non-cash benefits such as flexibility, status and autonomy Intrinsic reward A reward that comes from within the person Piece rate Payment based on output produced Fringe benefit A non-cash benefit such as a company car Job sharing Two employees sharing one full-time role Flextime Flexible start and finish times around core hours Separation The ending of the employment relationship Voluntary separation Retirement, resignation or voluntary redundancy Involuntary separation Redundancy, instant dismissal or summary dismissal Redundancy Where a job is no longer required by the business Summary dismissal Immediate dismissal for serious misconduct Unfair dismissal Dismissal that is harsh, unjust or unreasonable Fair Work Commission Body that hears unfair dismissal claims and approves agreements Award Industry-specific minimum pay and conditions Enterprise agreement Workplace-negotiated agreement
