passing the BOOT NES National Employment Standards — legislated minimum entitlements Common law contract The individual agreement between employer and employee Duty of care The employer's WHS obligation to provide a safe workplace EEO Employment decisions based on merit, with barriers removed Mediation A third party facilitates discussion without imposing a decision Conciliation A third party suggests solutions; the parties decide Arbitration A third party imposes a binding decision Strike Employees collectively stop work Lockout Employer prevents employees from working Span of control The number of employees a manager directly supervises Staff turnover The rate at which employees leave and are replaced Absenteeism Unplanned employee absence from work Benchmarking Comparing performance against industry best practice Corporate culture The shared values, attitudes and behaviours of the organisation Outsourcing (HR) Contracting HR functions to external providers Contractor A worker engaged under a contract for service See also: Marketing | Operations | Finance | Case Studies | MOC

title: Human Resources Syllabus Summary
text: Human Resources - Syllabus Summary 1. Role of Human Resource Management Align workforce capability and culture with strategic direction Attract, develop and retain employees; manage employee relations and legal compliance Treat employees as an asset to be developed Interdependence: Operations identifies staffing and skill requirements; HR recruits and trains Marketing depends on skilled and customer-facing employees Finance budgets wages and training; HR supports expenditure with productivity outcomes Outsourced HR functions: recruitment, payroll, training and specialist advice Contractors: domestic or global; flexibility and expertise against cost, control, communication and legal-jurisdiction risks 2. Influences on Human Resources Stakeholders: employers, employees, employer associations, unions, government organisations and society Stakeholder tensions: productivity, flexibility and cost vs fair pay, safety, security and development Legal influences: Fair Work Act 2009: workplace relations, minimum wages, NES, unfair dismissal and bargaining Awards: industry/occupation minimums; enterprise agreements: workplace-negotiated and subject to BOOT Common-law employment contracts and employer/employee obligations Work Health and Safety legislation: duty of care, risk control, training and consultation Anti-discrimination laws and Equal Employment Opportunity (merit-based decisions and removal of barriers) Workers compensation, termination protections and severance entitlements Economic influences: booms, downturns, unemployment, skills shortages, recruitment difficulty and wage pressure Technological influences: automation, HRIS, AI recruitment, remote work, changing skill needs and role displacement Social influences: ageing workforce, women's participation, cultural diversity and work-life balance expectations Ethics and CSR: fair pay, diversity, inclusion, bullying/harassment prevention, whistleblower protection and safe supply chains 3. Human Resource Processes HR cycle: acquisition → development → maintenance → separation Acquisition: Identify staffing and skill needs Prepare job descriptions and job specifications Recruit internally or externally Select through interviews, application forms, referee checks and tests Induct new employees into policies, safety, facilities, colleagues and entitlements Development: On-the-job training: coaching, mentoring, rotation, apprenticeships and shadowing Off-the-job training: TAFE, university, workshops and conferences Performance appraisals: strengths, skill gaps, goals and development needs Maintenance: Retain and motivate staff through pay, benefits, work conditions and development Participation, teamwork, flexible work, family-friendly programs and diversity Address bullying, harassment, low morale and avoidable turnover Separation: Voluntary: resignation, retirement and voluntary redundancy Involuntary: redundancy, dismissal and summary dismissal Manage notice, severance, accrued leave, consultation, fairness and documentation Consider survivor morale, corporate knowledge and unfair-dismissal risk 4. Human Resource Strategies Leadership styles: authoritarian, participative/democratic, delegative/laissez-faire, pacesetting, affiliative, coaching, coercive and transformational Job design: Job rotation, enlargement and enrichment Semi-autonomous work groups and team structures Flexible work structures Balance efficiency, motivation, autonomy, variety and job satisfaction Recruitment: right person for the right role; internal/external methods; general and role-specific skills Training and development: address skills shortages, safety, performance, innovation and retention Performance management: Set expectations and objectives, check in, give feedback and assess performance Teacher's distinction: administrative performance management records/audits skills and informs HR planning; developmental management plans and delivers training Rewards: Monetary and non-monetary; individual and group Performance-related, job-related and group incentives Align rewards with business strategy, objectives, viability, awards/agreements and employee motivation Global HR: Consider labour cost and supply, skills, quality, infrastructure, regulations, political stability, language and culture Balance access to skills and lower costs against domestic job losses and coordination risks Workplace disputes: Maintain a grievance procedure Resolution sequence: negotiation → mediation → conciliation → arbitration Distinguish overt action (strikes, bans, lockouts) from covert action (absenteeism, turnover, sabotage, underperformance) 5. Effectiveness of Human Resource Management Corporate culture Benchmarking key variables Changes in staff turnover Absenteeism Accidents Levels of disputation Worker satisfaction Match strategies to evidence: Leadership: culture, benchmarks, turnover, absenteeism and satisfaction Job design: turnover, absenteeism, accidents and satisfaction Recruitment: culture, benchmarks, turnover and absenteeism Training and development: turnover, absenteeism, accidents, culture and satisfaction Performance management and rewards: turnover, absenteeism, accidents and satisfaction Workplace disputes: turnover, absenteeism and satisfaction See also: Human Resources FULL | Human Resources 1 Role | Human Resources 2 Influences | Human Resources 3 Processes | Human Resources 4 Strategies | MOC

title: Marketing 1 · Role of Marketing
text: 📣 Marketing 1 · Role of Marketing Marketing · ① Role ← you are here · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Marketing module is examinable. This file covers the Role of marketing dot points only. Definition : Marketing is the total system of interacting activities designed to plan, promote, price and distribute products to present and potential customers. 1. Strategic Role Translates the business goal of profit maximisation into reality Develops a marketing plan with actions and strategies to attain greater sales Modern emphasis: customer-oriented marketing — viewing the business through the customer's eyes Marketing today places strong emphasis on understanding consumer behaviour and satisfying customer needs/wants 2. Marketing Plan A marketing plan is where the business applies marketing strategies based on market research to understand what to sell, their SWOT, and how to position themselves It is the roadmap for how the business will attract and retain customers Aligns marketing activities with overall business goals The steps in building the plan live in ③ Processes — don't confuse the plan (role) with the process of writing it. 3. Interdependence with Other Functions Function Relationship with Marketing Operations Marketing provides demand forecasts and customer preferences → operations modifies production. Operations produces goods → marketing sells them Finance Finance provides budgets and funds for marketing. Marketing generates revenue that flows to finance to cover expenses Human Resources HR recruits and trains employees for marketing roles. Untrained staff = wrong market assessments = lower conversion rates and profits Case Study — BYD : Operations produces the "Blade Battery" → marketing promotes vehicle safety/reliability. Marketing provides customer feedback → operations modifies cars. When operations delivers quality, affordable EVs, marketing can sell them in more international markets. Profits are reinvested into factories and research, creating a cycle of continuous improvement. 4. Marketing Approaches Approach Core Idea Focus Production Consumers buy based on product quality Taking orders and delivering products Sales Increased competition requires aggressive selling Advertising to stimulate demand Marketing Find what customers want, then satisfy that need Customer orientation, market research, integrated strategies Societal 📎 Balance company profits with societal well-being Environmental and social responsibility 📎 The syllabus names only three approaches: production, selling, marketing. The societal approach is textbook extension — safe to mention as a modern development, but the three above are what a "marketing approaches" question is testing. Apple : Early iPhones used a sales approach (educating customers on features). As expectations grew, shifted to a marketing approach (persuasive, research-driven). Customer feedback led to larger screens, thinner builds, better cameras. 2014: larger iPhones released in response to consumer demand. 5. Customer Orientation Customer relationship begins with the sale (doesn't end there) After-sale service, warranties, fulfilling needs and wants Example: free car servicing, longer warranty periods 6. Relationship Marketing Core: customer loyalty → repeat sales Achieved through reward programs, customer care, after-sales service Development of long-term cost-effective and strong relationships with customers 7. Types of Markets A market = group of individuals/organisations that need or want a product, have the money to purchase it, are willing to spend, and are socially and legally authorised to buy. Market Type Description Examples Resource Market Primary production (mining, agriculture, forestry, fishing) Farmers, miners Industrial Market Industries/businesses purchasing products for production or operations Factories buying raw materials Intermediate Market Wholesalers and retailers who purchase finished products and resell for profit Coles, Woolworths Consumer Market Individuals who plan to use/consume products End consumers Consumer Market Segments Segment Description Example Mass market Appeals to all consumers Electricity, basic food Market segment Focus on one area of a market Sports cars Niche market Smaller section of a segment Teenage girl magazines ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Sales approach vs Marketing approach Sales pushes what we already made . Marketing finds out what they want first Customer orientation vs Relationship marketing Orientation is the mindset (see it through their eyes). Relationship marketing is the tactic (loyalty programs, after-sales service) Market segment vs Niche market A niche sits inside a segment. Sports cars = segment. Vintage sports cars = niche Intermediate market vs Consumer market Intermediate buys to resell . Consumer buys to use 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Marketing The total system of interacting activities designed to plan, promote, price and distribute products to present and potential customers Market A group that needs/wants a product, has the money, is willing to spend, and is socially and legally authorised to buy Marketing plan A document applying marketing strategies based on market research to determine what to sell and how to position it Relationship marketing Developing long-term, cost-effective, strong relationships with customers to secure repeat sales Niche market A smaller section within a market segment Next: ② Influences on Marketing · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Marketing 2 · Influences on Marketing
text: 🌐 Marketing 2 · Influences on Marketing Marketing · ① Role · ② Influences ← you are here · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Marketing module is examinable. This file covers the Influences on marketing dot points only. 1. Factors Influencing Customer Choice Why marketers study customer choice : To understand what motivates an individual to purchase a particular product. Market researchers ask: Who are our customers? What do they buy? When do they buy? How often do they buy? Why do they buy? 1.1 Psychological (within the individual) Factor Key Point Perception How consumers view/interpret products Motives Internal drives to purchase Attitudes Learned predisposition towards a product Personality Unique psychological characteristics Self-image Buy products matching self-concept Learning Behaviour changes from experience Apple : iPhone 5c (colours) failed — quality expectations (psychological) were stronger than colour preference. iPhone 5s (metallic colours) succeeded — associated with quality/innovation. "Colour reveals your personality" — but consumers prioritised quality over colour. 1.2 Sociocultural (other people and groups) Factor Key Point Social class Grouping by income, occupation, education Culture/subculture Shared values, multicultural considerations — businesses cater for different cultural groups as Australia becomes more multicultural Family and roles Family members influence decisions Reference groups Peer influence on purchases Apple : Social media/gaming/streaming popularity → marketing promotes camera, screen, processing specs to differentiate from competitors. 1.3 Economic Condition Effect Marketing Response Boom Low unemployment, rising income, optimism Emphasise premium products; businesses expand production Recession High unemployment, falling income, caution Stress value and usefulness; customers seek functional, long-lasting products Apple : GFC → declining iPhone sales → developed low-cost iPhone 5c and continued selling older models. COVID-19 → released iPhone SE (2020) and "Mini" versions for price-conscious customers. 1.4 Government Four types of government influence: Fiscal Policy : The government budget showing revenue sources (taxes) and spending. Used to expand or contract economic activity. Example: introduction of the GST or increases in income tax. Monetary Policy : Government through the Reserve Bank uses interest rates to control money supply and inflation. RBA adjusts the cash rate → affects bank interest rates → encourages or discourages consumer spending. Regulations : Laws that directly impact marketing activities. Breaches may result in financial penalties. Government Regulations (direct impact) : Laws regulating marketing concerns — product contents, health/safety, pricing strategies, distribution channels, ethical promotion. Apple : iPhone 6 launch delayed in China (privacy concerns). India regulations prevented store expansion for years, eased in 2020. India's $6.6B incentive program boosted local smartphone manufacturing. 2. Ethical Influences 2.1 Unethical Practices Practice Definition Concealed facts Omitting information that could harm trust Puffery Exaggerated claims no reasonable person would take as factual Vague statements Ambiguous words consumers misinterpret Invasion of privacy Tracking web users for targeted advertising SUGGING Selling Under the Guise of a Survey — sales disguised as market research 2.2 Other Ethical Issues Good taste : Subjective, depends on community sensitivities Health-damaging products : Self-regulatory codes (children's advertising, alcohol, smoking) Fair competition : False promises, exaggerated descriptions, high-pressure selling 3. Consumer Law (Legal Influences) 3.1 Competition and Consumer Act 2010 — Two Purposes Protect consumers from misleading practices (misrepresenting products, deceptive advertising) Regulate trade practices that restrict competition Enforced by : ACCC (Australian Competition and Consumer Commission) and ASIC (Australian Securities and Investment Commission) 3.2 Deceptive & Misleading Conduct Tactic Example Fine print Important conditions too small to read Before/after ads Misleading comparisons Tests and surveys Unsubstantiated claims False country of origin "Made in Australia" when made overseas Misleading packaging Size/shape gives wrong impression of contents Fake special offers "Limited time" when offer is permanent Bait and switch Advertise cheap items, sell expensive ones when they run out Dishonest advertising Deceptive words, false quality claims, fake price reductions 3.3 Consumer Rights Right Details Implied conditions Unspoken/unwritten terms of contract — product must be fit for purpose; cannot claim false characteristics Warranties Promise to repair/replace faulty products — also a marketing tool if it includes superior options vs competitors Refunds Legally required if: faulty, doesn't match description, fails to work. NOT required if: customer changes mind, finds cheaper option, damages after purchase 3.4 Price Discrimination Different prices in different markets Possible because markets are geographically spread or product differentiation exists Prohibited if it substantially reduces competition Also applies to discounts, credits, rebates, services and payment arrangements 3.5 ACCC Case Studies Apple: iPhone/iPad misrepresentations — $9 million penalty Error 53 — staff misled customers about repair rights Consumer guarantee representations — ACCC took action Apple gave undertaking to improve policies Woolworths: ACCC court case over misleading grocery pricing/discount practices ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Psychological vs Sociocultural Psychological is inside one person's head . Sociocultural is other people influencing them Fiscal vs Monetary policy Fiscal = the government budget (tax and spend). Monetary = the RBA and interest rates Puffery vs Deceptive conduct Puffery is legal — obvious exaggeration nobody believes. Deceptive conduct is illegal — a reasonable person would be misled Ethical vs Legal influence Ethical = what you should do (no law forces you). Legal = what you must do (penalties apply) Price discrimination vs Price skimming Discrimination = different markets, different prices, same time . Skimming = same market, price falls over time ACCC vs ASIC ACCC = competition and consumers . ASIC = companies and financial services 📝 Exam habit that has cost you marks A legal influence question wants the Act named. Write Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) in full, then what it requires, then who enforces it ( ACCC ). Naming the regulator is often worth its own mark. 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Puffery Exaggerated claims about a product that no reasonable person would take as factual SUGGING Selling Under the Guise of a Survey — a sales pitch disguised as market research Implied conditions Unspoken, unwritten terms of a contract requiring a product to be fit for purpose Price discrimination Charging different prices for the same product in different markets; prohibited where it substantially reduces competition Monetary policy RBA action on interest rates to control the money supply and inflation Fiscal policy The government budget — revenue from taxation and government spending — used to expand or contract economic activity Next: ③ Marketing Processes · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Marketing 3 · Marketing Processes
text: ⚙️ Marketing 3 · Marketing Processes Marketing · ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes ← you are here · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Marketing module is examinable. This file covers the Marketing process dot points only. 1. The Six Steps in Developing a Marketing Plan 1. Situational analysis (SWOT + product life cycle) 2. Market research 3. Establish marketing objectives 4. Identify target markets 5. Develop marketing strategies → see [Marketing 4 Strategies](Marketing__Marketing_4_Strategies.html) 6. Implementation, monitoring and controlling Memorise the order. A "describe the marketing process" question is asking for these six in sequence. 2. Situational Analysis 2.1 SWOT The most crucial step — management must understand current position and where heading. Must be based on meaningful market research . Internal (controllable) External (monitor constantly) Positive Strengths Opportunities Negative Weaknesses Threats Apple SWOT : Strength = brand reputation | Weakness = high price | Opportunity = AI partnerships | Threat = Asian competitors (Xiaomi, OPPO) 2.2 Product Life Cycle Stage Strategy Introduction Build awareness, heavy promotion, limited range, high costs, low/negative profits Growth Differentiate brand, expand product line, competition increases, shift from "what it is" to "why ours is best" Maturity Defend market share, stress value, modify product, sales peak, market saturated Decline Reduce spending, consider product deletion, product becomes outdated CD = decline | PCs = maturity | EVs = growth | Tablets = maturity | Driverless cars = introduction McDonald's French fries : Introduction (1940s) → Growth (1940s–1990) → Maturity (1990, recipe change due to health campaign, share price fell) → Renewal (Loaded, Twisted, Waffle, Cheesy Bacon fries) Marketing strategies change through each stage — promotion emphasis, pricing approach, distribution channels, and product features all adapt to the current lifecycle position. 3. Market Research Definition : Systematic collection, recording and analysis of information concerning a specific marketing problem. 3.1 Steps Determine information needs Collect data (primary & secondary) Analyse and interpret data 3.2 Primary vs Secondary Primary Secondary Source Business conducts own research Others' research Methods Surveys, observations, focus groups Internet, Census, industry reports Pros Specific, current, controlled Cheap, available, broader context Cons Expensive, time-consuming May be outdated, not specific enough 3.3 What Market Research Reveals Consumer needs/wants and preferences Target market income → assists pricing decisions Feedback for product/service improvements Competitor analysis (prices, features, service) → assists product differentiation Census data → existing and potential customer characteristics Apple : Emails post-purchase feedback surveys. Monthly country-by-country surveys reveal: purchase drivers vs competitors, most-used features, demographics, satisfaction levels. "Every month, Apple surveys iPhone buyers" — reveals what drives customers to buy iPhone vs Android. Drives continuous improvement and competitive differentiation. 4. Marketing Objectives Definition : Realistic and measurable goals achieved through the marketing plan. Must be aligned to business goals but more customer oriented . 4.1 Three Common Objectives Objective Strategy Increase market share Promotional campaigns, competitive pricing, product differentiation Expand product mix New product development, product line extensions Maximise customer service Feedback forms, after-sales service, staff training 4.2 Market Share Formula Market Share (%) = (Company Sales ÷ Total Industry Sales) × 100 Why businesses want to increase market share : More customers → more sales → competitive advantage → customer satisfaction → repeat purchases → profit maximisation. Relationship between customer satisfaction and profits : Satisfied customers purchase again and recommend to peers → increased sales → increased profits. Extra cash reinvested back into the business for growth. 5. Identifying Target Markets ✅ Syllabus dot point: "identifying target markets" — step 4 of the marketing process. Target market : Group of present and potential customers a business intends to sell to. Primary : Most resources directed here Secondary : Smaller, less important segment Why identify target markets : To identify appropriate promotional strategies, improve ability to increase sales, ensure products meet customer needs/expectations. ⚠️ Segmentation and positioning are NOT in this section. The syllabus lists "market segmentation, product/service differentiation and positioning" as the first dot point under Marketing strategies → Marketing 4 Strategies §1. The distinction the syllabus draws: identifying which group you sell to is a process step. Dividing the market up, differentiating your product and positioning it are strategies . 6. Developing Marketing Strategies ✅ Syllabus dot point: "developing marketing strategies" — step 5 of the marketing process. This step is the whole of Marketing 4 Strategies — segmentation and positioning, the 4 Ps, the extended 3 Ps, e-marketing and global marketing. It sits inside the process as a stage, and is examined as its own syllabus section. 7. Implementation, Monitoring & Controlling ✅ Syllabus dot point: "implementation, monitoring and controlling — developing a financial forecast; comparing actual and planned results, revising the marketing strategy" — step 6, the last of the marketing process. 7.1 Definitions Implementation : Putting strategies into operation — the how, where and when Monitoring : Checking and observing actual progress of the marketing plan Controlling : Comparing planned vs actual performance, taking corrective action to ensure objectives are attained 7.2 Financial Forecasts Cost estimate + Revenue estimate Compare sales potential and revenue forecasts with anticipated expenditures Easier to forecast costs than revenue (costs are more controllable) 7.3 Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) KPI Purpose Sales analysis Evaluate current performance and strategy effectiveness using sales data Market share analysis Compare performance against competitors Marketing profitability analysis Break down total marketing costs into specific marketing activities 7.4 Revising the Marketing Strategy If objectives not met, changes include: Modify the 4Ps (marketing mix adjustments) New product development (add products) Product deletion (remove underperforming products) ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Monitoring vs Controlling Monitoring watches . Controlling acts — it's the corrective action that makes it control Primary vs Secondary research Primary = you collected it . Secondary = someone else already did Market segment vs Target market A segment is a group that exists . A target market is the segment you chose to sell to . ⭐ Choosing it is a process step; creating the segments is a strategy → Marketing 4 Strategies §1 Market share vs Market growth Share = your slice of the industry. Growth = the whole pie getting bigger Situational analysis vs market research Situational analysis is step 1 and asks where are we now (SWOT, PLC). Market research is step 2 and is the method that supplies the evidence for it 📝 Exam habits "Market research" is a marketing process, not an operations one. It sits at step 2 of the marketing plan. You have been caught on this before. If the stimulus gives you sales figures, calculate market share. A stated figure with no calculation done to it is a wasted mark. 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Situational analysis Assessment of a business's current position, most commonly through SWOT, based on meaningful market research Market research The systematic collection, recording and analysis of information concerning a specific marketing problem Marketing objective A realistic and measurable goal to be achieved through the marketing plan Target market The group of present and potential customers to which a business intends to sell Controlling Comparing planned with actual performance and taking corrective action so objectives are attained Segmentation, differentiation and positioning definitions live in Marketing 4 Strategies §1 — they are strategy dot points. Next: ④ Marketing Strategies · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Marketing 4 · Marketing Strategies
text: 🎯 Marketing 4 · Marketing Strategies Marketing · ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies ← you are here · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Marketing module is examinable. This file covers the Marketing strategies dot points only. ⭐ This is the highest-yield section in the module. Most 20-mark Marketing questions are answered mainly out of this file. 1. Market Segmentation, Differentiation and Positioning ✅ Syllabus dot point: "market segmentation, product/service differentiation and positioning" — the first dot point under Marketing strategies. ⚠️ This is not part of the marketing process. Identifying the target market is the process step ( Marketing 3 Processes §5). Segmenting, differentiating and positioning are strategies. 1.1 Market Segmentation Dividing the total market into distinct groups with similar characteristics, so the marketing mix can be tailored to each. Base Criteria Apple Example Geographic Location, region, climate Strong in Americas, Europe, Greater China Demographic Age, income, occupation, education Young to middle-aged, middle to high income, professionals/students Psychographic Lifestyle, values, attitudes, personality, socioeconomic groups Innovation-seekers, quality-focused, early adopters, brand-loyal Behavioural Buying patterns, brand loyalty, usage, benefits sought Apple ecosystem loyalty, repeat purchasers Apple's product-segment targets: iPhone : Broad audience — young adults, professionals, tech enthusiasts iPad : Creative professionals, students Mac : Developers, creative professionals Apple Watch : Fitness enthusiasts, professionals 1.2 Product / Service Differentiation Making a product that is the same as or similar to competitors' appear different from and better than theirs. This gives the seller greater control in the marketplace, especially over price — a differentiated product can command a premium instead of competing on cost alone. Differentiation can be achieved through: quality, features, design, branding, packaging, warranty, after-sales service, and for services, the expertise and time given. 1.3 Positioning Definition : How potential buyers from the target market perceive the product relative to competitors The business decides on the image it wishes to create for a product/service Brand names evoke certain images — e.g. No Frills (budget), Rolex (luxury) This image gives the product its position in the market Positioning is linked to the marketing mix — all 4Ps must reinforce the desired position The three work as one chain: segment the market → differentiate your product for the chosen segment → position it in their minds. A question naming any one of them usually wants all three. 2. Marketing Mix — the 4Ps 2.1 Product Decisions about: quality, packaging/labelling, design, brand name, guarantee. Strategies change with product life cycle stage. Total Product Concepts — Tangible and Intangible: Most products are a combination of tangible and intangible components Customers buy both tangible and intangible benefits A product includes: the package, brand name, warranty, after-sale service Product Branding: A brand is a name, term, symbol, design or combination that identifies a specific product and distinguishes it from competitors Brand symbol and logo : Graphic representation that identifies a business or product Branding strategies (by ownership): Manufacturer's/national brand : Manufacturer owns the brand name — high appeal, recognised across the country Private/household brand : Owned by a retailer or wholesaler Generic brands : Products with no brand name — normally used for supermarket products Branding must be linked to the reputation of the business Packaging: Development of container and graphic design for a product How easily is the package recognised — colours, branding, logo Packaging reinforces brand messaging and consumer perception 2.2 Price Pricing Methods: Method Description Cost-plus pricing Formula: Cost + (Cost × Markup %) = Price. Disadvantage: doesn't consider market conditions or other parts of the marketing mix Market-based pricing Sets prices according to supply and demand interaction — whatever the market is willing to pay. Prices constantly change with market fluctuations Competitive pricing Price covers costs and is comparable to competitor's price. Used in highly competitive markets — price below, equal to, or above competitors Pricing Strategies: Strategy When Used Price skimming New/innovative products — charge high initial price before competitors enter, then lower over time. E.g. iPhone launch ($2,199 Pro Max) Penetration pricing Entering competitive markets — lowest possible price that still covers cost. Quick market share gain ("mass market pricing"). Not long-term as it impacts revenue Competitive pricing Established markets with many competitors — match or slightly vary from price leader Loss leader Sell some products below cost to attract customers who also buy higher-margin items. E.g. supermarket specials at start of aisles Price points Psychological pricing at predetermined levels — e.g. watches at $55, $75, $95. Common in retail Prestige pricing Deliberately high price to signal quality/exclusivity — e.g. Rolex, Apple Price discrimination Different prices in different markets (prohibited if reduces competition) Price bundling Combining products at a lower total price — e.g. McValue Meals Dynamic pricing AI-powered adjustments based on real-time demand — e.g. McDonald's Apple pricing: Price skimming at launches, prestige pricing reinforces luxury image, selective price reductions on older models. 2.3 Promotion Definition : The methods used to communicate information about a product to persuade and remind the target market about its products. Elements of the Promotional Communication Process: Sender (business) → Message (advertisement) → Channel (medium) → Receiver (customer) Noise : Any interference or distraction that affects any stage in the promotional communication process Elements of the Promotion Mix: Method Details Advertising Paid, non-personal communication. Six main media: (1) Mass marketing (TV, radio), (2) Direct marketing catalogues, (3) Telemarketing, (4) Internet, (5) Social media advertising, (6) Billboards Personal selling Activities of a sales consultant directed to a customer — involves the human aspect of promotion. More persuasive than advertising because of direct interaction Sales promotion Short-term incentives: coupons, contests, samples, loyalty/rewards programs, free gifts, price discounts, two-for-one deals Publicity Free news about a business's products — NOT paid for Public Relations (PR) Activities aimed at creating and maintaining favourable relationships with stakeholders — planned, not free Direct marketing Direct communication with individual customers — email, mail, catalogues Distinction: Publicity vs Public Relations Publicity = free, unplanned media coverage PR = planned, strategic management of relationships 2.4 Place (Distribution) Definition : Not about location — about distribution channels and channel choices. How to get the product from factory to customer. Distribution Channels: Level Path Direct Manufacturer → Consumer (e.g. Apple website, Apple stores) One-level Manufacturer → Retailer → Consumer (e.g. Apple via JB Hi-Fi, Optus, Telstra) Two-level Manufacturer → Wholesaler → Retailer → Consumer Three-level Manufacturer → Agent → Wholesaler → Retailer → Consumer Most large businesses use at least 2 methods for flexibility. Channel Choice — Distribution Intensity: Type Description Example Intensive Saturate the market — product available everywhere Coca-Cola, Pepsi (supermarkets, vending machines, restaurants) Selective Moderate proportion of all possible outlets Apple (Apple stores + selected retailers like JB Hi-Fi) Exclusive Only one retail outlet in a large geographic area Ferrari, Tiffany jewellery (specific outlets only) Innovative Distribution Methods: Retailing activity conducted away from the traditional store Includes online retailing, pop-up stores, vending machines, direct-to-consumer platforms Physical Distribution Issues: All activities concerned with the efficient movement of products Includes warehousing, transport, inventory management, order processing 3. Extended Marketing Mix — People, Processes, Physical Evidence The traditional 4Ps focus on goods. The extra 3 Ps address services , which are intangible, inseparable, variable, and perishable. P Definition Apple Example People Quality of customer-employee interaction "Genius" and "Specialist" job titles; strong sales/customer service training; in-store, online, phone support Processes Flow of activities in service delivery Online ordering; free iOS upgrades; pre-ordering; roaming payment systems in stores Physical evidence Environment where service is delivered + tangible brand materials Stores designed for innovation/quality; hands-on "test-drive" approach; prime city locations; sleek packaging; professional website Apple : The extra 3 Ps strengthen premium brand image, increase customer satisfaction and loyalty, and maintain competitive advantage. 4. E-Marketing Definition : Internet marketing — allows a business with online operations to reach a global audience. 4.1 E-Marketing Technologies Technology Description Marketing Use Web pages Combination of text, graphics, animation and video Physical evidence (branding/packaging), process (ordering/communication), place (distribution), promotion (advertising on other sites) Podcasts Distribution of digital audio/video files over internet Publicity — promoting companies through talking/showcasing. Effective if aimed at same audience as target market SMS Short message service — text messages between mobile phones Direct promotion — cannot be ignored unless blocked. Used for sales notifications, tracking info, status updates, incentives Blogs Online diary allowing communication between business and customers Building relationships, feedback, product information Social media advertising Use of Facebook and Twitter to promote business Cost efficiency, vast global reach, higher market share. Disadvantage: anyone can comment (even without trying product) — can worsen brand reputation 4.2 Apple's E-Marketing Impact on the 4Ps P How E-Marketing Influences It Product Detailed specifications online; displayed alongside accessories; FAQs and technical specs reduce customer service costs Price Price transparency — comparison with competitors; price comparison websites; increased profit margins by selling online (no retail store costs) Place Global platform without retail costs; sell directly to customers; tailor websites for languages/cultures. Limitation: some customers prefer viewing before purchasing Promotion Images, audio, video, detailed info on website; new product launches published online; social media ads; database of existing/potential customers for email/social media promotion 5. Global Marketing Strategies Why businesses go global : TNCs (Transnational Corporations) operate beyond domestic operations to increase sales, further brand awareness, and establish markets in new countries. 5.1 Global Branding Worldwide use of a name, logo, term or symbol More effective and efficient to promote a brand rather than individual products A brand has the same meaning in any language Apple : Logo changed three times since 1979 — simple, globally recognisable. Competitive advantage due to global brand recognition. 5.2 Standardisation vs Customisation Approach Description Apple Example Standardisation Same marketing strategies worldwide — minor adjustments (language, actors) but overall script is the same Same iPhone in every country; iPhone 5c ad featured people of various nationalities speaking their own language Customisation Entirely different strategies for each country — changes based on culture, religion, tastes iPhone 6 Plus designed for Asian market (large screen); different pricing by market Combination Most businesses use both — standardise core elements, customise for local markets Apple changes language/actors (standardised) but adapts pricing and some features (customised) Why research the market : Differences in language, religion, tastes, and ethics require understanding before entering new markets. 5.3 Global Pricing Strategies Strategy Description Customised pricing Different prices for the same product in different markets. Uses cost-plus method covering: transportation, taxes, warehousing, tariffs Market customised pricing Prices set according to local market conditions and exchange rate fluctuations Standardised pricing Same price anywhere in the world — risky due to different purchasing powers iPhone X prices around the world (64GB $US) : Russia $1,390 | EU $1,377 | UK $1,330 | China $1,280 | Australia $1,259 | USA $999 Factors affecting global pricing : Currency exchange rates, transportation costs, local taxes, tariffs, competition in overseas markets. 5.4 Global Promotional Strategies Use variety of mediums: TV, Internet, radio Must consider language, religion, culture 5.5 Competitive Positioning Formal process of determining how to differentiate from competitors Value proposition includes: Operational excellence Customer intimacy Product leadership Apple : Historically positioned at high end (quality/design). As developed markets saturated, turned to high-growth emerging economies (China, India). 2014: secured contract with China Mobile (largest carrier) — significant sales increase. Huawei has since overtaken Apple in market share. 6. Section IV Essay Structures 6.1 Assess / Evaluate / Explain the Importance of (Judgement-Based) Introduction : Start with judgement sentence → state what you're evaluating (use syllabus dot points) → include all case studies. Body Paragraph Purpose Paragraph 1 Answer the question — judgement with brief overview. Define key concepts. Include case study. Paragraph 2 Advantages — prove they are advantages by linking to a topic-specific goal. Use stats. Paragraph 3 Disadvantages — prove they are disadvantages by linking to a topic-specific goal. Paragraph 4 Re-state judgement, link to long-term business goals. Conclusion : 1–2 summary sentences per body paragraph (including case study). 6.2 Analyse / Explain How (Cause-and-Effect) Introduction : Link two ideas together (cause and effect) → state what you're analysing (syllabus dot points) → include all case studies. Body Paragraph Purpose Paragraph 1 Cause/effect #1 — How is the business impacted? Why? Show cause and effect with case study. Paragraph 2 Cause/effect #2 — Same structure. Link to cause #1. Paragraph 3 Positive implications (LONG TERM) — Link to strategic role and business goals. Paragraph 4 Negative implications — Point out an issue. Conclusion : 1–2 summary sentences per body paragraph (including case study). 6.3 To Get 12+ Marks (20-mark questions) At least ONE paragraph on SWOT and one on Product Life Cycle SWOT: 2 body paragraphs — choose ONE part, do at least 2 examples Product Life Cycle: 1 body paragraph — show how ONE strategy changes through the PLC Full guides: Section IV Extended Response · Section III Business Report · Marketing Universal Essay ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Identifying target markets (process) vs segmentation and positioning (strategy) ⭐ Syllabus splits these. Identifying which group you sell to is step 4 of the marketing process . Dividing the market, differentiating the product and positioning it are the first dot point of marketing strategies . A "marketing strategies" question expects segmentation; a "marketing process" question expects target market identification Segmentation vs differentiation vs positioning Segmentation divides the market . Differentiation changes the product . Positioning changes the perception Price skimming vs Penetration pricing Skimming starts high and falls. Penetration starts low to buy share Publicity vs Public relations Publicity is free and unplanned . PR is planned and managed Cost-plus vs Competitive vs Market-based Cost-plus looks at your costs . Competitive looks at rivals . Market-based looks at supply and demand Selective vs Exclusive distribution Selective = several chosen outlets. Exclusive = one outlet per large area Standardisation vs Customisation Standardisation = same everywhere . Customisation = rebuilt per country Place vs location Place means distribution channels , not where the shop is. This is the single most misread P Loss leader vs Penetration pricing Loss leader = one product below cost to pull traffic. Penetration = the whole product's launch price 📝 Exam habits Never write about "Place" as if it means location. It is distribution: channel levels and channel intensity. In a 20-mark answer, name the strategy, then the business, then the outcome. "Apple uses price skimming" is 1 mark. "Apple uses price skimming, launching the Pro Max at $2,199 before reducing it once competitors respond, which maximises revenue from early adopters" is the full mark. 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Marketing mix The combination of product, price, promotion and place used to achieve marketing objectives Brand A name, term, symbol or design identifying a product and distinguishing it from competitors Price skimming Charging the highest possible price for a new or innovative product during the introduction stage before competitors enter Penetration pricing Charging the lowest price that still covers costs in order to gain market share quickly Loss leader Selling a product below cost price to attract customers who will also buy higher-margin items Publicity Free news or media coverage about a business's products Public relations Planned activities aimed at creating and maintaining favourable relationships with stakeholders E-marketing Internet marketing, allowing a business with online operations to reach a global audience Standardisation Using the same marketing strategy in every global market with only minor adjustments Back to: ① Role · 📕 Full note · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · MOC

title: Marketing — Full Module Note
text: 📕 Marketing — Full Module Note The whole module in one file. Split versions: ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies Scope: the full HSC Marketing module is examinable. 🔧 Maintenance note: sections 1–4 below are mirrored in the four split files. If one is corrected, correct both. Sections 5–8 exist only here. 1. Role of Marketing Definition : Marketing is the total system of interacting activities designed to plan, promote, price and distribute products to present and potential customers. 1.1 Strategic Role Translates the business goal of profit maximisation into reality Develops a marketing plan with actions and strategies to attain greater sales Modern emphasis: customer-oriented marketing — viewing the business through the customer's eyes Marketing today places strong emphasis on understanding consumer behaviour and satisfying customer needs/wants 1.2 Marketing Plan A marketing plan is where the business applies marketing strategies based on market research to understand what to sell, their SWOT, and how to position themselves It is the roadmap for how the business will attract and retain customers Aligns marketing activities with overall business goals 1.3 Interdependence with Other Functions Function Relationship with Marketing Operations Marketing provides demand forecasts and customer preferences → operations modifies production. Operations produces goods → marketing sells them Finance Finance provides budgets and funds for marketing. Marketing generates revenue that flows to finance to cover expenses Human Resources HR recruits and trains employees for marketing roles. Untrained staff = wrong market assessments = lower conversion rates and profits Case Study — BYD : Operations produces the "Blade Battery" → marketing promotes vehicle safety/reliability. Marketing provides customer feedback → operations modifies cars. When operations delivers quality, affordable EVs, marketing can sell them in more international markets. Profits are reinvested into factories and research, creating a cycle of continuous improvement. 1.4 Marketing Approaches Approach Core Idea Focus Production Consumers buy based on product quality Taking orders and delivering products Sales Increased competition requires aggressive selling Advertising to stimulate demand Marketing Find what customers want, then satisfy that need Customer orientation, market research, integrated strategies Societal Balance company profits with societal well-being Environmental and social responsibility Apple : Early iPhones used a sales approach (educating customers on features). As expectations grew, shifted to a marketing approach (persuasive, research-driven). Customer feedback led to larger screens, thinner builds, better cameras. 2014: larger iPhones released in response to consumer demand. 1.5 Customer Orientation Customer relationship begins with the sale (doesn't end there) After-sale service, warranties, fulfilling needs and wants Example: free car servicing, longer warranty periods 1.6 Relationship Marketing Core: customer loyalty → repeat sales Achieved through reward programs, customer care, after-sales service Development of long-term cost-effective and strong relationships with customers 1.7 Types of Markets A market = group of individuals/organisations that need or want a product, have the money to purchase it, are willing to spend, and are socially and legally authorised to buy. Market Type Description Examples Resource Market Primary production (mining, agriculture, forestry, fishing) Farmers, miners Industrial Market Industries/businesses purchasing products for production or operations Factories buying raw materials Intermediate Market Wholesalers and retailers who purchase finished products and resell for profit Coles, Woolworths Consumer Market Individuals who plan to use/consume products End consumers Consumer Market Segments Segment Description Example Mass market Appeals to all consumers Electricity, basic food Market segment Focus on one area of a market Sports cars Niche market Smaller section of a segment Teenage girl magazines 2. Influences of Marketing 2.1 Factors Influencing Customer Choice Why marketers study customer choice : To understand what motivates an individual to purchase a particular product. Market researchers ask: Who are our customers? What do they buy? When do they buy? How often do they buy? Why do they buy? Psychological (within the individual) Factor Key Point Perception How consumers view/interpret products Motives Internal drives to purchase Attitudes Learned predisposition towards a product Personality Unique psychological characteristics Self-image Buy products matching self-concept Learning Behaviour changes from experience Apple : iPhone 5c (colours) failed — quality expectations (psychological) were stronger than colour preference. iPhone 5s (metallic colours) succeeded — associated with quality/innovation. "Colour reveals your personality" — but consumers prioritised quality over colour. Sociocultural (other people and groups) Factor Key Point Social class Grouping by income, occupation, education Culture/subculture Shared values, multicultural considerations — businesses cater for different cultural groups as Australia becomes more multicultural Family and roles Family members influence decisions Reference groups Peer influence on purchases Apple : Social media/gaming/streaming popularity → marketing promotes camera, screen, processing specs to differentiate from competitors. Economic Condition Effect Marketing Response Boom Low unemployment, rising income, optimism Emphasise premium products; businesses expand production Recession High unemployment, falling income, caution Stress value and usefulness; customers seek functional, long-lasting products Apple : GFC → declining iPhone sales → developed low-cost iPhone 5c and continued selling older models. COVID-19 → released iPhone SE (2020) and "Mini" versions for price-conscious customers. Government Four types of government influence: Fiscal Policy : The government budget showing revenue sources (taxes) and spending. Used to expand or contract economic activity. Example: introduction of the GST or increases in income tax. Monetary Policy : Government through the Reserve Bank uses interest rates to control money supply and inflation. RBA adjusts the cash rate → affects bank interest rates → encourages or discourages consumer spending. Regulations : Laws that directly impact marketing activities. Breaches may result in financial penalties. Government Regulations (direct impact) : Laws regulating marketing concerns — product contents, health/safety, pricing strategies, distribution channels, ethical promotion. Apple : iPhone 6 launch delayed in China (privacy concerns). India regulations prevented store expansion for years, eased in 2020. India's $6.6B incentive program boosted local smartphone manufacturing. 2.2 Ethical Influences Unethical Practices Practice Definition Concealed facts Omitting information that could harm trust Puffery Exaggerated claims no reasonable person would take as factual Vague statements Ambiguous words consumers misinterpret Invasion of privacy Tracking web users for targeted advertising SUGGING Selling Under the Guise of a Survey — sales disguised as market research Other Ethical Issues Good taste : Subjective, depends on community sensitivities Health-damaging products : Self-regulatory codes (children's advertising, alcohol, smoking) Fair competition : False promises, exaggerated descriptions, high-pressure selling 2.3 Consumer Law (Legal Influences) Competition and Consumer Act 2010 — Two Purposes Protect consumers from misleading practices (misrepresenting products, deceptive advertising) Regulate trade practices that restrict competition Enforced by : ACCC (Australian Competition and Consumer Commission) and ASIC (Australian Securities and Investment Commission) Deceptive & Misleading Conduct Tactic Example Fine print Important conditions too small to read Before/after ads Misleading comparisons Tests and surveys Unsubstantiated claims False country of origin "Made in Australia" when made overseas Misleading packaging Size/shape gives wrong impression of contents Fake special offers "Limited time" when offer is permanent Bait and switch Advertise cheap items, sell expensive ones when they run out Dishonest advertising Deceptive words, false quality claims, fake price reductions Consumer Rights Right Details Implied conditions Unspoken/unwritten terms of contract — product must be fit for purpose; cannot claim false characteristics Warranties Promise to repair/replace faulty products — also a marketing tool if it includes superior options vs competitors Refunds Legally required if: faulty, doesn't match description, fails to work. NOT required if: customer changes mind, finds cheaper option, damages after purchase Price Discrimination Different prices in different markets Possible because markets are geographically spread or product differentiation exists Prohibited if it substantially reduces competition Also applies to discounts, credits, rebates, services and payment arrangements ACCC Case Studies Apple: iPhone/iPad misrepresentations — $9 million penalty Error 53 — staff misled customers about repair rights Consumer guarantee representations — ACCC took action Apple gave undertaking to improve policies Woolworths: ACCC court case over misleading grocery pricing/discount practices 3. Marketing Processes 3.1 Steps in Developing a Marketing Plan Situational Analysis Market Research Establish marketing objectives Identify target markets Develop marketing strategies Implementation, monitoring and controlling 3.2 Situational Analysis SWOT The most crucial step — management must understand current position and where heading. Must be based on meaningful market research . Internal (controllable) External (monitor constantly) Positive Strengths Opportunities Negative Weaknesses Threats Apple SWOT : Strength = brand reputation | Weakness = high price | Opportunity = AI partnerships | Threat = Asian competitors (Xiaomi, OPPO) Product Life Cycle Stage Strategy Introduction Build awareness, heavy promotion, limited range, high costs, low/negative profits Growth Differentiate brand, expand product line, competition increases, shift from "what it is" to "why ours is best" Maturity Defend market share, stress value, modify product, sales peak, market saturated Decline Reduce spending, consider product deletion, product becomes outdated CD = decline | PCs = maturity | EVs = growth | Tablets = maturity | Driverless cars = introduction McDonald's French fries : Introduction (1940s) → Growth (1940s–1990) → Maturity (1990, recipe change due to health campaign, share price fell) → Renewal (Loaded, Twisted, Waffle, Cheesy Bacon fries) Marketing strategies change through each stage — promotion emphasis, pricing approach, distribution channels, and product features all adapt to the current lifecycle position. 3.4 Market Research Definition : Systematic collection, recording and analysis of information concerning a specific marketing problem. Steps Determine information needs Collect data (primary & secondary) Analyse and interpret data Primary vs Secondary Primary Secondary Source Business conducts own research Others' research Methods Surveys, observations, focus groups Internet, Census, industry reports Pros Specific, current, controlled Cheap, available, broader context Cons Expensive, time-consuming May be outdated, not specific enough What Market Research Reveals Consumer needs/wants and preferences Target market income → assists pricing decisions Feedback for product/service improvements Competitor analysis (prices, features, service) → assists product differentiation Census data → existing and potential customer characteristics Apple : Emails post-purchase feedback surveys. Monthly country-by-country surveys reveal: purchase drivers vs competitors, most-used features, demographics, satisfaction levels. "Every month, Apple surveys iPhone buyers" — reveals what drives customers to buy iPhone vs Android. Drives continuous improvement and competitive differentiation. 3.5 Marketing Objectives Definition : Realistic and measurable goals achieved through the marketing plan. Must be aligned to business goals but more customer oriented . Three Common Objectives Objective Strategy Increase market share Promotional campaigns, competitive pricing, product differentiation Expand product mix New product development, product line extensions Maximise customer service Feedback forms, after-sales service, staff training Market Share Formula Market Share (%) = (Company Sales / Total Industry Sales) × 100 Why businesses want to increase market share : More customers → more sales → competitive advantage → customer satisfaction → repeat purchases → profit maximisation. Relationship between customer satisfaction and profits : Satisfied customers purchase again and recommend to peers → increased sales → increased profits. Extra cash reinvested back into the business for growth. 3.6 Target Markets & Segmentation ⚠️ Syllabus placement. Only "identifying target markets" is a marketing process dot point (step 4). "Market segmentation, product/service differentiation and positioning" is the first dot point under marketing strategies (§4). They are grouped here for teaching, but in an exam a "marketing strategies" question expects segmentation and positioning. Target market : Group of present and potential customers a business intends to sell to. Primary : Most resources directed here Secondary : Smaller, less important segment Why identify target markets : To identify appropriate promotional strategies, improve ability to increase sales, ensure products meet customer needs/expectations. Segmentation Bases Base Criteria Apple Example Geographic Location, region, climate Strong in Americas, Europe, Greater China Demographic Age, income, occupation, education Young to middle-aged, middle to high income, professionals/students Psychographic Lifestyle, values, attitudes, personality, socioeconomic groups Innovation-seekers, quality-focused, early adopters, brand-loyal Behavioural Buying patterns, brand loyalty, usage, benefits sought Apple ecosystem loyalty, repeat purchasers Apple's Product-Segment Targets iPhone : Broad audience — young adults, professionals, tech enthusiasts iPad : Creative professionals, students Mac : Developers, creative professionals Apple Watch : Fitness enthusiasts, professionals 3.7 Product Positioning ⚠️ Positioning is a marketing STRATEGY in the syllabus , not a process. See the note at §3.6. Product/service differentiation belongs with it: making a similar product appear different from and better than competitors', which gives the seller control over price. Definition : How potential buyers from the target market perceive the product The business decides on the image it wishes to create for a product/service Brand names evoke certain images — e.g. No Frills (budget), Rolex (luxury) This image gives the product its position in the market Positioning is linked to the marketing mix — all 4Ps must reinforce the desired position 3.8 Implementation, Monitoring & Controlling Definitions Implementation : Putting strategies into operation — the how, where and when Monitoring : Checking and observing actual progress of the marketing plan Controlling : Comparing planned vs actual performance, taking corrective action to ensure objectives are attained Financial Forecasts Cost estimate + Revenue estimate Compare sales potential and revenue forecasts with anticipated expenditures Easier to forecast costs than revenue (costs are more controllable) Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) KPI Purpose Sales analysis Evaluate current performance and strategy effectiveness using sales data Market share analysis Compare performance against competitors Marketing profitability analysis Break down total marketing costs into specific marketing activities Revising the Marketing Strategy If objectives not met, changes include: Modify the 4Ps (marketing mix adjustments) New product development (add products) Product deletion (remove underperforming products) 4.
