Uses cost-plus method covering: transportation, taxes, warehousing, tariffs Market customised pricing Prices set according to local market conditions and exchange rate fluctuations Standardised pricing Same price anywhere in the world — risky due to different purchasing powers iPhone X prices around the world (64GB $US) : Russia $1,390 | EU $1,377 | UK $1,330 | China $1,280 | Australia $1,259 | USA $999 Factors affecting global pricing : Currency exchange rates, transportation costs, local taxes, tariffs, competition in overseas markets. Global Promotional Strategies Use variety of mediums: TV, Internet, radio Must consider language, religion, culture Competitive Positioning Formal process of determining how to differentiate from competitors Value proposition includes: Operational excellence Customer intimacy Product Leadership Apple : Historically positioned at high end (quality/design). As developed markets saturated, turned to high-growth emerging economies (China, India). 2014: secured contract with China Mobile (largest carrier) — significant sales increase. Huawei has since overtaken Apple in market share. 4.5 Section IV Essay Structures Assess/Evaluate/Explain the Importance of (Judgement-Based) Introduction : Start with judgement sentence → state what you're evaluating (use syllabus dot points) → include all case studies. Body Paragraph Purpose Paragraph 1 Answer the question — judgement with brief overview. Define key concepts. Include case study. Paragraph 2 Advantages — prove they are advantages by linking to a topic-specific goal. Use stats. Paragraph 3 Disadvantages — prove they are disadvantages by linking to a topic-specific goal. Paragraph 4 Re-state judgement, link to long-term business goals. Conclusion : 1-2 summary sentences per body paragraph (including case study). Analyse/Explain How (Cause-and-Effect) Introduction : Link two ideas together (cause and effect) → state what you're analysing (syllabus dot points) → include all case studies. Body Paragraph Purpose Paragraph 1 Cause/effect #1 — How is the business impacted? Why? Show cause and effect with case study. Paragraph 2 Cause/effect #2 — Same structure. Link to cause #1. Paragraph 3 Positive Implications (LONG TERM) — Link to strategic role and business goals. Paragraph 4 Negative Implications — Point out an issue. Conclusion : 1-2 summary sentences per body paragraph (including case study). To Get 12+ Marks (20-mark questions) At least ONE paragraph on SWOT AND one on Product Life Cycle SWOT: 2 body paragraphs — choose ONE part, do at least 2 examples Product Life Cycle: 1 body paragraph — show how ONE strategy changes through PLC 5. McDonald's Marketing — Detailed Case Study Source : "BUSINESS CASE STUDY — McDonald's" by A.J. Stanshall (2024) Strategic Role "Accelerating the Arches" (2020) → "Accelerating the Arches 2.0" (2023) Focus: maximise marketing, brand and affordability Goal: shift from brand engagement to brand advocacy (customers recommending the brand) Factors Influencing Customer Choice Factor McDonald's Example Psychological Crocs collab (2023) — nostalgia, belonging; "Health halo" effect (fries next to salad = perceived healthier) Sociocultural China middle class expansion: 80M (2002) → 500M+ (2024) = more disposable income Economic Rising inflation increases input costs; efficiency gains to offset (can't always raise prices) Government UK Calorie Labelling Regulations (2022) — mandatory calorie info at all touchpoints Consumer Laws Labelling : Australia NZ Food Standards Code; NSW Food Act 2003; mandatory kilojoule labelling. 2015 breach: animated menu boards hid kilojoule info. 2018 Cancer Council study: labelling had limited impact on consumer behaviour Advertising : Quebec forbids advertising to children under 13. 2013 class action — Happy Meal toys timed with films. Settled 2020: $1M donation + changed practices Ethical Considerations 1997 McLibel case : McDonald's UK guilty of exploiting children with advertising 2020 breach : TV ad "naughty girl" rewarded with McDonald's — aimed at children, only unhealthy options 2023 breach : "Player of the Week" awards gave children occasional food products (violated voluntary code) Part of Australian Association of National Advertisers (self-regulatory) SWOT Strengths Diversified income; global brand; high-quality standards; growth plan; ~uniform menu; access to capital; large market share; technology Weaknesses Lack of central control over franchises (2023 IT glitch); perception of unhealthiness; multiple jurisdictions Opportunities Innovation/differentiation; reinvest in restaurants; digital media; social/environmental performance; new products Threats Negative publicity; environmental regulations; supply chain interruptions; inflation; competition (BK, Domino's, Starbucks, Wendy's); wage costs; legal complexity Product Life Cycle Burgers = mature; Chicken & coffee = growth French fries : Introduction (1940s) → Growth (1940s–1990) → Maturity (1990, recipe change due to health campaign, share price fell) → Renewal (Loaded, Twisted, Waffle, Cheesy Bacon fries) Market Research Traditional: surveys, questionnaires, sales data Modern: apps provide real-time data (what sells, when, where, to whom) AI-powered dynamic pricing : adjusts menu prices, tests consumer price resistance Moving towards hyper-personalised segmentation using loyalty data — "thousands of customer cohorts, where we used to have less than ten" Market Segmentation Base Examples Demographic Happy Meals (age); McCafé (older); campaigns for Black/Hispanic/Asian consumers (US); Halal/Kosher/No beef in India (religion); Family Bundles (family size) Psychographic Interests, attitudes, values, lifestyles; data-driven personalised segmentation Behavioural Loyalty, purchase frequency, transaction value; paper cards → app-only loyalty (2019); rewards points; predict future patterns Geographic Malaysian soup, McAloo Tikki (India), Teriyaki Mac (Japan), Prosperity Burger (Chinese New Year) Product Strategies COVID simplified menu → core products = ~70% of sales in top 6 markets Branding : Golden arches more recognisable than the Christian cross; 17 "billion-dollar brands"; Big Mac alone >US$1B Packaging : Reinforces brand messaging; new worldwide packaging launched late 2020 Pricing Strategies Strategy McDonald's Example Loss leaders Loose Change Menu (AU$1+) — attracts customers who also buy higher-margin items Price points "Value ladder" from Loose Change → Standard → Gourmet (Chicken Deluxe) Price bundling McValue Meals — Big Mac meal $13.35 = 14% saving vs individual items AI pricing Dynamic pricing models test consumer price resistance at different stores Promotion US$4 billion/year on promotion worldwide; 3rd largest ad spender in Australia Regional "co-ops" for local advertising; shift from advertising to engaging 2022 FIFA World Cup : Largest global campaign — McDelivery in 75 countries, 10 languages; double-digit delivery sales increases Publicity : Negative — Super Size Me, McLibel, China meat scandal, McMillion$, Israeli soldiers (2024) Sales promotions : FIFA World Cup — yellow/red card = free items in Canada Place/Distribution Producer → Retailer → Customer channel; ~42,000 restaurants; selective distribution Delivery : 55,000 orders at any moment; US$16B delivery sales (2023) Focus on Drive-Thru expansion Global Marketing "One McDonald's Way" : Best innovations rolled out across multiple markets Standardisation : ~2.5M Big Macs/day; ~15 core global items; economies of scale; McCafé becoming exclusive global coffee brand (100+ equipment types → 5 suppliers) Customisation : Adapted to local tastes and cultures in different markets 6. Extended Response Scaffolds & Worked Examples 2021 HSC — "Analyse how a situational analysis (SWOT, product life cycle) may affect marketing strategies" Model body paragraph (Threats → Product Strategy): Apple has threats such as competition from low-cost Asian providers (Huawei, Xiaomi). Threats are external factors the business cannot control. This has impacted Apple's product strategy — they position as high-quality/luxury with recognisable branding (bitten apple logo) and minimalist white/silver packaging. However, focus on camera improvements raised questions about innovation, affecting market share (17% vs Samsung's 20% in Q2 2023, though improved to 23% vs 16% by Q4 2024). This meets customer expectations, minimising impact of low-cost competitors. Answering "Assess" on Promotional Mix "Assess why a promotional mix is important in marketing goods and services" Assess = judgement of value and importance Structure: Intro (define + case studies) → 3 body paragraphs (one per strategy) → Conclusion (restate judgement + link to business goal) 2025 Past HSC — "Explain how target market impacts on people, processes and physical evidence strategies" Must cover ALL 3 strategies for top marks. Use PEEL structure. PEEL example (Processes): P: Processes are influenced by the target market because businesses design processes to meet target market needs. Apple's target market values convenience, speed, and innovation. E: Apple uses online ordering, pre-orders, roaming payment systems, free iOS upgrades. E: These processes reduce waiting times, improve convenience, and reflect Apple's innovative brand image. Efficient processes help Apple provide seamless customer experience. L: Therefore, Apple's target market strongly influences its processes, maintaining customer satisfaction, loyalty, and competitive advantage. 2025 Past HSC — Q26 Q26 (20 marks) : "Analyse the relationship between market segmentation and marketing strategies" 2012 Section IV : "Why are ethical behaviour and government regulation important in marketing?" (analyse question) 7. HSC Exam Tips Key Verb Requirements Verb Action Identify/State Name it — no explanation needed Define One clear meaning Describe Characteristics and features Explain How/why — cause and effect Discuss For AND against, then judgement Analyse Break down, examine relationships Evaluate/Assess Weighed judgement with evidence Justify Support a decision with evidence PEEL Structure P oint → E xplain → E vidence (case study) → L ink back to question "Explain" Scaffold Define → Relationship/impact → Implications → Link (Therefore...) "Describe" Scaffold Definition → Characteristics and features → Relationship between components → Implications → Link Always Include Specific case study examples (Apple, McDonald's, BYD, etc.) Business terminology from the syllabus Cause-and-effect reasoning (how → therefore → which leads to) Links to business goals (profit maximisation, growth, competitive advantage) 8. Key Definitions Quick Reference Term One-Line Definition Marketing Total system to plan, promote, price and distribute products Marketing plan Actions and strategies to attain greater sales Marketing objectives Realistic, measurable goals from the marketing plan Target market Group of customers a business intends to sell to Market segmentation Dividing a market into distinct similar-characteristic groups Marketing mix Combination of Product, Price, Promotion, Place SWOT Internal strengths/weaknesses + external opportunities/threats Market research Systematic collection and analysis of marketing information Primary data First-hand data collected by the business Secondary data Others' research (Census, industry reports) Market share Company sales ÷ total industry sales × 100 Product life cycle Introduction → Growth → Maturity → Decline Customer orientation Relationship begins with the sale Relationship marketing Focus on loyalty and repeat sales E-marketing Internet marketing using digital technologies Global branding Worldwide use of name, logo, term or symbol Standardisation Same marketing strategies worldwide Customisation Different strategies for each country/market Puffery Exaggerated claims no reasonable person believes SUGGING Selling disguised as market research Price discrimination Different prices in different markets ACCC Enforces Competition and Consumer Act 2010 TNC Transnational Corporation — operates beyond domestic market Fiscal policy Government budget showing revenue (taxes) and spending Monetary policy RBA adjusts interest rates to control money supply and inflation Product positioning How potential buyers perceive the product in the market Intensive distribution Product available everywhere (saturate market) Selective distribution Moderate proportion of outlets Exclusive distribution One retail outlet in large geographic area See also: Finance | Operations | Human Resources | Case Studies | MOC

title: Marketing Syllabus Summary
text: Marketing - Syllabus Summary 1. Role of Marketing Strategic role: translate business objectives, including profit maximisation, into customer-focused plans and sales activity Marketing plan: research-based objectives, target markets and strategies aligned with business goals Customer orientation: understand and satisfy customer needs; continue the relationship after the sale Relationship marketing: loyalty, repeat sales, customer care, rewards and after-sales service Marketing approaches: production, sales, marketing and societal Market types: resource, industrial, intermediate and consumer markets Consumer markets: mass market, market segment and niche market Interdependence: Operations uses demand forecasts and customer feedback to plan production Finance funds marketing and receives revenue generated by sales HR recruits and trains marketing and customer-facing staff 2. Influences on Marketing Customer choice: Psychological: perception, motives, attitudes, personality, self-image and learning Sociocultural: social class, culture, family, roles and reference groups Economic: boom, recession, income, employment and consumer confidence Government: fiscal policy, monetary policy, regulation and industry incentives Ethical influences: Concealed facts, puffery, vague claims, privacy concerns and SUGGING Good taste, health-damaging products, fair competition and pressure selling Legal influences: Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), including the Australian Consumer Law ACCC and ASIC enforcement Misleading or deceptive conduct, false claims, fine print, bait-and-switch and misleading packaging Consumer guarantees, implied conditions, warranties and refunds for faulty or misdescribed goods Price discrimination restrictions where competition is substantially reduced 3. Marketing Processes Marketing plan sequence: situational analysis → market research → objectives → identify target markets → develop strategies → implementation, monitoring and control Situational analysis: SWOT: internal strengths and weaknesses; external opportunities and threats Product life cycle: introduction, growth, maturity and decline; adapt the mix at each stage Market research: Identify information needs → collect primary/secondary data → analyse and interpret Primary sources: surveys, observation and focus groups; specific and current, but costly and time-consuming Secondary sources: Census, industry reports and existing research; accessible and lower-cost, but may be outdated or broad Marketing objectives: measurable goals aligned with the business, including market share, product mix and customer service Target markets: primary and secondary groups; identify customers to guide product, price, promotion and distribution choices Implementation: put strategies into action, including how, where and when Monitoring and control: compare actual and planned results; use corrective action KPIs: sales analysis, market-share analysis and marketing profitability analysis Strategy revision: modify the 4Ps, develop new products or delete underperforming products 4. Marketing Strategies Market segmentation: geographic, demographic, psychographic and behavioural bases Differentiation: distinguish the offer from competitors; align features and benefits with customer priorities Positioning: desired place/image in the target market; reinforce it across the marketing mix Product: Quality, design, features, packaging, labelling, brand and guarantees Tangible and intangible product elements; adapt product strategy to the life-cycle stage Price: Methods: cost-plus, market-based and competitive pricing Strategies: skimming, penetration, competitive, loss leader, price points, prestige, bundling and dynamic pricing Legal limit: price discrimination must not substantially reduce competition Promotion: Advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, publicity, public relations and direct marketing Match message and channel to target market; distinguish free publicity from planned PR Place/distribution: Direct, one-level, two-level and three-level channels Intensive, selective and exclusive distribution Online retailing, direct-to-consumer sales, warehousing, transport and order processing Extended marketing mix for services: People: staff skills, service and customer interactions Processes: service-delivery steps and convenience Physical evidence: service environment and tangible brand cues E-marketing: web pages, podcasts, SMS, blogs and social media; digital channels affect product information, price comparison, distribution and promotion Global marketing: Global branding and positioning Standardisation, customisation or a combination Global pricing: standardised, customised and market-customised pricing Adjust for exchange rates, transport, taxes, tariffs, language, culture, religion and local tastes Choose promotional channels suited to each market See also: Marketing FULL | Marketing 1 Role | Marketing 2 Influences | Marketing 3 Processes | Marketing 4 Strategies | MOC

title: Universal Marketing Essay — McDonald's Case Study
text: Universal Marketing Essay — McDonald's Case Study Replace [BRACKETED TEXT] with question-specific content. Covers influences, processes, and strategies. Introduction [TERM 1] refers to the [formal definition from syllabus]. [TERM 2] refers to [formal definition]. In the context of McDonald's, the world's largest Quick Service Restaurant (QSR) chain operating 45,356 locations across 100+ countries with global systemwide sales of $139 billion in 2025, these concepts are critical to sustaining competitive advantage. McDonald's has effectively implemented [APPROACH/STRATEGY] to address [CHALLENGE/OPPORTUNITY]. This essay will evaluate [TOPIC FROM QUESTION] by examining [POINT 1], [POINT 2], and the interdependence with [POINT 3], demonstrating that McDonald's approach has been [EFFECTIVENESS JUDGEMENT]. Body 1 — Role of Marketing The strategic role of marketing at McDonald's extends beyond promotion to encompass the entire process of identifying, anticipating, and satisfying customer requirements profitably. McDonald's generated $25.9 billion in consolidated revenue in 2024, growing to $26.9 billion in 2025, while serving over 70 million customers daily worldwide and 1.7 million in Australia alone. In the Australian market, McDonald's holds approximately 23.2% market share of fast food revenue, operating 1,092 restaurants with over 110,000 employees, making it the largest employer of youth in the country. Marketing is interdependent with other business functions at McDonald's. Human Resources supports marketing through the 'Mates Make It Maccas' employer branding campaign, which recruits staff while simultaneously reinforcing the brand's community-oriented image. Finance supports marketing decisions through the allocation of approximately $1.4 billion in global annual advertising expenditure. Operations ensures consistent product quality across 45,000+ locations, which underpins the brand promise communicated through marketing. This interdependence ensures that marketing strategies are both financially viable and operationally deliverable, creating a cohesive approach to achieving McDonald's organisational objectives. Body 2 — Influences on Marketing McDonald's operates within a complex environment of ethical, legal, economic, and social influences that shape its marketing approach. Under the Australian Consumer Law (Schedule 2 of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010), McDonald's must ensure all products meet consumer guarantees of acceptable quality, fitness for purpose, and accurate description. The ACCC actively monitors McDonald's for misleading conduct, requiring transparent nutritional labelling including kilojoule counts on all menu items, which directly influences how products are promoted. Ethical influences significantly affect McDonald's marketing decisions. The company avoids SUGGING (suggestive selling that pressures customers) by training staff in consultative approaches rather than aggressive upselling. Marketing communications avoid vague or exaggerated health claims, instead providing specific nutritional information. McDonald's must balance the invasion of privacy concerns arising from its MyMcDonald's Rewards app, which collects purchase data from 150 million+ global loyalty members, requiring compliance with the Australian Privacy Act 1988. Furthermore, economic conditions heavily influence marketing strategy — during the current cost-of-living crisis, McDonald's Loose Change Menu (items priced from $1 to $5 AUD) has become a critical tool for maintaining customer traffic, demonstrating how fiscal policy, monetary policy, and consumer confidence directly shape pricing and promotional decisions. Body 3 — Marketing Processes McDonald's marketing process begins with clearly defined organisational objectives: increasing global systemwide sales (achieved 7% growth to $139 billion in 2025), growing digital revenue to 40% of total sales by 2027, and expanding to 50,000 restaurants worldwide. These objectives inform target market identification — McDonald's primary target is families with children (served through Happy Meals and playground facilities), secondary targets include youth aged 16-24 reached through social media marketing and McCafé positioning, and tertiary targets encompass working adults seeking convenience through drive-thru (60-70% of Australian sales) and delivery services. Market research underpins all marketing decisions. McDonald's employs primary research including customer satisfaction surveys, taste tests for new product development (such as the 'Menu Heist' campaign bringing international items to Australia in 2025), and focus groups. Secondary research from IBISWorld, ABS data, and competitor financial reports informs strategic planning. The SWOT analysis reveals McDonald's strengths (brand recognition, scale, digital infrastructure) against threats (health-conscious consumer trends, rising input costs, competitor innovation such as KFC's 'Saucy' rebranding). Market segmentation further refines the approach — geographic segmentation drives localised menus (McOz in Australia, McArabia in the Middle East), demographic segmentation targets different age groups, and psychographic segmentation addresses lifestyle preferences from budget-conscious to premium McCafé consumers. Body 4 — Marketing Strategies McDonald's employs a comprehensive 7Ps marketing mix to achieve its objectives. The pricing strategy combines loss leaders (Loose Change Menu items like $2 Cheeseburgers and $1.50 Soft Serve cones that drive foot traffic) with psychological pricing ($9.95 meals) and competitive pricing benchmarked against KFC and Hungry Jack's. The product strategy centres on 17 billion-dollar brands, continuous innovation (McPlant, McSpicy), and menu localisation — demonstrated by the VEGEMITE McShaker Fries exclusive to Australia launched in January 2025. Promotional strategies represent a $1.4 billion global investment encompassing digital marketing through the McDonald's App (personalised offers and loyalty rewards driving $40 billion in loyalty-member sales), traditional advertising maintaining the iconic 'I'm Lovin' It' global campaign, and sales promotions such as the McDonald's Monopoly six-week prize giveaway in September 2024. Distribution strategies leverage the franchise model (95% franchise-owned globally, 80%+ in Australia) to minimise capital risk while maximising market coverage, complemented by drive-thru innovation including AI-powered ordering and delivery partnerships with Uber Eats. The digital transformation — with $10 billion in digital sales in 2025 representing 20% of system revenue — positions McDonald's to meet its 2027 target of 40% digital revenue, demonstrating effective integration of e-marketing strategies within the broader marketing framework. Body 5 — Evaluation and Challenges While McDonald's marketing approach has delivered consistent growth — evidenced by 3.1% global comparable sales growth in 2025 and 23.2% Australian market share — significant challenges remain. Health-conscious consumer trends continue to threaten the core fast-food positioning, requiring ongoing investment in healthier menu options and transparent nutritional communication. The competitive landscape intensifies as KFC invests in rebranding ('Saucy' campaign), Hungry Jack's pursues aggressive flame-grilled differentiation, and new entrants like Wendy's (opening its first Australian store in January 2025) increase market fragmentation. Economic headwinds including inflation, rising food costs, and fluctuating consumer confidence directly impact marketing effectiveness. However, McDonald's demonstrates strategic agility — the Loose Change Menu was specifically developed to address cost-of-living pressures, while the MyMcDonald's Rewards loyalty program (150 million+ active members generating $40 billion in sales) creates switching costs that insulate against competitive threats. The interdependence between marketing and operations ensures that strategic decisions are implementable across 45,000+ locations, while the franchise model distributes marketing costs while maintaining brand consistency. Overall, McDonald's marketing approach has been [EFFECTIVE/INEFFECTIVE] in achieving [OBJECTIVE FROM QUESTION], though continued adaptation to health trends, digital transformation, and economic conditions will determine long-term success. Conclusion In conclusion, McDonald's comprehensive approach to marketing — encompassing the strategic role of marketing, response to ethical, legal, and economic influences, systematic marketing processes, and integrated 7Ps strategies — has enabled the company to maintain its position as the world's largest QSR chain. Through value-based pricing strategies, digital transformation generating $10 billion in 2025, and market segmentation targeting families, youth, and budget-conscious consumers, McDonald's has achieved 7% systemwide sales growth to $139 billion. While challenges persist regarding health perceptions, competitive intensity, and economic uncertainty, the evidence demonstrates that McDonald's marketing strategy remains [OVERALL JUDGEMENT]. The company's ability to balance global brand consistency with local market adaptation — exemplified by Australian innovations such as the Loose Change Menu and 'Mates Make It Maccas' campaign — positions McDonald's to achieve its ambitious 2027 targets of 50,000 locations and 40% digital revenue.

LIQUIDITY Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities ideal 2:1 SOLVENCY Gearing Ratio = Total Liabilities / Owners' Equity ideal 0.5:1 to 1:1 PROFITABILITY Gross Profit Ratio = (Gross Profit / Sales) x 100 higher is better Net Profit Ratio = (Net Profit / Sales) x 100 higher is better Return on Owners' = (Net Profit / Owners' Equity) x 100 higher is better Equity EFFICIENCY Expense Ratio = (Total Expenses / Sales) x 100 lowest possible Accounts Receivable = Step 1: Sales / Accounts Receivable Turnover Step 2: 365 / Step 1 answer ideal 30 days BREAK-EVEN Break-Even (units) = Fixed Costs / (Selling Price - Variable Cost) Contribution = Selling Price - Variable Cost per unit Margin of Safety = Actual sales - Break-even sales The Three Financial Statements CASH FLOW STATEMENT Opening Cash Balance + Cash Receipts - Cash Payments = Closing Cash Balance INCOME STATEMENT Sales Less Sales Returns = NET SALES Less COGS (Opening Stock + Purchases - Closing Stock) = GROSS PROFIT Less Expenses (selling + administrative + financial) = NET PROFIT Check: Gross Profit Ratio - Expense Ratio = Net Profit Ratio BALANCE SHEET Owners' Equity = Assets (Current + Non-Current) - Liabilities (Current + Non-Current) The Verbs Verb What to do Marks guide Identify / State Name it — no explanation 1–2 Outline Sketch in general terms 2–3 Describe Features and characteristics 2–3 Distinguish Differences between two things 3–4 Explain Cause and effect — how and why 3–4 Analyse Relationships and implications 4–6 Discuss For and against, then judgement 5–6 Assess / Evaluate Weighted judgement with evidence 7–8 Recommend Course of action with justification 7–8 Exam Tips Always apply theory to a case study — Apple, McDonald's, BYD. Use specific data — ratios, figures, percentages, dates. Show interdependence between the four functions. Interpret, don't just calculate — a ratio means nothing without a judgement on it. Link back to the strategic role — cost leadership/differentiation (Ops), profit maximisation (Marketing), the five objectives (Finance), effectiveness indicators (HR). Know your verbs and match answer length to marks. Cross-Topic Threads Top-band answers integrate across topics. These are the highest-value links. Thread Where it connects JIT inventory Operations 4 Strategies (management strategy) → Finance 4 Strategies (frees working capital, improves liquidity) Interdependence Every module's ① Role file — required in almost every extended response Globalisation Operations 4 Strategies (global sourcing) · Marketing 4 Strategies (standardisation vs customisation) · Finance 4 Strategies (exchange rates, hedging) · Human Resources 4 Strategies (global HR) Technology Influences all four functions — automation, e-marketing, HRIS, e-procurement. Each module's ② Influences file Cost leadership Operations 1 Role (strategic role) → Finance 4 Strategies (cost controls, expense ratio) Training Human Resources 3 Processes (development) → Operations 4 Strategies (quality, productivity) → Finance 4 Strategies (cost vs return) Ethics and CSR Operations 2 Influences (triple bottom line) · Marketing 2 Influences (deceptive conduct) · Finance 3 Processes (window dressing) · Human Resources 2 Influences (fair treatment) Legislation Operations 2 Influences (the ten Acts) · Marketing 2 Influences (Competition and Consumer Act) · Human Resources 2 Influences (Fair Work Act, WHS)

title: Operations 1 · Role of Operations Management
text: ⚙️ Operations 1 · Role of Operations Management Operations · ① Role ← you are here · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Operations module is examinable. This file covers the Role of operations management dot points only. Definition : Operations refers to the business processes of transformation and value adding . Transformation : converting inputs into outputs Value adding : creating extra value as inputs become outputs. In manufacturing this is physical change; in services it is the application of knowledge and skills 1. Strategic Role of Operations Operations contributes to the strategic direction of the business through two generic strategies : Strategy Definition How it is achieved Cost leadership Having the lowest costs and being the most price-competitive while remaining profitable Economies of scale, automation, bulk buying, eliminating waste, standardisation, global sourcing Goods/services differentiation Distinguishing goods or services from competitors Goods : vary features, quality, augmented features (warranty, delivery). Services : vary the amount of time, level of expertise, qualifications of staff ⭐ Exam link : Almost every Operations extended response should end by linking back to cost leadership or differentiation . That is the strategic role. 2. Goods vs Services Goods Services Tangible — can be stored Intangible — produced and consumed simultaneously Standardised or customised Standardised (fast food) or customised (legal advice) Quality measured by durability and fitness for purpose Quality measured by professionalism and reliability Classification of goods: Pure goods — no service component (e.g. tinned food) Pure services — no goods component (e.g. financial advice) Goods with a service component — (e.g. a car with a warranty) 3. Interdependence with Other Key Business Functions Function Relationship with Operations Marketing Marketing provides demand forecasts and customer preferences → operations modifies production. Operations produces the goods → marketing sells them Finance Finance provides budgets for equipment, technology and inputs. Operations controls costs, which drives profitability Human Resources HR recruits and trains production staff. Operations determines skill needs and staffing levels. Productivity depends directly on workforce quality ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Cost leadership vs lowest price Cost leadership is about your costs . A low-cost business can still charge a premium and pocket the margin Transformation vs value adding Transformation is the conversion . Value adding is the extra worth created by it Goods vs services Goods can be stored . Services are produced and consumed at the same moment 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Operations The business process of transformation and value adding Transformation Converting inputs into outputs Value adding Creating extra value as inputs become outputs Cost leadership Having the lowest costs and being the most price competitive while remaining profitable Differentiation Distinguishing goods or services from those of competitors Next: ② Influences on Operations · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Operations 2 · Influences on Operations
text: 🌐 Operations 2 · Influences on Operations Operations · ① Role · ② Influences ← you are here · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Operations module is examinable. This file covers the Influences on operations management dot points only. 1. The Seven Influences Influence Detail Globalisation Removal of trade barriers; operations structured around global production facilities. Opportunity : global markets, economies of scale, global sourcing. Threat : intensified competition Technology Increased efficiency, reduced costs, consistent quality, higher productivity. Includes both administrative and processing technology Quality expectations Goods : design, fitness for purpose, durability. Services : professionalism, reliability, level of customisation. Failure → dissatisfaction, returns, damaged reputation Cost-based competition Pressure to lower production costs. Methods: eliminate waste, standardise, high volume, automate, economies of scale, bulk buying Government policies Changes in taxation, industrial relations, environmental regulation, training requirements — all create compliance costs Legal regulation Compliance with legislation across WHS, environment, food safety, fair trading and industrial relations. Compliance costs are the expenses of meeting these requirements — see §2 below Environmental sustainability Operating without compromising resources for future generations. Methods: minimise waste, recycle, reduce carbon footprint 2. Legal Regulation — The Actual Acts Naming the Act with its year and jurisdiction is a mark. "The Environmental Protection Act" is not an answer — no NSW Act has that name. (Cth) = Commonwealth, national. (NSW) = state. Act What the Act actually requires What it costs operations Regulator Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) Imposes a duty of care — the employer must eliminate or minimise risks so far as is reasonably practicable, identify hazards, train and supervise staff, and consult workers on safety decisions Safety equipment, training time, signage, incident reporting systems, safety audits SafeWork NSW Workers Compensation Act 1987 (NSW) Every employer must hold a workers compensation insurance policy . Injured workers receive income support and medical costs on a no-fault basis — they don't have to prove the employer was negligent Insurance premiums, which rise with the business's claims history icare · SIRA Protection of the Environment Operations Act 1997 (NSW) (the POEO Act) Businesses conducting scheduled activities (chemical production, waste processing, electricity generation, intensive livestock) must hold an environment protection licence . Empowers the EPA to issue clean-up, prevention and prohibition notices . Penalties to $5 million for corporations Licence fees, emissions monitoring, effluent treatment, waste disposal contracts NSW EPA Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (Cth) (the EPBC Act) Any action likely to have a significant impact on a matter of national environmental significance — threatened species, world heritage areas, wetlands — must be referred for federal approval Environmental impact assessment, project delays, redesign Federal environment department Waste Avoidance and Resource Recovery Act 2001 (NSW) Sets NSW waste reduction targets and imposes a waste levy on material sent to landfill, deliberately making disposal more expensive than recovery The levy itself, plus separation and recycling systems NSW EPA Food Act 2003 (NSW) Businesses handling food must notify the authority, appoint a food safety supervisor , and keep premises, equipment and handling practices to the Food Standards Code. Creates offences for selling unsafe or falsely described food Supervisor training, temperature monitoring, cleaning schedules, inspections NSW Food Authority Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (contains the Australian Consumer Law, Schedule 2) Bans misleading and deceptive conduct , guarantees goods are of acceptable quality and fit for purpose , and imposes product safety standards and mandatory recalls. Also bans anti-competitive conduct such as price fixing and resale price maintenance Quality assurance systems, accurate labelling, recall capability, warranty servicing ACCC Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) Establishes the National Employment Standards (11 minimum entitlements), minimum wages, awards, enterprise bargaining, and protection from unfair dismissal . Includes the right to rest and meal breaks under the relevant award Wage costs, rostering constraints, penalty rates, redundancy entitlements Fair Work Commission · Fair Work Ombudsman Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) Businesses with annual revenue over $100 million must publish an annual modern slavery statement describing the risks of forced labour in their operations and supply chains , and what they are doing about them Supplier auditing, due diligence, annual reporting Anti-Slavery Commissioner Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 and 1997 (Cth) · A New Tax System (GST) Act 1999 (Cth) Company tax on assessable income, and 10% GST collected on taxable supplies and remitted to the ATO Record keeping, BAS lodgement, accounting systems ATO ⚠️ The Trade Practices Act 1974 no longer exists. It was renamed the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) . It appears as an MCQ distractor and is never correct for anything current. 2.1 How to use an Act in an answer Naming it is one mark. The mark after it comes from the consequence . 1. NAME Under the [ACT YEAR (JURISDICTION)], 2. DUTY the business [OBLIGATION]. 3. BREACH [STIMULUS FACT] constitutes a breach, 4. COST exposing it to [PENALTY / CLAIM / REPUTATIONAL DAMAGE]. 5. ACTION The business should therefore [COMPLIANCE MEASURE]. Worked: Under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) , the business owes a duty of care to provide a safe environment for employees and customers. Floors that are often wet and slippery constitute a direct breach, exposing it to workers compensation claims, public liability claims and regulatory penalties. Operations should therefore introduce scheduled cleaning, hazard signage and staff safety training, accepting the compliance cost as substantially cheaper than a single serious injury claim. The two phrases that pay in any legal question: compliance costs (the expense of meeting the law) and duty of care (the WHS obligation). Both appear in marking criteria constantly. 2.2 Which Act for which scenario Scenario Act A worker slips on a wet floor Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) That worker claims medical costs and lost income Workers Compensation Act 1987 (NSW) A factory discharges effluent into a creek Protection of the Environment Operations Act 1997 (NSW) A restaurant serves food causing illness Food Act 2003 (NSW) A product injures a customer through a manufacturing fault Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) Staff are made to work through their breaks Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) A business cannot verify its overseas supplier's labour conditions Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) 3. Corporate Social Responsibility CSR = open and accountable business actions based on respect for people, community, society and the environment. The triple bottom line = financial + social + environmental performance. The cost of CSR : Environmentally sustainable practices often cost more in the short term (new equipment, sustainable inputs, waste treatment), which conflicts with cost leadership . The counter-argument is long-term reputation, customer loyalty and avoided regulatory penalties. ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Legal compliance vs ethical responsibility Compliance = the letter of the law , the minimum required. Ethics = the spirit of the law . A business can be fully compliant and still be criticised as unethical Compliance cost vs penalty Compliance cost is the expense of meeting the law. A penalty is what you pay for breaching it Government policies vs legal regulation Policies are what the government chooses to do (tax rates, training programs). Regulation is what the law requires Triple bottom line vs being green Triple bottom line is three measures — financial, social, environmental. Not just environmental 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Compliance cost The expense incurred by a business in meeting legal requirements Duty of care The WHS obligation on an employer to eliminate or minimise risks so far as is reasonably practicable CSR Open and accountable business actions based on respect for people, community, society and the environment Triple bottom line Measuring performance across financial, social and environmental dimensions Environmental sustainability Operating without compromising the resources of future generations Next: ③ Operations Processes · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Operations 3 · Operations Processes
text: 🔄 Operations 3 · Operations Processes Operations · ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes ← you are here · ④ Strategies · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Operations module is examinable. This file covers the Operations processes dot points only. INPUTS → TRANSFORMATION PROCESSES → OUTPUTS ⭐ The sequence MCQ — 2025 HSC Q19, and you lost it. "Which of the following is the correct sequence for its operations process?" Every option is three terms. Do not read them as a story — label each term first , then check the order reads input → transformation → output. Label Terms that belong here INPUT Materials · information · customers · human resources · facilities TRANSFORMATION Volume/variety/variation/visibility · sequencing and scheduling · technology · task design · process layout · monitoring · control · improvement OUTPUT Customer service · warranties Worked on the real question: Option Labels Verdict A. Product → task design → materials output → transformation → input ❌ backwards — you chose this B. Facilities → control → customer service input → transformation → output ✅ correct C. Information → warranties → improvement input → output → transformation ❌ out of order D. Human resources → planning → customers input → ? → input ❌ ends on an input The trap: "Product" sounds like a starting point because it's what the business makes. It is the finished good — an output. And customers are an INPUT (a transformed resource), not the end of the line. 1. Inputs Type Definition Examples Transformed resources The inputs changed by the process Materials (raw materials, intermediate goods), Information (internal and external), Customers (where the customer themselves is changed, e.g. a haircut) Transforming resources The inputs that carry out the change Human resources (skills, training, motivation), Facilities (plant, machinery, factory layout) Exam trap : When a question mentions customised products , the key point is that customers become a transformed resource — they enter the process and shape it directly. 2. Transformation Processes — The Four Vs V What it means High Low Volume How much is produced Efficient, automated, low unit cost, capital intensive Manual, skilled labour, high unit cost Variety Range of products offered Complex, flexible, expensive, process layout Simple, efficient, standardised, product layout Variation in demand How much demand fluctuates Need flexible resources, accurate forecasting, casual staff Stable planning, consistent resource use Visibility Degree of customer contact Skilled staff, responsive, quality interaction matters Speed, consistency, cost control 3. Technology, Task Design and Process Layout 3.1 Technology Type Definition Leading edge The most advanced technology available — new, gives competitive advantage, but untested and expensive Established Proven technology that has been widely adopted — reliable and cheaper, but no advantage over competitors Benefits: faster production, fewer errors, consistent quality, long-term labour cost savings. 3.2 Task Design Task design : The process of classifying job activities so employees can perform them easily. Steps: define the job → analyse it into duties → allocate difficulty and time → match to awards → articulate through job descriptors . 3.3 Process Layout Types Type Use Characteristics Example Process (functional) layout High variety, low volume Equipment grouped by function ; flexible; slower Hospital, bank, printery Product layout High volume, standardised Assembly line ; consistent quality; inflexible Car factory, Foxconn Fixed position layout Large, immovable products Workers and equipment come to the site Construction, shipbuilding Office layout Information flow Arranged for communication and workflow Open-plan offices 4. Monitoring, Control and Improvement ✅ This is a PROCESS, not a strategy. The syllabus lists "monitoring, control and improvement" as the fourth bullet under transformation processes , inside Operations processes — alongside the 4 Vs, sequencing and scheduling, and technology/task design/layout. ⚠️ Why it feels like a strategy: the words control and improvement appear a second time in the syllabus, under Operations strategies → "quality management — control, assurance, improvement" . Two different dot points, same two words. See the confusing pair below. Stage Definition Monitoring Measuring actual performance against planned performance using KPIs Controlling Assessing KPIs against targets, investigating variances , and taking corrective action Improvement The systematic reduction of inefficiencies, waste and bottlenecks Common operations KPIs : lead times, inventory turnover, defect rates, capacity utilisation, unit costs, waste levels, warranty claims. Areas of improvement : time, process flows, quality, cost, efficiency. Continuous improvement = an ongoing commitment to achieving perfection. Requires staff involvement at every level — it cannot be imposed from the top alone. Confusing term — Bottleneck : The point in a process with the lowest capacity , which limits the output of the entire system. Improving anything other than the bottleneck does not increase total output. 5. Outputs Output element Detail Customer service How well the business meets and exceeds customer expectations Warranties A promise to repair or replace faulty goods. Warranty claims are a key source of feedback about quality failures — they signal where the transformation process is going wrong 6. Sequencing and Scheduling Definitions — learn these exact wordings Sequencing refers to the order in which activities in the operations process occur. Scheduling refers to the length of time activities take within the operations process. 6.1 Gantt Charts Gantt chart : outlines the activities that need to be performed, the order in which they should be performed, and how long each activity is expected to take. Task Week 1 Week 2 Week 3 Week 4 Week 5 Week 6 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Shop refit ████████████████ Purchase ─────────────────████████████ stock Staff ─────────────────████████ training Marketing ─────────────────────────████████████ Opening ───────────────────────────────────────────█ Advantages of Gantt charts: Show which activities can be performed concurrently (at the same time) Identify bottlenecks and scheduling conflicts Easy to communicate the plan to staff and stakeholders Show total project duration at a glance Allow progress to be tracked against plan 6.2 Critical Path Analysis (CPA) Critical path analysis : shows what needs to be done , how long tasks take , and what order is necessary to complete those tasks. The critical path is the shortest time to complete all of the tasks. How this actually works — read this once and it will never confuse you again. A CPA diagram contains several possible paths from start to finish. You add up the durations along each path. The longest path is the critical path . Because every task must be finished, that longest path is the shortest possible time in which the whole project can be completed. So "longest path" and "shortest completion time" are the same number viewed two ways. The path is longest; the project time it produces is the shortest achievable. Both phrasings are correct — don't let them trip you up. Key CPA terms Term Meaning Critical path The sequence of activities that determines the total project duration Critical activity An activity on the critical path — it cannot be delayed without delaying the whole project Float (slack) The amount of time a non-critical activity can be delayed without delaying the project. Critical activities have zero float Concurrent activities Activities that can be carried out at the same time Dependency An activity that cannot start until another finishes Worked example — Critical Path Analysis Activity Duration (days) Must follow A 3 — B 4 — C 2 A D 5 B E 3 C and D Network: A (3) C (2) ┌──────────►○──────────►┐ START ├──► E (3) ──► FINISH └──────────►○──────────►┘ B (4) D (5) Step 1 — list every path and total it: Path 1: A → C → E = 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 days Path 2: B → D → E = 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 days Step 2 — identify the critical path: the longest path is B → D → E . Step 3 — state the project duration: the shortest time to complete all tasks is 12 days . Step 4 — calculate float on the non-critical path: Path A→C→E takes 8 days but has 12 days available, so A and C each have 4 days of float . They can be delayed up to 4 days without delaying the opening. Answering the question "which task determines when E can be performed?" → D , because E cannot begin until both C (finished day 5) and D (finished day 9) are complete. The later of the two — D — is the constraint. How CPA assists the transformation process: Identifies which activities are critical , so management allocates resources there first Reveals float , allowing staff and equipment to be redeployed from non-critical tasks Reduces lead time by showing which activities can run concurrently Improves dependability by producing a realistic completion date Supports the speed performance objective ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Monitoring, control and improvement (process) vs quality management: control, assurance, improvement (strategy) ⭐ Both exist in the syllabus. The process one is about performance against plan — measure, find the variance, fix it. The strategy one is about defect prevention — inspection, ISO 9000 systems, TQM. If the question is about KPIs and corrective action it's the process ; if it's about quality standards and defects it's the strategy Transformed vs transforming resources Transformed resources are changed . Transforming resources do the changing Sequencing vs scheduling Sequencing = order . Scheduling = duration Gantt chart vs CPA Gantt shows activities against a timeline — best for visualising progress. CPA shows dependencies and what cannot be delayed — best for managing time and resources Critical path vs number of tasks The critical path is about time , not how many activities are on it Float vs critical activity Critical activities have zero float by definition Lead time vs cycle time Lead time = ordering to receiving. Cycle time = time to produce one unit Monitoring vs controlling Monitoring measures . Controlling investigates the variance and acts Process layout vs product layout Process = grouped by function , high variety. Product = assembly line , high volume 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Transformed resources Inputs changed by the process — materials, information, customers Transforming resources Inputs that carry out the change — human resources and facilities Sequencing The order in which activities occur Scheduling The length of time activities take Gantt chart A chart outlining activities, their order and their expected duration Critical path analysis A technique showing what must be done, how long it takes and in what order Critical path The shortest time to complete all of the tasks Float The time a non-critical activity can be delayed without delaying the project Bottleneck The lowest-capacity point in a process, which limits total system output Continuous improvement An ongoing commitment to achieving perfection Next: ④ Operations Strategies · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · Back to MOC

title: Operations 4 · Operations Strategies
text: 🎯 Operations 4 · Operations Strategies Operations · ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies ← you are here · 📕 Full note Scope: the full HSC Operations module is examinable. This file covers the Operations strategies dot points only. ⭐ The highest-yield section in the module. Most 20-mark Operations questions are answered mainly out of this file. 1. Performance Objectives Objective Definition Quality Design quality (how well it matches consumer understanding of what it should do) + conformance quality (how well it meets specifications) + quality of service Speed Fast response to market changes; reduced lead times and waiting times Dependability Consistency and reliability — the product works as promised, and delivery arrives when promised Flexibility The ability to adjust production to change quickly — in volume, product or delivery Customisation Creating individualised products to meet specific customer needs; mass customisation delivers this at volume Cost Minimising expenses so the business can compete on price while remaining profitable 2. New Product or Service Design and Development Two approaches: Approach Definition Consumer-driven Customer preferences and market research determine the design Technology-driven Innovation and new technology enable products consumers had not asked for Steps : Market research → Design and prototype → Testing → Refinement → Production and launch Key considerations : supply chain (do we need new suppliers?), quality (can standards be maintained?), capacity (do we need new resources or technology?), cost. Service design : Explicit service — the tangible parts: the time taken, the expertise applied Implicit service — the intangible parts: the feeling of wellbeing, status, comfort Cost is determined after both elements are specified 3. Supply Chain Management SCM = the integration and management of the flow of supplies from inputs, through transformation, to outputs. Sourcing = deciding which suppliers to use. Factors: consumer demand, quality of inputs, flexibility and timeliness, cost. Trends in sourcing: Supplier rationalisation — reducing the number of suppliers to gain better terms and consistency Backwards vertical integration — acquiring your own supplier Cost minimisation — moving sourcing offshore Building flexible and responsive supply chains Global sourcing = purchasing inputs without being constrained by location. Advantages Disadvantages Lower costs Quality risk Reduced lead times (if well managed) Impact on domestic businesses and jobs Access to materials unavailable domestically Communication, cultural and time-zone barriers Access to specialist expertise Longer, more fragile supply lines E-commerce = using the internet in supply chain management. E-procurement systems automate ordering. B2B (business to business — automatic restocking between firms) and B2C (business to consumer — direct sales). Logistics = distribution, transportation, storage (warehousing and distribution centres), materials handling and packaging. 4. Outsourcing Outsourcing = the use of external providers to perform business activities — either domestic or global . Advantages Disadvantages Cost savings Communication and language barriers Improved efficiency Loss of direct quality control Access to specialist skills Security and confidentiality risks Focus on core business Dependency on the partner Increased accountability through contracts Loss of corporate memory and in-house skill Simplification of the business Reputation affected by the partner's conduct 5. Technology Type Detail Leading edge Newest available; competitive advantage; expensive and untested Established Proven and widely used; reliable and cheaper; no differentiation Key applications: CAD (computer-aided design), CAM (computer-aided manufacture), robotics , automation . 6. Inventory Management ⚠️ Critical exam distinction If the question asks about inventory MANAGEMENT → answer Holding stock (JIC) or Just in Time (JIT) . If the question asks about a strategy to VALUE inventory, or an inventory VALUATION method → answer FIFO or LIFO . Mixing these up is one of the most common ways students lose marks in this topic. 6.1 Holding Stock — "Just in Case" (JIC) Advantages Disadvantages Can always meet customer demand Holding costs : storage, insurance, theft, spoilage, security Alternatives available if an item is out of stock Capital tied up in stock that could be used elsewhere Reduced lead times for customers Risk of obsolescence (stock becoming outdated) Immediate revenue from available stock Damage and deterioration Bulk-buying cost savings Requires warehouse space 6.2 Just in Time (JIT) Produce or order only what is needed, when it is needed. Advantages Disadvantages Greatly reduced storage costs Lead time increases when demand varies unexpectedly No theft or damage risk from stored stock Total dependence on supplier reliability No obsolescence A single delivery failure can shut down production Frees working capital Loses bulk-buying discounts 6.3 Inventory Valuation — FIFO, LIFO and Weighted Average Method Definition FIFO (First In First Out) Assumes the oldest stock is sold first LIFO (Last In First Out) Assumes the newest stock is sold first Weighted average Uses the average cost of all inventory; smooths price fluctuations The decision table — memorise this: Understate / minimise profit (to reduce tax) Overstate / maximise profit (for potential investors) Cost of inventory is increasing LIFO FIFO Cost of inventory is decreasing FIFO LIFO Worked example — FIFO vs LIFO with rising costs Purchases: Date Units Cost per unit Total 1 Jan 100 $10 $1,000 1 Feb 100 $12 $1,200 1 Mar 100 $14 $1,400 Total 300 $3,600 150 units are sold at $20 each → Sales revenue = $3,000 FIFO (oldest sold first): COGS = (100 × $10) + (50 × $12) = 1,000 + 600 = $1,600 Closing stock = (50 × $12) + (100 × $14) = 600 + 1,400 = $2,000 Gross profit = 3,000 − 1,600 = $1,400 LIFO (newest sold first): COGS = (100 × $14) + (50 × $12) = 1,400 + 600 = $2,000 Closing stock = (50 × $12) + (100 × $10) = 600 + 1,000 = $1,600 Gross profit = 3,000 − 2,000 = $1,000 Weighted average : $3,600 ÷ 300 units = $12 per unit COGS = 150 × 12 = $1,800 → Gross profit = $1,200 Conclusion : With rising costs, FIFO reports the higher profit ($1,400) — chosen to impress investors. LIFO reports the lower profit ($1,000) — chosen to reduce tax. Weighted average sits between the two. Note COGS + closing stock = $3,600 in every method: the total cost is the same, only its allocation differs. EOQ (Economic Order Quantity) : the optimal order quantity that minimises total inventory costs — balancing ordering costs (which fall as you order less often in bigger batches) against holding costs (which rise as you store more). LIFO note : LIFO is permitted for HSC analysis but is not permitted under Australian Accounting Standards for external financial reporting. Answer the question as asked, using the table above. 7. Quality Management Approach Key feature Quality control Inspection at various points in production. Define standards, test against them, take corrective action. Detects defects after they occur Quality assurance A system designed to prevent defects — "right the first time." Certified against external standards such as ISO 9000 Total Quality Management (TQM) Holistic — every employee is responsible for quality; the total business is managed for quality. Elements: customer focus, continuous improvement, employee empowerment Six Sigma Data-driven; targets 3.4 defects per million opportunities. Uses DMAIC : Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control Kaizen Continuous incremental improvement involving all employees; eliminating waste ( muda ) Quality circles Small groups of employees who meet regularly to identify and solve quality problems ⭐ The three-way tell — this was 2025 HSC Q8 and you lost it. If the stem says… The answer is Inspecting, checking, testing, detecting faults Control A system, a standard, certification, preventing defects, "right the first time", ISO 9000 Assurance "Ongoing commitment", continuous, never-ending, always getting better, Kaizen Improvement 2025 HSC Q8 read "demonstrates an ongoing commitment to make its operations more efficient and effective" → Improvement . You answered Assurance. Assurance is something you install once and certify ; improvement is something you keep doing . 8. Overcoming Resistance to Change Two sources of resistance: Source Detail Financial costs Purchasing new equipment, redundancy payouts , retraining costs, reorganising plant layout Psychological (inertia) Fear and uncertainty → less motivated staff → lower productivity → quality issues → increased lead times and defects → lost customers Inertia = the tendency of people and organisations to keep doing what they have always done and resist any change to it. Managing change effectively: Identify the sources of change and assess the need for it Communicate with employees and build widespread support Use change agents — people who champion and drive the change Apply change models (e.g. Lewin's unfreeze → change → refreeze) 9. Global Factors Factor Detail Global sourcing Sourcing inputs anywhere in the world for cost or quality advantage Economies of scale Higher volumes → lower per-unit costs , through capital investment, technology, global branding and centralised training Scanning and learning Actively studying and adopting global best practice from other markets and competitors Research and development Investing in leading-edge technologies; global expertise increases the opportunity base ⚠️ Confusing pairs in this section Pair The tell Speed vs dependability Speed = how fast . Dependability = how reliably you deliver when you said you would . You can be fast and undependable Quality control vs quality assurance Control inspects to find defects (reactive). Assurance designs the process so they don't happen (proactive) JIT/JIC vs FIFO/LIFO JIT/JIC = inventory management . FIFO/LIFO = inventory valuation Outsourcing vs offshoring Outsourcing = an external provider . Offshoring = overseas , which may still be in-house Global sourcing vs outsourcing Global sourcing buys inputs . Outsourcing contracts out an activity Leading edge vs established technology Leading edge = advantage but untested and dear. Established = reliable and cheap but no advantage Economies of scale Lower per-unit cost. Total cost still rises with volume Design quality vs conformance quality Design = matches what consumers think it should do . Conformance = meets the specification Explicit vs implicit service Explicit = tangible (time, expertise). Implicit = intangible (comfort, status) Obsolescence vs spoilage Obsolescence = outdated . Spoilage = physically deteriorated EOQ vs reorder point EOQ = how much to order. Reorder point = when to order 📝 Exam habits Every extended response ends at cost leadership or differentiation. That is the strategic role, and markers look for the link. Don't list influences or strategies — explain the impact on the operations process. A list is a Band 3 answer. 📖 Definitions to quote Term Definition Quality Design quality + conformance quality + quality of service Dependability The consistency and reliability of the product and its delivery Supply chain management Integrating and managing the flow of supplies through the business Global sourcing Purchasing inputs without being constrained by location Outsourcing Using external providers to perform business activities JIT Producing or ordering only what is needed, when it is needed FIFO Valuing inventory on the assumption the oldest stock is sold first EOQ The order quantity that minimises total inventory costs Quality assurance A system designed to prevent defects, certified against standards such as ISO 9000 TQM A holistic approach in which every employee is responsible for quality Six Sigma A data-driven method targeting 3.4 defects per million opportunities, using DMAIC Kaizen Continuous incremental improvement involving all employees Inertia The tendency to keep doing what has always been done and resist change Economies of scale Lower per-unit costs achieved through higher volume Back to: ① Role · 📕 Full note · Drill sheet: Confusing Pairs · MOC

title: Operations — Full Module Note
text: 📕 Operations — Full Module Note The whole module in one file. Split versions: ① Role · ② Influences · ③ Processes · ④ Strategies Scope: the full HSC Operations module is examinable. 🔧 Maintenance note: sections 1–4 below are mirrored in the four split files. If one is corrected, correct both. Sections 5–9 exist only here. 1. Role of Operations Management Definition : Operations refers to the business processes of transformation and value adding . Transformation : converting inputs into outputs Value adding : creating extra value as inputs become outputs. In manufacturing this is physical change; in services it is the application of knowledge and skills 1.1 Strategic Role of Operations Operations contributes to the strategic direction of the business through two generic strategies : Strategy Definition How it is achieved Cost leadership Having the lowest costs and being the most price-competitive while remaining profitable Economies of scale, automation, bulk buying, eliminating waste, standardisation, global sourcing Goods/services differentiation Distinguishing goods or services from competitors Goods : vary features, quality, augmented features (warranty, delivery). Services : vary the amount of time, level of expertise, qualifications of staff Exam link : Almost every Operations extended response should end by linking back to cost leadership or differentiation . That is the strategic role. 1.2 Goods vs Services Goods Services Tangible — can be stored Intangible — produced and consumed simultaneously Standardised or customised Standardised (fast food) or customised (legal advice) Quality measured by durability and fitness for purpose Quality measured by professionalism and reliability Classification of goods: Pure goods — no service component (e.g. tinned food) Pure services — no goods component (e.g. financial advice) Goods with a service component — (e.g. a car with a warranty) 1.3 Interdependence with Other Key Business Functions Function Relationship with Operations Marketing Marketing provides demand forecasts and customer preferences → operations modifies production. Operations produces the goods → marketing sells them Finance Finance provides budgets for equipment, technology and inputs. Operations controls costs, which drives profitability Human Resources HR recruits and trains production staff. Operations determines skill needs and staffing levels. Productivity depends directly on workforce quality 2. Influences on Operations Influence Detail Globalisation Removal of trade barriers; operations structured around global production facilities. Opportunity : global markets, economies of scale, global sourcing. Threat : intensified competition Technology Increased efficiency, reduced costs, consistent quality, higher productivity. Includes both administrative and processing technology Quality expectations Goods : design, fitness for purpose, durability. Services : professionalism, reliability, level of customisation. Failure → dissatisfaction, returns, damaged reputation Cost-based competition Pressure to lower production costs. Methods: eliminate waste, standardise, high volume, automate, economies of scale, bulk buying Government policies Changes in taxation, industrial relations, environmental regulation, training requirements — all create compliance costs Legal regulation Compliance with legislation across WHS, environment, food safety, fair trading and industrial relations. Compliance costs are the expenses of meeting these requirements — see §2.1 below Environmental sustainability Operating without compromising resources for future generations. Methods: minimise waste, recycle, reduce carbon footprint 2.1 Legal Regulation — The Actual Acts Naming the Act with its year and jurisdiction is a mark. "The Environmental Protection Act" is not an answer — no NSW Act has that name. (Cth) = Commonwealth, national. (NSW) = state. Act What the Act actually requires What it costs operations Regulator Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) Imposes a duty of care — the employer must eliminate or minimise risks so far as is reasonably practicable, identify hazards, train and supervise staff, and consult workers on safety decisions Safety equipment, training time, signage, incident reporting systems, safety audits SafeWork NSW Workers Compensation Act 1987 (NSW) Every employer must hold a workers compensation insurance policy . Injured workers receive income support and medical costs on a no-fault basis — they don't have to prove the employer was negligent Insurance premiums, which rise with the business's claims history icare · SIRA Protection of the Environment Operations Act 1997 (NSW) (the POEO Act) Businesses conducting scheduled activities (chemical production, waste processing, electricity generation, intensive livestock) must hold an environment protection licence . Empowers the EPA to issue clean-up, prevention and prohibition notices . Penalties to $5 million for corporations Licence fees, emissions monitoring, effluent treatment, waste disposal contracts NSW EPA Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (Cth) (the EPBC Act) Any action likely to have a significant impact on a matter of national environmental significance — threatened species, world heritage areas, wetlands — must be referred for federal approval Environmental impact assessment, project delays, redesign Federal environment department Waste Avoidance and Resource Recovery Act 2001 (NSW) Sets NSW waste reduction targets and imposes a waste levy on material sent to landfill, deliberately making disposal more expensive than recovery The levy itself, plus separation and recycling systems NSW EPA Food Act 2003 (NSW) Businesses handling food must notify the authority, appoint a food safety supervisor , and keep premises, equipment and handling practices to the Food Standards Code. Creates offences for selling unsafe or falsely described food Supervisor training, temperature monitoring, cleaning schedules, inspections NSW Food Authority Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (contains the Australian Consumer Law, Schedule 2) Bans misleading and deceptive conduct , guarantees goods are of acceptable quality and fit for purpose , and imposes product safety standards and mandatory recalls. Also bans anti-competitive conduct such as price fixing and resale price maintenance Quality assurance systems, accurate labelling, recall capability, warranty servicing ACCC Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) Establishes the National Employment Standards (11 minimum entitlements), minimum wages, awards, enterprise bargaining, and protection from unfair dismissal . Includes the right to rest and meal breaks under the relevant award Wage costs, rostering constraints, penalty rates, redundancy entitlements Fair Work Commission · Fair Work Ombudsman Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) Businesses with annual revenue over $100 million must publish an annual modern slavery statement describing the risks of forced labour in their operations and supply chains , and what they are doing about them Supplier auditing, due diligence, annual reporting Anti-Slavery Commissioner Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 and 1997 (Cth) · A New Tax System (GST) Act 1999 (Cth) Company tax on assessable income, and 10% GST collected on taxable supplies and remitted to the ATO Record keeping, BAS lodgement, accounting systems ATO ⚠️ The Trade Practices Act 1974 no longer exists. It was renamed the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) . It appears as an MCQ distractor and is never correct for anything current. How to use an Act in an answer Naming it is one mark. The mark after it comes from the consequence . 1. NAME Under the [ACT YEAR (JURISDICTION)], 2. DUTY the business [OBLIGATION]. 3. BREACH [STIMULUS FACT] constitutes a breach, 4. COST exposing it to [PENALTY / CLAIM / REPUTATIONAL DAMAGE]. 5. ACTION The business should therefore [COMPLIANCE MEASURE]. Worked: Under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) , the business owes a duty of care to provide a safe environment for employees and customers. Floors that are often wet and slippery constitute a direct breach, exposing it to workers compensation claims, public liability claims and regulatory penalties. Operations should therefore introduce scheduled cleaning, hazard signage and staff safety training, accepting the compliance cost as substantially cheaper than a single serious injury claim. The two phrases that pay in any legal question: compliance costs (the expense of meeting the law) and duty of care (the WHS obligation). Both appear in marking criteria constantly. Which Act for which scenario Scenario Act A worker slips on a wet floor Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) That worker claims medical costs and lost income Workers Compensation Act 1987 (NSW) A factory discharges effluent into a creek Protection of the Environment Operations Act 1997 (NSW) A restaurant serves food causing illness Food Act 2003 (NSW) A product injures a customer through a manufacturing fault Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) Staff are made to work through their breaks Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) A business cannot verify its overseas supplier's labour conditions Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) 2.2 Corporate Social Responsibility CSR = open and accountable business actions based on respect for people, community, society and the environment. The triple bottom line = financial + social + environmental performance. Confusing pair — Legal compliance vs Ethical responsibility Legal compliance = obeying the letter of the law — the minimum required. Ethical responsibility = acting in the spirit of the law — doing what is right even where no law compels it. A business can be fully legally compliant and still be criticised as unethical. The cost of CSR : Environmentally sustainable practices often cost more in the short term (new equipment, sustainable inputs, waste treatment), which conflicts with cost leadership . The counter-argument is long-term reputation, customer loyalty and avoided regulatory penalties. 3. Operations Processes INPUTS → TRANSFORMATION PROCESSES → OUTPUTS 3.1 Inputs Type Definition Examples Transformed resources The inputs changed by the process Materials (raw materials, intermediate goods), Information (internal and external), Customers (where the customer themselves is changed, e.g. a haircut) Transforming resources The inputs that carry out the change Human resources (skills, training, motivation), Facilities (plant, machinery, factory layout) Exam trap : When a question mentions customised products , the key point is that customers become a transformed resource — they enter the process and shape it directly. 3.2 Transformation Processes — The Four Vs V What it means High Low Volume How much is produced Efficient, automated, low unit cost, capital intensive Manual, skilled labour, high unit cost Variety Range of products offered Complex, flexible, expensive, process layout Simple, efficient, standardised, product layout Variation in demand How much demand fluctuates Need flexible resources, accurate forecasting, casual staff Stable planning, consistent resource use Visibility Degree of customer contact Skilled staff, responsive, quality interaction matters Speed, consistency, cost control 3.3 Technology, Task Design and Process Layout Technology Type Definition Leading edge The most advanced technology available — new, gives competitive advantage, but untested and expensive Established Proven technology that has been widely adopted — reliable and cheaper, but no advantage over competitors Benefits: faster production, fewer errors, consistent quality, long-term labour cost savings. Task design : The process of classifying job activities so employees can perform them easily. Steps: define the job → analyse it into duties → allocate difficulty and time → match to awards → articulate through job descriptors . Process layout types Type Use Characteristics Example Process (functional) layout High variety, low volume Equipment grouped by function ; flexible; slower Hospital, bank, printery Product layout High volume, standardised Assembly line ; consistent quality; inflexible Car factory, Foxconn Fixed position layout Large, immovable products Workers and equipment come to the site Construction, shipbuilding Office layout Information flow Arranged for communication and workflow Open-plan offices 3.4 Monitoring, Controlling and Improvement Stage Definition Monitoring Measuring actual performance against planned performance using KPIs Controlling Assessing KPIs against targets, investigating variances , and taking corrective action Improvement The systematic reduction of inefficiencies, waste and bottlenecks Common operations KPIs : lead times, inventory turnover, defect rates, capacity utilisation, unit costs, waste levels, warranty claims. Areas of improvement : time, process flows, quality, cost, efficiency. Continuous improvement = an ongoing commitment to achieving perfection. Requires staff involvement at every level — it cannot be imposed from the top alone. Confusing term — Bottleneck : The point in a process with the lowest capacity , which limits the output of the entire system. Improving anything other than the bottleneck does not increase total output. 3.5 Outputs Output element Detail Customer service How well the business meets and exceeds customer expectations Warranties A promise to repair or replace faulty goods.
