Warranty claims are a key source of feedback about quality failures — they signal where the transformation process is going wrong 3.6 Sequencing and Scheduling Definitions — learn these exact wordings Sequencing refers to the order in which activities in the operations process occur. Scheduling refers to the length of time activities take within the operations process. Gantt Charts Gantt chart : outlines the activities that need to be performed, the order in which they should be performed, and how long each activity is expected to take. Task Week 1 Week 2 Week 3 Week 4 Week 5 Week 6 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Shop refit ████████████████ Purchase ─────────────────████████████ stock Staff ─────────────────████████ training Marketing ─────────────────────────████████████ Opening ───────────────────────────────────────────█ Advantages of Gantt charts: Show which activities can be performed concurrently (at the same time) Identify bottlenecks and scheduling conflicts Easy to communicate the plan to staff and stakeholders Show total project duration at a glance Allow progress to be tracked against plan Critical Path Analysis (CPA) Critical path analysis : shows what needs to be done , how long tasks take , and what order is necessary to complete those tasks. The critical path is the shortest time to complete all of the tasks. How this actually works — read this once and it will never confuse you again. A CPA diagram contains several possible paths from start to finish. You add up the durations along each path. The longest path is the critical path . Because every task must be finished, that longest path is the shortest possible time in which the whole project can be completed. So "longest path" and "shortest completion time" are the same number viewed two ways. The path is longest; the project time it produces is the shortest achievable. Both phrasings are correct — don't let them trip you up. Key CPA terms Term Meaning Critical path The sequence of activities that determines the total project duration Critical activity An activity on the critical path — it cannot be delayed without delaying the whole project Float (slack) The amount of time a non-critical activity can be delayed without delaying the project. Critical activities have zero float Concurrent activities Activities that can be carried out at the same time Dependency An activity that cannot start until another finishes Worked example — Critical Path Analysis Activity Duration (days) Must follow A 3 — B 4 — C 2 A D 5 B E 3 C and D Network: A (3) C (2) ┌──────────►○──────────►┐ START ├──► E (3) ──► FINISH └──────────►○──────────►┘ B (4) D (5) Step 1 — list every path and total it: Path 1: A → C → E = 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 days Path 2: B → D → E = 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 days Step 2 — identify the critical path: the longest path is B → D → E . Step 3 — state the project duration: the shortest time to complete all tasks is 12 days . Step 4 — calculate float on the non-critical path: Path A→C→E takes 8 days but has 12 days available, so A and C each have 4 days of float . They can be delayed up to 4 days without delaying the opening. Answering the question "which task determines when E can be performed?" → D , because E cannot begin until both C (finished day 5) and D (finished day 9) are complete. The later of the two — D — is the constraint. How CPA assists the transformation process: Identifies which activities are critical , so management allocates resources there first Reveals float , allowing staff and equipment to be redeployed from non-critical tasks Reduces lead time by showing which activities can run concurrently Improves dependability by producing a realistic completion date Supports the speed performance objective Gantt vs CPA — the distinction examiners look for A Gantt chart shows activities against a timeline — it is best for visualising schedule and progress. CPA shows dependencies and identifies which activities cannot be delayed — it is best for managing time and resources. 4. Operations Strategies 4.1 Performance Objectives Objective Definition Quality Design quality (how well it matches consumer understanding of what it should do) + conformance quality (how well it meets specifications) + quality of service Speed Fast response to market changes; reduced lead times and waiting times Dependability Consistency and reliability — the product works as promised, and delivery arrives when promised Flexibility The ability to adjust production to change quickly — in volume, product or delivery Customisation Creating individualised products to meet specific customer needs; mass customisation delivers this at volume Cost Minimising expenses so the business can compete on price while remaining profitable Confusing pair — Speed vs Dependability Speed = how fast you deliver. Dependability = how reliably you deliver when you said you would . A business can be fast but undependable (quick sometimes, late others), or slow but perfectly dependable. 4.2 New Product or Service Design and Development Two approaches: Approach Definition Consumer-driven Customer preferences and market research determine the design Technology-driven Innovation and new technology enable products consumers had not asked for Steps : Market research → Design and prototype → Testing → Refinement → Production and launch Key considerations : supply chain (do we need new suppliers?), quality (can standards be maintained?), capacity (do we need new resources or technology?), cost. Service design : Explicit service — the tangible parts: the time taken, the expertise applied Implicit service — the intangible parts: the feeling of wellbeing, status, comfort Cost is determined after both elements are specified 4.3 Supply Chain Management SCM = the integration and management of the flow of supplies from inputs, through transformation, to outputs. Sourcing = deciding which suppliers to use. Factors: consumer demand, quality of inputs, flexibility and timeliness, cost. Trends in sourcing: Supplier rationalisation — reducing the number of suppliers to gain better terms and consistency Backwards vertical integration — acquiring your own supplier Cost minimisation — moving sourcing offshore Building flexible and responsive supply chains Global sourcing = purchasing inputs without being constrained by location. Advantages Disadvantages Lower costs Quality risk Reduced lead times (if well managed) Impact on domestic businesses and jobs Access to materials unavailable domestically Communication, cultural and time-zone barriers Access to specialist expertise Longer, more fragile supply lines E-commerce = using the internet in supply chain management. E-procurement systems automate ordering. B2B (business to business — automatic restocking between firms) and B2C (business to consumer — direct sales). Logistics = distribution, transportation, storage (warehousing and distribution centres), materials handling and packaging. 4.4 Outsourcing Outsourcing = the use of external providers to perform business activities — either domestic or global . Advantages Disadvantages Cost savings Communication and language barriers Improved efficiency Loss of direct quality control Access to specialist skills Security and confidentiality risks Focus on core business Dependency on the partner Increased accountability through contracts Loss of corporate memory and in-house skill Simplification of the business Reputation affected by the partner's conduct 4.5 Technology Type Detail Leading edge Newest available; competitive advantage; expensive and untested Established Proven and widely used; reliable and cheaper; no differentiation Key applications: CAD (computer-aided design), CAM (computer-aided manufacture), robotics , automation . 4.6 Inventory Management Critical exam distinction If the question asks about inventory MANAGEMENT → answer Holding stock (JIC) or Just in Time (JIT) . If the question asks about a strategy to VALUE inventory, or an inventory VALUATION method → answer FIFO or LIFO . Mixing these up is one of the most common ways students lose marks in this topic. Holding Stock — "Just in Case" (JIC) Advantages Disadvantages Can always meet customer demand Holding costs : storage, insurance, theft, spoilage, security Alternatives available if an item is out of stock Capital tied up in stock that could be used elsewhere Reduced lead times for customers Risk of obsolescence (stock becoming outdated) Immediate revenue from available stock Damage and deterioration Bulk-buying cost savings Requires warehouse space Just in Time (JIT) Produce or order only what is needed, when it is needed. Advantages Disadvantages Greatly reduced storage costs Lead time increases when demand varies unexpectedly No theft or damage risk from stored stock Total dependence on supplier reliability No obsolescence A single delivery failure can shut down production Frees working capital Loses bulk-buying discounts Inventory Valuation — FIFO, LIFO and Weighted Average Method Definition FIFO (First In First Out) Assumes the oldest stock is sold first LIFO (Last In First Out) Assumes the newest stock is sold first Weighted average Uses the average cost of all inventory; smooths price fluctuations The decision table — memorise this: Understate / minimise profit (to reduce tax) Overstate / maximise profit (for potential investors) Cost of inventory is increasing LIFO FIFO Cost of inventory is decreasing FIFO LIFO Worked example — FIFO vs LIFO with rising costs Purchases: Date Units Cost per unit Total 1 Jan 100 $10 $1,000 1 Feb 100 $12 $1,200 1 Mar 100 $14 $1,400 Total 300 $3,600 150 units are sold at $20 each → Sales revenue = $3,000 FIFO (oldest sold first): COGS = (100 × $10) + (50 × $12) = 1,000 + 600 = $1,600 Closing stock = (50 × $12) + (100 × $14) = 600 + 1,400 = $2,000 Gross profit = 3,000 − 1,600 = $1,400 LIFO (newest sold first): COGS = (100 × $14) + (50 × $12) = 1,400 + 600 = $2,000 Closing stock = (50 × $12) + (100 × $10) = 600 + 1,000 = $1,600 Gross profit = 3,000 − 2,000 = $1,000 Weighted average : $3,600 ÷ 300 units = $12 per unit COGS = 150 × 12 = $1,800 → Gross profit = $1,200 Conclusion : With rising costs, FIFO reports the higher profit ($1,400) — chosen to impress investors. LIFO reports the lower profit ($1,000) — chosen to reduce tax. Weighted average sits between the two. Note COGS + closing stock = $3,600 in every method: the total cost is the same, only its allocation differs. EOQ (Economic Order Quantity) : the optimal order quantity that minimises total inventory costs — balancing ordering costs (which fall as you order less often in bigger batches) against holding costs (which rise as you store more). LIFO note : LIFO is permitted for HSC analysis but is not permitted under Australian Accounting Standards for external financial reporting. Answer the question as asked, using the table above. 4.7 Quality Management Approach Key feature Quality control Inspection at various points in production. Define standards, test against them, take corrective action. Detects defects after they occur Quality assurance A system designed to prevent defects — "right the first time." Certified against external standards such as ISO 9000 Total Quality Management (TQM) Holistic — every employee is responsible for quality; the total business is managed for quality. Elements: customer focus, continuous improvement, employee empowerment Six Sigma Data-driven; targets 3.4 defects per million opportunities. Uses DMAIC : Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control Kaizen Continuous incremental improvement involving all employees; eliminating waste ( muda ) Quality circles Small groups of employees who meet regularly to identify and solve quality problems Confusing pair — Quality control vs Quality assurance Control = inspecting output to find defects (reactive, after the fact). Assurance = designing the process so defects don't happen (proactive, before the fact). 4.8 Overcoming Resistance to Change Two sources of resistance: Source Detail Financial costs Purchasing new equipment, redundancy payouts , retraining costs, reorganising plant layout Psychological (inertia) Fear and uncertainty → less motivated staff → lower productivity → quality issues → increased lead times and defects → lost customers Inertia = the tendency of people and organisations to keep doing what they have always done and resist any change to it. Managing change effectively: Identify the sources of change and assess the need for it Communicate with employees and build widespread support Use change agents — people who champion and drive the change Apply change models (e.g. Lewin's unfreeze → change → refreeze) 4.9 Global Factors Factor Detail Global sourcing Sourcing inputs anywhere in the world for cost or quality advantage Economies of scale Higher volumes → lower per-unit costs , through capital investment, technology, global branding and centralised training Scanning and learning Actively studying and adopting global best practice from other markets and competitors Research and development Investing in leading-edge technologies; global expertise increases the opportunity base 5. Key Case Study — Apple Topic Example Inputs Transformed : screens, chips, circuitry, customer feedback. Transforming : Foxconn factories, Chinese labour 4 Vs High volume at Foxconn; wide variety (iPhone, iPad, Mac, Watch); variation risky (over/under ordering); high visibility (customer-driven design) Quality 5M iPhones returned (2013) — lack of training, $1.6bn cost; defective Apple Maps (2012); facial recognition failure on iPhone X (2018) Outsourcing Production to Foxconn: lower cost, expertise, economies of scale — but loss of quality control, security risks, cultural barriers Supply chain 785 suppliers across 31 countries; COVID delayed iPhone 12; chip shortage (2021); Tim Cook reduced suppliers and warehouses Cost objectives iPhone SE cheaper components; in-house chip development; Samsung→TSMC supplier switch; China→India production shift; purchased Intel's 5G division Global factors Components from USA, Korea, Taiwan, Europe, China; global branding; growing R&D investment 6. Section IV & Short Answer Structures HSC Verb Frameworks Verb What to do Identify / State Name it — no explanation needed Outline Sketch in general terms; answer + brief details Describe Features and characteristics; define + give 2 or more features Distinguish Differences between two things: define 1 → define 2 → state differences → link Explain Cause and effect: answer → how → why → link to goals Analyse Show the relationship and draw out implications Assess Make a judgement based on criteria Discuss Issues, advantages and disadvantages, then judgement Evaluate Weighted judgement supported by evidence Worked Structure — "Assess the impact of customised products on the operations process" (Q21c) Assess = make a judgement based on criteria. 1. Judgement sentence: "Customised products have a large impact on the operations process of [business]…" + define the operations process 2. Inputs: Customers become a TRANSFORMED RESOURCE 3. Process: Technology, task design and layout are all affected 4. Effect: Flexible production needed, skilled workers, process layouts 5. Implication: What this means for the business 6. Restate the judgement Worked Structure — "Analyse the use of outsourcing in achieving the strategic role of Operations" Analyse = show the relationship and draw out implications. 1. Define outsourcing 2. How does outsourcing impact operations? (cost reduction, access to expertise) 3. Effect: link to a PERFORMANCE OBJECTIVE (cost, quality, flexibility) 4. Implication: link to COST LEADERSHIP or DIFFERENTIATION 5. Use relational verbs: therefore, as a result, consequently, this means PEEL Structure P oint → E xplain → E vidence (case study) → L ink back to the question 7. Common Exam Pitfalls Inventory MANAGEMENT (JIT/JIC) vs VALUATION (FIFO/LIFO) — read the verb in the question. Critical path : the longest path through the network gives the shortest possible project time. Both phrasings describe the same number. Sequencing = order. Scheduling = length of time. Don't swap them. Quality control (detects) vs quality assurance (prevents). Always link back to cost leadership or differentiation — that is the strategic role. Transformed resources are changed; transforming resources do the changing. Customers can be both an input (transformed resource) and an output recipient. Don't list influences — explain the impact on the operations process. Leading edge vs established technology: the trade-off is advantage versus reliability and cost. Compliance costs are the expenses of meeting legal requirements, not the fines for breaching them. 8. Glossary — Terms Students Mix Up Term Plain meaning Don't confuse with Transformed resources Inputs that are changed (materials, information, customers) Transforming resources — those that do the changing Transforming resources Human resources and facilities Transformed resources Sequencing The order of activities Scheduling — the duration Critical path Longest path through the network The number of tasks — it's about time , not count Float / slack Spare time a non-critical activity has Critical activities have zero float Lead time Time between ordering and receiving Cycle time — time to produce one unit Bottleneck The lowest-capacity point limiting total output A general "delay" Quality control Inspecting to find defects Quality assurance — preventing them Quality assurance System preventing defects; ISO 9000 TQM — whole-of-business philosophy JIT Inventory management strategy FIFO/LIFO — inventory valuation FIFO / LIFO Inventory valuation methods JIT/JIC — inventory management EOQ Order size minimising total inventory cost Reorder point ( when to order) Obsolescence Stock becoming outdated and unsellable Spoilage (physical deterioration) Outsourcing Using an external provider for an activity Offshoring — moving it overseas (may still be in-house) Global sourcing Buying inputs from anywhere in the world Outsourcing — contracting out an activity Economies of scale Lower per-unit cost at higher volume Lower total cost (total cost still rises) Inertia Resistance to change from habit and fear Financial resistance (cost-based) Compliance cost Expense of meeting legal requirements Penalty for breaching them Cost leadership Competing by being the lowest cost Lowest price — a low-cost firm may still charge a premium Design quality Matching consumer understanding of the product Conformance quality — meeting the specification Explicit service Tangible service elements (time, expertise) Implicit service — intangible feelings Triple bottom line Financial + social + environmental Just "being green" 9. Key Definitions Quick Reference Term One-Line Definition Operations The business process of transformation and value adding Transformation Converting inputs into outputs Value adding Creating extra value as inputs become outputs Cost leadership Having the lowest costs and being most price competitive while profitable Differentiation Distinguishing goods or services from those of competitors Transformed resources Inputs changed by the process — materials, information, customers Transforming resources Inputs that carry out the change — human resources and facilities Volume How much of a product is produced Variety The range of products offered Variation in demand The degree to which demand fluctuates Visibility The degree of customer contact with the process Leading edge technology The most advanced technology available Established technology Proven, widely adopted technology Task design Classifying job activities so employees can perform them easily Process layout Equipment grouped by function; high variety, low volume Product layout Assembly line; high volume, standardised Fixed position layout Workers come to a large immovable product Monitoring Measuring actual performance against planned performance Controlling Assessing KPIs against targets and taking corrective action Continuous improvement Ongoing commitment to achieving perfection Sequencing The order in which activities occur Scheduling The length of time activities take Gantt chart Chart outlining activities, their order and expected duration Critical path analysis Shows what must be done, how long it takes, and in what order Critical path The shortest time to complete all of the tasks Float Time a non-critical activity can be delayed without delaying the project Quality Design quality + conformance quality + quality of service Speed Fast response to market change; reduced lead times Dependability Consistency and reliability of product and delivery Flexibility Ability to adjust production quickly Customisation Creating individualised products for specific needs Supply chain management Integrating and managing the flow of supplies through the business Global sourcing Purchasing inputs without location constraint Logistics Distribution, transport, warehousing, materials handling, packaging Outsourcing Using external providers to perform business activities JIC (holding stock) Keeping inventory on hand to meet demand JIT Producing or ordering only to meet immediate demand FIFO Valuing inventory assuming oldest stock is sold first LIFO Valuing inventory assuming newest stock is sold first EOQ Order quantity that minimises total inventory costs Quality control Inspection at points of production to detect defects Quality assurance A system preventing defects; ISO 9000 TQM Holistic approach where every employee is responsible for quality Six Sigma Data-driven method targeting 3.4 defects per million; DMAIC Kaizen Continuous incremental improvement eliminating waste Inertia Psychological resistance to change Change agent A person who champions and drives change Economies of scale Lower per-unit costs achieved through higher volume CSR Open and accountable business actions respecting people and environment See also: Marketing | Finance | Human Resources | Case Studies | MOC

title: Operations Syllabus Summary
text: Operations - Syllabus Summary 1. Role of Operations Management Strategic contribution: cost leadership and goods/services differentiation Transformation: inputs → transformation processes → outputs; value added through production or service delivery Goods and services: tangible/storable goods; intangible services produced and consumed together; quality measured against different expectations Goods with service components, pure goods and pure services Interdependence: Marketing forecasts demand and communicates customer preferences; operations supplies products for sale Finance funds equipment, technology and inputs; operations controls production costs HR supplies and trains staff; operations identifies skill and staffing needs 2. Influences on Operations Globalisation: global markets, sourcing and production; economies of scale; stronger competition Technology: administrative and processing technology; efficiency, consistency, productivity and cost effects Quality expectations: design, fitness for purpose, durability, professionalism and reliability Cost-based competition: waste reduction, standardisation, automation, bulk buying and economies of scale Government policy: tax, industrial relations, environmental and training requirements; compliance costs Legal regulation: Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW): duty of care, hazard control, training and worker consultation Workers Compensation Act 1987 (NSW): compulsory workers compensation insurance Protection of the Environment Operations Act 1997 (NSW): environment protection licences and pollution controls Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (Cth): federal approval for significant environmental impacts Waste Avoidance and Resource Recovery Act 2001 (NSW): waste reduction and landfill levy Food Act 2003 (NSW): food safety supervision and safe handling Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth): consumer guarantees, product safety, recalls and fair trading Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth): minimum employment conditions, awards and workplace relations Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth): supply-chain risk reporting for qualifying large businesses Income Tax Assessment Acts and A New Tax System (GST) Act 1999 (Cth): tax and GST obligations Environmental sustainability: reduce waste, recycle, lower emissions and protect future resources CSR and triple bottom line: financial, social and environmental performance; short-term cost trade-offs against reputation and long-term risk 3. Operations Processes Inputs: Transformed resources: materials, information and customers Transforming resources: human resources and facilities Transformation process and the four Vs: Volume: production quantity and scale Variety: product range and process flexibility Variation in demand: fluctuation and capacity planning Visibility: customer contact and service requirements Technology choices: leading-edge or established; cost, reliability, quality and competitive effects Task design: duties, skills, time and role requirements Process layouts: process/functional, product/assembly line, fixed-position and office Monitoring: actual results against plans using KPIs Controlling: investigate variances and take corrective action Improvement: reduce waste, inefficiency and bottlenecks; involve staff in continuous improvement Operations KPIs: lead times, inventory turnover, defects, capacity utilisation, unit costs, waste and warranty claims Outputs: goods/services, customer service, warranties and quality feedback Sequencing: activity order; scheduling: activity duration Gantt charts: task order, duration, concurrency, progress and scheduling conflicts Critical path analysis: dependencies, critical activities, project duration and float/slack Bottleneck: lowest-capacity point that limits total output 4. Operations Strategies Performance objectives: quality, speed, dependability, flexibility, customisation and cost New product/service design: Consumer-driven or technology-driven design Research → prototype → testing → refinement → production/launch Supply, quality, capacity and cost considerations Supply chain management: Supplier choice: demand, quality, flexibility, timeliness and cost Supplier rationalisation, backward vertical integration and responsive supply chains Global sourcing: cost and expertise benefits against quality, communication and supply risks E-commerce and e-procurement; B2B and B2C ordering Logistics: transport, storage, distribution, materials handling and packaging Outsourcing: cost, efficiency, specialist skills and focus on core work; quality-control, security, dependency and skill-loss risks Technology: CAD, CAM, robotics and automation Inventory management: Just in Case (JIC): availability and bulk savings against holding costs, tied-up capital and obsolescence Just in Time (JIT): lower storage costs and freed working capital against supplier and interruption risk FIFO, LIFO and weighted average for inventory valuation; EOQ balances ordering and holding costs Quality management: Quality control: inspection and corrective action Quality assurance: systems that prevent defects TQM: whole-business responsibility, customer focus and continuous improvement Six Sigma: DMAIC and defect reduction Kaizen: incremental improvement and waste elimination Quality circles: employee groups solving quality problems Resistance to change: equipment, redundancy and retraining costs; fear, uncertainty and inertia Managing change: assess need, communicate, build support, use change agents and apply change models Global factors: global sourcing, economies of scale, scanning and learning, research and development See also: Operations FULL | Operations 1 Role | Operations 2 Influences | Operations 3 Processes | Operations 4 Strategies | MOC

title: Section III — How to Write the Business Report
text: 📋 Section III — The Business Report 20 marks · about 35 minutes · answered in a separate writing booklet A hypothetical business is described, followed by three or four bullet points . Each bullet is a section of your report. There is no choice — everyone answers this question. Worked examples: Trial Practice Killara 2022 · Theory: Operations | Marketing | Finance | Human Resources 1. What You Are Marked On NESA prints the criteria above the question. All four are worth marks. Criterion What it actually means Demonstrate knowledge and understanding relevant to the question Correct syllabus content, defined Apply the hypothetical business situation Quote the stimulus. Name the business. Use its numbers Communicate using relevant business terminology and concepts Syllabus terms, not everyday words Present a sustained, logical and cohesive response in the form of a business report Headings. Executive summary. Conclusion "In the form of a business report" is a criterion, not a suggestion. An unheaded essay loses marks even if the content is perfect. 2. The Structure EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Who the business is · what the report covers · name the recommendations up front ONE HEADED SECTION PER BULLET IN THE QUESTION Use the bullet's own wording as the heading RECOMMENDATION ONE ← if the question says "recommend TWO" RECOMMENDATION TWO these are TWO separate headed sections, never combined CONCLUSION Restate the findings, the recommendations, and the business's stated objective ⚠️ The rule that cost marks in the Killara trial: "Recommend TWO strategies" means two separate headed paragraphs , each with two reasons . Combining them reads as one recommendation and caps the mark. Teacher's note: "Do as 2 separate paragraphs, 2 reasons for each." The heading trick Read the bullets. They are your headings. Question bullet Your heading "Describe the role of operations management for this business" THE ROLE OF OPERATIONS MANAGEMENT "Demonstrate how legal regulation and CSR can influence operations management" INFLUENCE OF LEGAL REGULATION AND CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY "Recommend TWO human resource management strategies" RECOMMENDATION ONE — [STRATEGY] and RECOMMENDATION TWO — [STRATEGY] You cannot go off-topic if your headings are the question. 3. The Executive Summary Four moves, about 85 words, written first and never skipped. 1. WHO [Business] operates [what, where]. 2. CONTEXT One line on the problem from the stimulus. 3. SCOPE This report describes… demonstrates… and recommends… 4. OBJECTIVE …to assist in achieving [THE STATED GOAL]. From the teacher-marked Jumbo Movies report: Jumbo Movies Pty Ltd operates a cinema complex in a large shopping centre in Western Sydney, competing in an entertainment market disrupted by streaming services and declining attendance among consumers under 30. This report describes the role of operations management for the business, demonstrates how legal regulation and corporate social responsibility influence that function, and recommends two human resource strategies, being training and development as well as rewards, to assist the new owners in achieving their objective of increasing profits by 20% within 12 months. Naming the recommendations in the executive summary is free marks. The marker knows where you're going before they start. 4. The Body Sections 1 TOPIC Judgement-first sentence answering the bullet. 2 DEFINE The syllabus concept, briefly. 3 APPLY The stimulus detail as evidence — quote it. 4 EFFECT What that means for this business. 5 CLOSE "Therefore / Consequently…" linking to the objective. Every stimulus bullet must appear somewhere. The review points are not decoration — each one is a mark waiting to be claimed. Jumbo Movies review point Where it landed Wet, slippery floors WHS duty of care breach Run down environment and uniforms High visibility (4 Vs) + non-monetary rewards Coffee machine took 6 months Dependability failure Ticketing machine errors Quality failure + training Working through lunch breaks Fair Work / NES + non-monetary rewards Unhappy with training Training and development Before you write, tick each stimulus bullet off against a section. Any bullet with no home is a mark you're about to leave behind. 5. The Recommendation Sections One heading each. Two reasons each. Name the syllabus category. 1 NAME It is recommended that [BUSINESS] implement [STRATEGY], a [FUNCTION] strategy within [SYLLABUS CATEGORY]. 2 REASON 1 The first reason is [X]. [STIMULUS EVIDENCE]. 3 REASON 2 The second reason is [Y]. [EFFECT + INDICATOR]. 4 LINK …contributing directly to [THE STATED OBJECTIVE]. Worked, from the corrected Jumbo Movies report: RECOMMENDATION ONE — TRAINING AND DEVELOPMENT It is recommended that Jumbo Movies implement a structured training and development program, a human resource strategy within the development stage of the HR cycle. The first reason is that it directly addresses the errors identified in the review. Employees are dissatisfied with the training received on the new ticketing machines and regular errors are occurring, indicating the technology was introduced without adequate skill development, so on the job training combined with customer service training would reduce these errors and improve the performance objectives of quality and speed. The second reason is retention. Employees who are supported to develop are more motivated and less likely to leave, reducing staff turnover , a key indicator of human resource effectiveness, which lowers recruitment and induction costs and contributes directly to the 20% profit objective. 6. Worked Example — Your Full-Marks Apple Report This is the structure that earned full marks on your Finance assessment. Same shape, different subject. Full text: Brain/Business_Studies/Past_Essays/Finance_Assessment_Draft.md EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Apple Inc. is a large global technology company that designs, manufactures and sells consumer electronics, software and digital services worldwide. This report assesses Apple's financial performance over the 2024 and 2025 financial years using the net profit ratio, expense ratio, and accounts receivable turnover (days). It also recommends the use of factoring… PROFITABILITY — NET PROFIT RATIO ← one heading per ratio EFFICIENCY — EXPENSE RATIO EFFICIENCY OF COLLECTION — ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE TURNOVER RECOMMENDATION — IMPROVE ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE TURNOVER CONCLUSION Why each body section scored: 1 JUDGEMENT "Apple's profitability improved between 2024 (23.97%) and 2025 (26.92%), as shown by the net profit ratio, which measures how much profit is retained after expenses." 2 DATA Both years' raw figures and the calculation. 3 MEANING "…meaning Apple retained approximately 24 cents for every $1 of revenue." 4 CAUSE "…driven by growth in services revenue, which increased from $96,169m to $109,158m." 5 BENCHMARK "Compared to Samsung, which operates with a net profit ratio of approximately 10%…" 6 IMPLICATION "…supports reinvestment, expansion, and long term growth." The move that made it full marks: a benchmark in every section. Samsung for profitability, Samsung again for the expense ratio, the 30-day ideal for receivables. Never a number without a comparison. 7. Timing and Length Phase Time Read the stimulus, tick each bullet to a section 3 min Executive summary 4 min Body sections 20 min Recommendations 6 min Conclusion 2 min 750–800 words , roughly 20 words a minute handwritten. If you're running out of time, cut examples and detail from the body sections. Never cut the recommendations or the conclusion — they carry their own marks and the "sustained and cohesive" criterion. 8. Checklist □ Executive summary present, names the recommendations □ One heading per question bullet, using the bullet's wording □ Recommendations in SEPARATE headed sections, two reasons each □ Every stimulus detail used somewhere □ Business named repeatedly, not "the business" □ Syllabus terminology throughout □ Every judgement has a benchmark or comparison □ Conclusion restates findings + recommendations + the stated objective The four most common ways to lose marks here: No headings. Loses the "form of a business report" criterion outright. Generic content. Theory that could describe any business. Quote the stimulus. Combining two recommendations. Two means two sections. Ignoring the stated objective. If the question says "increase profits by 20% within 12 months", every recommendation must link back to it. See also: Section IV Extended Response | Trial Practice Killara 2022 | MOC | Confusing Pairs

title: Section IV — How to Write the Extended Response
text: 📝 Section IV — The Extended Response 20 marks · about 35 minutes · choose ONE of two questions · separate writing booklet No stimulus. You bring the case study. The two questions cover different topics, so pick the one where your case study evidence is strongest. Scaffolds below follow your teacher's Section IV Essay Structures handout. Case study data: Case Studies · Theory: Operations | Marketing | Finance | Human Resources 1. What You Are Marked On Criterion What it actually means Demonstrate knowledge and understanding relevant to the question Correct syllabus content, defined Apply relevant business case study/studies and contemporary business issues Real businesses. Real figures. Real dates. This is where most marks are lost Communicate using relevant business terminology and concepts Syllabus terms, not everyday words Present a sustained, logical and cohesive response Judgement in the introduction, sustained through every paragraph, restated at the end No headings here. Section III is a report. Section IV is an essay — continuous prose, paragraphed. 2. Identify the Verb First The verb dictates the entire structure. Get it wrong and the content can't save you. Verb What to do Structure Assess / Evaluate / Explain the importance of Make a judgement §3 scaffold Analyse / Explain how Show relationships and draw out implications §4 scaffold Discuss For and against, then judge §3 scaffold, balanced Examine Identify components and their relationships §4 scaffold 3. Assess · Evaluate · Explain the importance of Judgement based on criteria — does it help the business achieve ________? Introduction 1. Start with the JUDGEMENT SENTENCE. 2. State specifically what you are evaluating — use the syllabus dot points by name. 3. Name every case study you will use. Your teacher's model: "This essay will evaluate how Apple effectively uses their operational strategies of Supply Chain Management, Inventory Management and Outsourcing to respond to the globalisation, ethical and legal influences ." Notice: the dot points are named, not gestured at. Each body paragraph 1 JUDGEMENT Answer the question — a judgement with a brief overview of reasons. 2 DEFINE Define and describe the key concept(s). 3 ADVANTAGES Prove they ARE advantages by linking to a topic-specific goal. Use statistics as evidence. 4 DISADVANT. Prove they ARE disadvantages by linking to a topic-specific goal. 5 RESTATE Re-state the judgement, linked to long-term business goals. "Prove they are advantages by linking to a topic-specific goal." An advantage isn't an advantage because you say so. It's an advantage because it helps achieve cost leadership , or market share , or liquidity , or staff retention . Name the goal. Conclusion One to two summary sentences per body paragraph, each including the case study . 4. Analyse · Explain how · Examine Show the relationship between things and draw out implications. Introduction 1. Start by LINKING THE TWO IDEAS TOGETHER — cause and effect in the first sentence. 2. State specifically what you are analysing — name the syllabus dot points. 3. Name every case study. Your teacher's model: "This essay will analyse the impacts for Apple of globalisation, ethical and legal influences on their operational strategies of Supply Chain Management, Inventory Management and Outsourcing ." Each body paragraph 1 LINK Open by linking the two ideas — cause and effect — for the case study. 2 CAUSE/EFFECT 1 HOW is the business impacted? (observable changes) WHY is it affected? (link to a topic-specific goal) 3 CAUSE/EFFECT 2 HOW · WHY · and link back to cause #1. 4 IMPLICATIONS LONG TERM. Link to the strategic role and business goals. Positive, negative, or both — but detailed and tied to the case study. You do not have to give both positive and negative implications. You do have to make them detailed and tied to the case study. 5. Worked Body Paragraph — 2021 HSC Marketing Question: Analyse how a situational analysis (SWOT, product life cycle) may affect marketing strategies. Teacher's structural rule for this question: To score above 12, you must have at least one paragraph on SWOT and one on Product Life Cycle . SWOT — 2 body paragraphs. Each takes ONE element and does at least two of it (2 strengths, or 2 threats, etc.). Product Life Cycle — 1 body paragraph showing how ONE marketing strategy changes across the cycle. The paragraph, annotated: Apple has numerous threats such as competition in its smartphone market which impacts on their marketing strategy such as their Product strategy. [LINK — cause and effect up front] Threats are external factors that could impact on the business that they have no control over [DEFINITION] and for Apple one of their major threats is the increased competition especially from low cost Asian providers such as Huawei, Xiaomi. The product strategy includes their branding, packaging and after sales services [DEFINITION] . For Apple to compete against low cost competitors they have positioned their product as a high quality, luxury smartphone. Apple's branding is easily recognizable with the apple with a bite out of it and they have linked the branding to their reputation of producing a high quality, innovative product [HOW] . However there has been some issues with whether they have been innovative over the last few years as their focus has been on improving the camera. This has impacted on their market share as it was lower than Samsung from Quarter 2 2023 (17% compared to 20%) until Quarter 4, 2024 when their market share improved to be higher than Samsung (23% compared to 16%) [EFFECT — with statistics] . … This meets the needs of the customers expectations when purchasing Apple products therefore their target market is more likely to purchase their products rather than their cheaper competitors [WHY/EFFECT] . Therefore by using their product strategy of branding and packaging Apple is able to maintain or increase the number of their customers and have been able to minimise the threat of competitors and improve their market share in the last quarter of 2024. [IMPLICATION] What makes it work: Move Where Cause and effect in sentence 1 "threats… which impacts on their marketing strategy such as their Product strategy" Both concepts defined threats, then product strategy Named competitors Huawei, Xiaomi, Samsung Dated statistics 17% vs 20% Q2 2023 → 23% vs 16% Q4 2024 Honest weakness "issues with whether they have been innovative" Implication closes market share improved, threat minimised The dated statistic is the difference between Band 5 and Band 6. "Apple has a large market share" is worth nothing. "23% compared to Samsung's 16% in Q4 2024" is worth a mark. 6. Short-Answer Verb Scaffolds Same logic, compressed. From your teacher's 2024 Operations Past Paper short answer structure . Assess — "Assess the impact of customised products on the operations process of the sports shoe store." 1 Judgement sentence: "It has a large impact on the operational process of…" 2 Define the process 3 How is it impacting the operational process 4 Effect on the business 5 What it means for the business (implication) 6 Restate the judgement Analyse — "Analyse the use of outsourcing in achieving the strategic role of Operations Management." 1 Define outsourcing 2 How does outsourcing impact operations 3 Effect — link to the performance objective 4 What it means for the business (implication) — linking to cost leadership 7. The Marker's Comments — What Full Marks Looks Like From your Past HSC Finance Model Answer 2025 pack. These are the actual reasons marks were awarded. A 2-mark answer scored 2/2 because the student: showed all the working for the calculation stated what it means for the business compared it to the industry average related it to the scenario A 4-mark answer scored 4/4 because the student: linked it to the scenario showed clear cause and effect relationships using relational verbs provided implications , even if limited Marker's note on that response: "This is probably not the best 4 that a student will write but it does enough to reach the 4 in the HSC." You do not need brilliance. You need the four moves, every time. Relational verbs are the ones that carry cause and effect: causes · results in · leads to · means that · therefore · consequently impacts on · which in turn · thereby · so that · enabling 8. Case Study Evidence You Must Be Able to Quote Full data: Case Studies Case study Strongest for Apple Operations (supply chain, outsourcing, new product design) · Marketing (positioning, global branding) · Finance (ratios 2024–25, services margin) McDonald's Marketing (standardisation vs customisation, global promotion) · Finance (comparative ratios 2022–23) Figures worth memorising: Apple net profit ratio 23.97% (2024) → 26.92% (2025) expense ratio 14.7% (2024) → 14.93% (2025) AR turnover 32 days → 35 days (ideal 30) services revenue $96,169m → $109,158m Samsung NPR ~10% — the benchmark market share 17% vs Samsung 20% (Q2 2023) 23% vs Samsung 16% (Q4 2024) McDonald's current ratio 1.43:1 (2022) → 1.16:1 (2023) net profit 27% (2022) → 33% (2023) revenue $25.92 billion (2024) restaurants 40,000+ in 100+ countries advertising ~$4.5 billion annually 9. Timing and Checklist Phase Time Choose the question, identify the verb, plan 3 paragraphs 5 min Introduction 4 min Body ×3 7 min each Conclusion 3 min 800–900 words , three body paragraphs. □ Verb identified — judgement scaffold or relationship scaffold □ Introduction states the judgement or the link, in sentence 1 □ Syllabus dot points named specifically in the introduction □ Case studies named in the introduction □ Every paragraph contains the case study □ At least one DATED STATISTIC per paragraph □ Every advantage/disadvantage linked to a topic-specific goal □ Implications are LONG TERM and tied to the strategic role □ Conclusion: 1–2 sentences per body paragraph, each naming the case study The three most common ways to lose marks here: Theory with no business. Every paragraph needs the case study, not just paragraph one. Undated, unsourced figures. "A large market share" earns nothing. Answering the wrong verb. Describing when asked to evaluate caps you at mid-band regardless of content. See also: Section III Business Report | Case Studies | MOC | Confusing Pairs | Trial Practice Killara 2022

title: Killara 2022 Trial — Marked Paper and Model Answers
text: Killara 2022 Trial — Marked Paper and Model Answers ✅ TEACHER-MARKED. Section I 16/20 · Section II 35/40 · Section III 16–17/20 Total 67–68/80 (84%) Theory: Operations | Marketing | Finance | Human Resources · Drill: Confusing Pairs 1. Section I — Multiple Choice · 16/20 Q Ans Q Ans Q Ans Q Ans 1 D 6 C 11 D 16 D 2 D 7 A 12 C 17 B 3 C 8 D 13 D 18 B 4 B 9 A 14 B 19 D 5 B 10 C 15 A 20 C The four missed Q Chose Correct The lesson 4 C Industrial B Resource Farmers operate in the resource market, where raw materials are sold. The industrial market is who they sell to . The question asked which market they sell in 6 D Performance appraisal C Unfair dismissal Performance appraisal is an evaluation process, not a termination. Justin was sacked for reporting a colleague — harsh, unjust and unreasonable 10 B Enterprise Agreement C Common Law Contract Enterprise agreements are collective and must pass the BOOT. One solicitor negotiating a bespoke $300k package individually is a common law contract 17 C Employees B Finance The stem says "which key business function" . There are only four: operations, marketing, finance, HR. Employees, Customers and Outsourcing aren't functions — Finance was the only possible answer Q5 — double-highlighted Correct is (B) Volume . "Produces standardised steel bars" = high volume, low variety. Variation in demand means demand fluctuating over a cycle, which the stem never describes. A one-off increase is not variation. The three calculation traps Q11 — GP ratio 35% → GP = $630,000. COGS = Sales − GP = $1,170,000 . Option (B) is the GP, not the COGS. Q15 — run the balance month by month: 10k → 20k → 10k → 5k → $20,000 . Don't net the totals. Q20 — market share , not viewer count. P3 goes 21.43% → 24.14% = +2.71pp . P4 held 400,000 viewers but lost share. 2. Section II — Short Answer · 35/40 (teacher-marked) Q Mark Teacher's margin note 21(a) 2/2 — 21(b) 4/4 "reducing lead time" ✓ 21(c) 3/4 "how? better to link to more satisfied customers or reduced costs" 22(a) 2/2 — 22(b) 3/4 "flow?" · "not sure what you mean" 22(c) 3/4 "…to meet market needs" 23(a) 1/2 reason (i) crossed out 23(b) 4/4 — 23(c) 3/4 "not necessarily" — the recession detour 24(a) 2/2 — 24(b) 4/4 ✓ throughout 24(c) 4/4 ✓ throughout ⚠️ Two hard lessons from the marked script 1. "Identify TWO" means two distinct reasons. Reason (i) was crossed out entirely in 23(a). "Cost saving" and "time saving" are effectively the same reason stated twice , and the induction-training claim is wrong — the outsourcing provider still runs induction. Pick reasons from genuinely different categories: Valid distinct reasons for outsourcing HR Cost reduction — avoids maintaining an in-house HR department Access to specialist expertise — external providers hold current legal and industrial relations knowledge Allows focus on core business — management attention redirected to revenue-generating activity Scalability — capacity flexes with business need without hiring 2. End on a tangible outcome, not a syllabus category. The 21(c) model closed on "the performance objectives of quality, dependability and cost are met." That is abstract. The teacher wants the business consequence : …ensuring fewer defective products reach customers, which reduces warranty replacement costs and restores customer satisfaction . Applies to every Operations answer. Name the concrete benefit, then the syllabus term — not the term alone. The three patterns costing marks Not using the data given. The industry averages in Q24 were printed directly above the question and went uncited. If a figure is in the stimulus, quote it back. Warm-up sentences. "X plays a distinct role in…" , "One key factor that can influence…" , "Financial reports can be complicated…" — roughly 15% of the writing restated the question. Start at the definition. Answering beyond the question. A third of 23(c) covered a recession when the question asked about an increase in economic activity. Nothing outside the verb's scope earns anything. Length and time budget Marks Words Time 2 35–45 3 min 4 90–110 6 min 6 140–160 9 min Anything past this isn't earning. It's costing you Section III. 3. Model Answers — Short Answer 21(a) · Outline how measuring warranty claims assists assessment of operations effectiveness · 2 marks Warranty claims are a key performance indicator of quality . Measuring them against a target allows TWG to compare actual to planned performance, locate where the transformation process is producing defects, and take corrective action. 38 words. The two words that pay are KPI and quality . ⚠️ Terminology trap: a bottleneck is a capacity constraint slowing throughput, not a defect. Warranty claims reveal defects. 21(c) · Explain why controls are important in the operations process · 4 marks ⚠️ This scored 3/4 as originally written. The corrected final sentence is below. Controls in the operations process involve comparing actual performance against planned performance using key performance indicators such as defect rates, lead times and warranty claims, then investigating the variance and taking corrective action . Controls are important because they convert monitoring into improvement: measurement alone identifies a problem, but control resolves it. For TWG, if warranty claims are targeted at 2% but reach 7%, control would trigger an investigation of the transformation process, potentially revealing inadequate quality assurance at the assembly stage. Controls also prevent minor variances escalating into systemic failure, as detecting a defect during production costs substantially less than replacing products under warranty. Consequently, controls ensure fewer defective appliances reach customers, reducing warranty replacement costs and restoring the customer satisfaction TWG is currently losing — achieving the performance objectives of quality and dependability , and enabling product differentiation . Original ending (3/4) Corrected ending (4/4) Closes on "the performance objectives of quality, dependability and cost are met" "fewer defective appliances reach customers, reducing warranty replacement costs and restoring customer satisfaction" Why Names the syllabus category Names the business outcome , then the category The words markers look for: variance and corrective action . Inventing a benchmark (2% vs 7%) shows you understand control needs something to compare against. The mark most people drop: ending on abstraction. Always finish with what actually changes for the business — customers retained, costs reduced, orders delivered on time. 22(a) · Outline ONE factor influencing consumer choice · 2 marks Sociocultural influences, particularly reference groups such as peers and fitness influencers. Activewear is worn publicly, so women buy the brands their peers and influencers endorse, treating the product as a marker of social identity. 35 words. The trap: influences on consumer choice = why the customer buys. Branding, packaging, price = what the business does. Don't cross the two. The four factors: Factor Meaning Psychological Inside the individual — perception, motives, attitudes, personality, self-image, learning Sociocultural Other people — family, peers and reference groups, social class, culture and subculture Economic Boom vs recession, disposable income, level of economic activity Government Legislation, taxes, interest rates, regulations affecting spending 22(b) · Explain how consumer laws influence marketing practices · 4 marks The five consumer laws — memorise as a list: deceptive and misleading advertising price discrimination implied conditions warranties resale price maintenance Correct citation: Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) , containing the Australian Consumer Law (ACL) , enforced by the ACCC . Application example: Nellie and Ellie could not pin or clip garments on models to alter the fit shown, as this constitutes deceptive and misleading conduct by misrepresenting how the product performs. 22(c) · How can this business conduct market research · 4 marks The question says conduct , so the process is the spine: 1. Determining information needs 2. Data collection (primary / secondary) 3. Data analysis and interpretation Primary and secondary alone is step 2 only. Add step 1 ( what do they need to know — price sensitivity, preferred fabrics, purchase frequency? ) and step 3, and name market segmentation by demographic and psychographic. 23(c) · Explain how an increase in economic activity may impact HR · 4 marks Boom only. Say nothing about recession. Low unemployment → skills shortages → upward wage pressure → harder to attract and retain staff → HR shifts spending toward retention strategies , training and non-financial rewards, while labour costs rise as a proportion of expenses. 24(b) · Discuss the profitability of Wacky Widgets · 4 marks Wacky Widgets' net profit ratio is 24.2% ($206,000 ÷ $850,000) — 24 cents retained per sales dollar, well below the industry average of 50%. However, its gross profit ratio of 82.9% shows cost of goods sold is well controlled, so the weakness lies in operating expenses. This is confirmed by the expense ratio of 58.7%, far above the industry average of 36%, with wages alone absorbing $310,000. Profitability is therefore weak but correctable. Expense minimisation through cost centre analysis, and refinancing the $110,000 in loan repayments, would lift the net profit ratio toward the benchmark. 95 words. The three ratios read against each other: Ratio Wacky Widgets Industry Gross profit 82.9% — Net profit 24.2% 50% Expense 58.7% 36% The move that lifts this from 2 to 4: high GP + low NP means the money is leaking between them, i.e. operating expenses . Part (a) already proved it — reuse the figure. ⚠️ A ratio without a comparison is a number, not analysis. Always answer: compared to what? Over time, industry, or target. And if the paper hands you an industry average, use it — that was the mark lost here. 24(c) · Why are capitalising expenses and normalised earnings limitations · 4 marks Capitalising expenses records a cost as part of a non-current asset's value rather than as an expense, writing it off as depreciation over time. This understates expenses and overstates both net profit and asset values, so the business appears stronger than it is. Normalised earnings are profits adjusted to remove one-off items such as an asset sale. Because management decides what counts as unusual, the adjustment is subjective, earnings can be smoothed, and comparability between years and between businesses is lost. Both therefore prevent financial reports giving a true and fair view. 92 words. What it is Why it's a limitation Capitalising expenses Adding a cost to the value of a non-current asset instead of expensing it now Understates expenses, overstates profit and asset values Normalised earnings Adjusting profit to remove one-off or cyclical items Management decides what is "unusual" — subjective, destroys comparability The hook: Capitalising expenses flatters the numbers. Normalised earnings flatter the story. Both are limitations because management chooses . ⚠️ Capitalised costs are written off as depreciation , not "as income." 4. Section III — Model Business Report Question 25 (20 marks). Jumbo Movies Pty Ltd, cinema complex, Western Sydney. Decline in under-30 attendance, growing demand for streaming. New owners want profits up 20% in 12 months. Review revealed: wet and slippery floors · run down environment and uniforms · broken coffee machine took 6 months to replace · regular ticketing machine errors · employees working through lunch breaks · dissatisfaction with training on new machines. Required: describe the role of operations management · demonstrate how legal regulation and CSR influence operations · recommend TWO HR strategies. ✅ Teacher-marked 16–17/20. Margin note beside the legal and CSR section: "great paragraphs." Marks lost for combining the two HR strategies into one section. Teacher: "Do as 2 separate paragraphs, 2 reasons for each" · "link to HR" · "if you did the HR strategies separately you would get 18/20." The version below is corrected. ~780 words. If short on time, trim the CSR social examples rather than the HR section. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Jumbo Movies Pty Ltd operates a cinema complex in a large shopping centre in Western Sydney, competing in an entertainment market disrupted by streaming services and declining attendance among consumers under 30. This report describes the role of operations management for the business, demonstrates how legal regulation and corporate social responsibility influence that function, and recommends two human resource strategies, being training and development as well as rewards, to assist the new owners in achieving their objective of increasing profits by 20% within 12 months. THE ROLE OF OPERATIONS MANAGEMENT Operations management involves the transformation of inputs into outputs, and for Jumbo Movies the output is intangible and perishable, as an unsold seat for a session cannot be recovered. The strategic role of operations is cost leadership or good and service differentiation, and Jumbo Movies cannot compete with streaming on cost, as Netflix carries no venue or staffing overheads, so it must pursue service differentiation by delivering an experience that cannot be replicated at home. Cinema operations are also high visibility, as customers are physically present and directly observe the facilities, staff and uniforms, which is why the run down environment identified in the review damages this business far more than it would a manufacturer. The review further reveals failures in the performance objectives of dependability, as a broken coffee machine took six months to replace, and quality, evidenced by regular ticketing machine errors. Operations is therefore interdependent with finance, as the 20% profit objective requires both cost control and higher revenue per customer, and with marketing, as an outdated environment contradicts any promotional message about a premium experience. INFLUENCE OF LEGAL REGULATION AND CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY Under the Work Health and Safety Act, Jumbo Movies owes a duty of care to employees and customers, and floors that are often wet and slippery constitute a direct breach, exposing the business to workers compensation claims, public liability claims and regulatory penalties. Operations must therefore build compliance into its processes through scheduled cleaning between sessions, hazard signage and staff safety training, while the Fair Work Act and National Employment Standards require that employees receive their entitled breaks, meaning rostering must be redesigned. Although compliance raises operating costs, a single serious injury claim would cost far more. Corporate social responsibility requires the business to move beyond this legal minimum, considering its impact on people, the community and the environment, and is voluntary and reputational rather than mandatory. As a cinema consumes substantial electricity through projection and air conditioning, Jumbo Movies could install laser projectors and LED lighting, eliminate single use plastics at the candy bar and introduce recycling. Although these initiatives raise short term costs and create tension with the profit objective, they support the triple bottom line and differentiate the business to consumers under 30, the very segment being lost to streaming. RECOMMENDATION ONE — TRAINING AND DEVELOPMENT It is recommended that Jumbo Movies implement a structured training and development program, a human resource strategy within the development stage of the HR cycle. The first reason is that it directly addresses the errors identified in the review. Employees are dissatisfied with the training received on the new ticketing machines and regular errors are occurring, indicating the technology was introduced without adequate skill development, so on the job training combined with customer service training would reduce these errors and improve the performance objectives of quality and speed. The second reason is retention. Employees who are supported to develop are more motivated and less likely to leave, reducing staff turnover , a key indicator of human resource effectiveness, which lowers recruitment and induction costs and contributes directly to the 20% profit objective. RECOMMENDATION TWO — REWARDS It is secondly recommended that Jumbo Movies introduce a combination of monetary and non monetary rewards, a maintenance strategy within the HR cycle. The first reason is that the review identifies clear sources of dissatisfaction that cost almost nothing to resolve. Guaranteed rostered lunch breaks, flexible rostering around peak demand, new uniforms and formal staff recognition address the complaints raised at minimal expense. The second reason is alignment. Monetary rewards linked to performance, such as a bonus tied to confectionery revenue per customer, align employee behaviour with the owners' profit objective. Together these reduce absenteeism and staff turnover , and produce the motivated, well presented workforce on which the cinema's service differentiation depends. CONCLUSION Service differentiation is Jumbo Movies only viable response to streaming competition. Legal regulation imposes safety and employment obligations, while corporate social responsibility differentiates it to a younger market. Training and development combined with a rewards system would improve service quality, morale and productivity, supporting the 20% profit objective within 12 months. Every stimulus detail is used Review point Where it lands Wet, slippery floors WHS duty of care breach Run down environment and uniforms High visibility (4 Vs) + non-monetary rewards Coffee machine, 6 months Dependability failure Ticketing machine errors Quality failure + training Working through lunch breaks Fair Work / NES + non-monetary rewards Unhappy with training Training and development If short on time, cut in this order: the CSR social examples, then the variation-in-demand sentence, then the performance-pay risk sentence. Takes you to ~850 without losing a criterion. 5. Section III Report Template The structure that earns the "form of a business report" criterion: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY who the business is, what the report covers, name the recommendations up front BODY SECTION 1 one heading per bullet in the question BODY SECTION 2 judgement-first topic sentence stimulus detail as evidence "Therefore..." closer RECOMMENDATION ONE ← ONE HEADING PER RECOMMENDATION RECOMMENDATION TWO never combine them CONCLUSION restate findings + the recommendations + the objective ⚠️ The rule that cost marks here: if the question says "Recommend TWO strategies" , that is two separate headed paragraphs , each with two reasons , each explicitly named as a strategy of the relevant business function. Combining them reads as one recommendation and caps the mark. Each recommendation paragraph: 1 NAME It is recommended that [BUSINESS] implement [STRATEGY], a [FUNCTION] strategy within [SYLLABUS CATEGORY]. 2 REASON 1 The first reason is [X]. [STIMULUS EVIDENCE]. 3 REASON 2 The second reason is [Y]. [EFFECT + INDICATOR]. 4 LINK …contributing directly to [THE STATED OBJECTIVE]. Word budget: 750–800 words, ~35 minutes. Roughly 20 words a minute handwritten. See also: MOC | Operations | Human Resources | Finance | Marketing

text: McDonald's Case Study — Section IV Essay Resource Added note — not from the TheSashi notes. Added 25 Oct 2026 from your McDonald's Section IV resource screenshot. For Section IV (Case Study Essay) — Trial Aug 5, 2026. Complete data pack: company profile, key stats, strategies, policies, financial ratios, and essay-ready paragraphs. Sections 6 (Strategy → Objective Matrix) and 7 (Essay-Ready Paragraph Templates) were listed in the resource's Quick Jump but were cut off at the bottom of your screenshot, so they are not included here. Send the rest and they can be added. Quick Jump Company Profile & Key Statistics Operations — Strategies, Policies & Data Marketing — Strategies, Policies & Data Finance — Ratios, Strategies & Analysis HR — Policies, Legal Compliance & Case Law Strategy → Objective Matrix — not shown in screenshot Essay-Ready Paragraph Templates — not shown in screenshot 1. Company Profile & Key Statistics McDonald's Corporation Founded 1940 (franchise model since 1955) HQ Chicago, USA Global Stores >40,000 in 100+ countries Australian Stores >1,000 (80% franchised) Employees (Aus) >100,000 Revenue 2023 $25.49 billion USD Revenue 2022 $23.18 billion USD Business Model Franchise (~93% franchised globally) Key Essay Statistics (2023) Statistic Value Note NP Ratio 33% +6pp from 2022 Current Ratio 1.16:1 Down from 1.43:1 Gearing (D/E) (869)% Negative (share buyback) AR Turnover 32.88 days Stable Operating Costs $13.85B Only 0.3% increase Inventory ~$52M Stable across 2022–23 How to use these stats in an essay: "McDonald's improved its Net Profit ratio from 27% in 2022 to 33% in 2023, outpacing competitor Yum Brands (23%), demonstrating the effectiveness of its integrated marketing and cost control strategies in achieving the financial objective of profitability." 2. Operations — Strategies, Policies & Data Supply Chain Management — Global Sourcing Tags: Cost, Dependability, Quality McDonald's sources ingredients from approved suppliers in multiple countries. In Australia, >90% of ingredients are locally sourced. The global supply chain uses regional distribution centres to minimise lead times. Data point: McDonald's Australia works with >150 Australian farmers and suppliers, reducing transport costs and supporting the cost performance objective while ensuring dependability of supply. Quality Management — TQM Tags: Quality, Cost McDonald's uses a Total Quality Management (TQM) approach: quality assurance systems at every stage from supplier audits to in-store cooking protocols. The "Made For You" system ensures burgers are assembled to order, reducing waste. Data point: Standardised cooking times and temperatures across all 40,000+ stores ensure consistency — a core element of quality assurance. Technology — Automation Tags: Cost, Speed Self-service kiosks installed in the majority of Australian stores. Mobile app ordering with geofencing for pickup timing. Automated inventory tracking systems link POS data to supply orders. Data point: Kiosks reduce front-counter labour costs by ~15–20% per store while increasing average order value by 20% (upselling prompts). Inventory Management — JIT Tags: Cost, Quality Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory: perishable ingredients (lettuce, buns, meat patties) delivered multiple times per week. Reduces holding costs and spoilage. Data point: Inventory held at a stable ~$52M despite revenue growth from $23.2B to $25.5B — JIT improving efficiency. Global Factors — Economies of Scale Tags: Cost, Flexibility With >40,000 stores, McDonald's achieves massive economies of scale in purchasing (bulk buying packaging, ingredients). Global R&D centres develop menu innovations that roll out across markets. Environmental Sustainability — CSR Tags: Customisation, Cost Australian stores: recycled building cladding, sheep's wool insulation, solar panels. "Daisy and Liam" robots in the USA disassemble old iPhones to recover rare minerals — part of circular economy commitment. Policy: 100% of guest packaging from renewable/recycled sources by 2025 (global target). 3. Marketing — Strategies, Policies & Data Promotion — Integrated Campaigns Tags: Growth, Profitability 2023 Marvel Cinematic Universe partnership: movie figurines with large meals — incentivised upsizing + repeat visits + word-of-mouth. Data point: Revenue increased from $23,182M to $25,493M (+10%) — this promotion was a key driver alongside maintaining costs at ~$13.8B. Pricing — Penetration + Loss Leader Tags: Growth, Profitability Loss Leader: $1 Frozen Coke / $1 McFlurry — brings customers in, they buy high-margin items. Penetration: McValue menu at lower price points to capture price-sensitive consumers during a cost-of-living crisis. Global Marketing — Glocalisation Tags: Growth, Customisation Standardisation: Golden Arches, "I'm Lovin' It" slogan, core menu (Big Mac, Fries) are globally consistent. Customisation / Localisation: Australia: McCafé (premium coffee), Chicken Salt on fries, Aussie Angus Burger. India: no beef, McAloo Tikki. Japan: Teriyaki Burger. Consumer Law Compliance (CCA 2010) Tags: Ethics, Reputation Previously scrutinised by the ACCC for advertising food as "healthy" despite high sugar/fat content (misleading conduct under the CCA). Response: Introduced clear nutritional labelling on packaging and menu boards, accurate calorie counts in all advertising. E-Marketing — Digital Ecosystem Tags: Growth, Efficiency MyMacca's app with loyalty program, personalised offers based on purchase history, geolocation-based promotions. >30 million app downloads in Australia. Market Segmentation Demographic: Families (Happy Meals), young adults (value deals, late-night), coffee drinkers (McCafé). Behavioural: Loyalty app users get targeted deals. Geographic: Regional menu variations. 4. Finance — Ratios, Strategies & Analysis Financial Ratio Data (2022 vs 2023) Ratio 2022 2023 Trend What It Means NP Ratio (Profitability) 27% 33% Improved Revenue rose 10% while operating costs rose only ~0.3%, so profit margin expanded. Yum Brands: 23% in 2023, so McDonald's outperforms its competitor. Current Ratio (Liquidity) 1.43:1 1.16:1 Worsened Below ideal 2:1. Still >1:1, so it can meet short-term obligations, but the declining trend is a concern. Gearing / D/E (Solvency) (598)% (869)% Negative Negative due to an aggressive share buyback program reducing equity. Still relies more on debt than equity — high financial risk, but characteristic of mature franchise businesses with stable cash flows. AR Turnover (Efficiency) 31.74 days 32.88 days Stable Collects receivables in ~32 days (~11.4x/year). Slight slowdown but not material for a business that is mostly cash-based. Inventory ~$52M ~$52M Stable JIT working — revenue grew 10% but inventory didn't increase, showing efficiency gains. Finance Strategies at McDonald's Profitability Management — Cost Control Tags: Profitability, Efficiency Cost centres: Each store is treated as a cost centre with local P&L responsibility. Managers control labour scheduling, food waste, and utilities. Data: Operating costs rose only 0.3% ($13,811.6M → $13,847M) while revenue rose 10%, demonstrating effective cost control. Working Capital Management Tags: Liquidity, Efficiency Cash-based business model minimises receivables; franchisees pay royalties and rent monthly. Tight inventory via JIT keeps current assets lean. However, the declining current ratio (1.43 → 1.16) signals a need for improved working capital management. Global Financial Management Tags: Growth, Solvency Hedging: McDonald's operates in 100+ countries, exposed to ~50 currencies. Uses forward contracts and currency swaps to hedge against exchange rate fluctuations, protecting AUD-denominated profits when repatriating to US HQ. Cash Flow Management Tags: Liquidity, Profitability Franchise model ensures steady cash inflows (royalties ~4–5% of gross sales + rent). Discounts for early payment from franchisees. Factoring is not typically used due to mostly cash-based operations. 5. HR — Policies, Legal Compliance & Case Law NES Compliance McDonald's Australia complies with all 11 NES including: Max 38hr/week for full-time 4 weeks annual leave Parental leave (12mo unpaid + 24wks paid) Minimum wage $26.64/hr (above award for some roles) Casual loading 25% WHS Act 2011 Compliance PPE provided: non-slip shoes, heat-resistant gloves Mandatory safety training for all new hires Workers compensation insurance for all employees (incl. casuals) Return-to-work plans for injured workers SafeWork Australia compliance audits Enterprise Agreement McDonald's Australia operates under an Enterprise Agreement negotiated between the company and employee representatives (SDA — Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees' Association). It must pass the BOOT (Better Off Overall Test) compared to the Fast Food Industry Award. WFH Case Law (Fair Work Act 2009) Key precedent: The Fair Work Commission ruled in favour of an employee's flexible working request (WFH under NES #2), allowing WFH despite employer pushback. The Commission upheld the employee's right to flexible arrangements to accommodate school drop-offs, citing strengthened workplace flexibility laws (2023 amendments to the Fair Work Act). Source: Yun, J. (2026) "Mum wins WFH rights" — Fair Work Commission arbitration. HR Essay Strategy: Even though HR Strategies is not assessed, HR Influences (legal framework, stakeholders, economic/tech/social) and HR Processes (acquisition, development, maintenance, separation) CAN appear in a cross-topic Section III or in the SA section. The WFH case above is an excellent contemporary example of the Fair Work Act in action for any essay discussing legal influences on business.
